Measured across 400 questions, four sittings Hazzard is 81% of the paper; Beers is 0.5%

This is not the Shlav A study plan. It is a consolidation block for the months before you start at Sheba — September to the end of January — built to harden what you already know rather than to get you through an exam that is still nine or ten months away and whose date is not yet fixed.

Why it is still built on the past papers. The eight sittings are the best available evidence about which parts of geriatrics carry weight, and that is as useful for walking onto a ward as it is for sitting a paper. Nine Hazzard chapters appear in every recent sitting; they are also, read plainly, the nine things a geriatrician is asked about most.

The real exam plan comes later, once the date is published and once you know what the first months at Sheba leave you. Expect it to look different: more question volume, less reading, and timed mocks that have no place in this block.

Daily shape

Six days a week, one fixed day off — pick it now and keep it. The day off is scheduled, not earned; the plans that fail are the ones that run seven days until a bad week ends them. Each working day: 75 min on the chapter, 35 min on 50 questions from the whole bank, 10 min reviewing every miss. That is 7.5 hours of reading a week, which is what the schedule below is built on.

Read the chapter in your own copy. The sections in this file are a scaffold and a drill set — they are not a substitute for the text the questions are written from.

January: no new chapters

The reading ends on 3 January — 16 weeks, about 112 hours. The rest of January is for going back over the nine core chapters, clearing the missed cards in the drill, and picking up anything from the deferred list below that you have appetite for. Arriving at Sheba mid-consolidation is better than arriving three chapters into something new.

Deliberately not scheduled0h
  • Harrison's — 3–5 questions per sitting in your track, and the 50-question Harrison block belongs to the base track you are not taking
  • The AGS GRS — 30% of the June 2022 paper and zero in every paper before or since. The syllabus still mandates it; four consecutive papers say otherwise

An explicit, US, consensus list of potentially inappropriate medications for adults 65 and over. Learn the architecture, because questions test which table a drug sits in as often as whether it is on the list.

Read this section knowing what the papers say about it. Beers is the stated source for 2 questions in 500 across eight sittings. Its content still reaches you through Hazzard chapters — the drug material is not wasted — but do not spend reading hours here at the expense of the nine core chapters.

Four framing points the panel states outright, each a plausible stem: PIMs are potentially inappropriate, not definitely; “avoid” is not an absolute contraindication unless the label says so; the criteria exclude hospice and end-of-life care; and they are US-designed, so other countries must adapt.

The criteria tables — 2 to 10

Exam pearl

Questions ask which table a drug sits in as often as whether it is on the list. Learn Beers as a set of tables, not as a drug list. The document runs Tables 1 to 10; Table 1 is the evidence-grading key and the criteria themselves live in Tables 2 to 10.

TableContents
2PIMs to avoid in most older adults
3PIMs to avoid in specific diseases or syndromes
4Use with caution
5Drug–drug interactions to avoid
6Renal dose adjustment
7Drugs with strong anticholinergic properties
8Removed since 2019 (low US use or off-market — still PIMs elsewhere)
9 · 10Added and modified since 2019 — read these first

What changed in 2023

New criteria: warfarin · dextromethorphan-quinidine in heart failure · opioids as delirium precipitants · anticholinergics in falls and fractures · ticagrelor (caution) · SGLT2 inhibitors (caution) · skeletal muscle relaxants folded into the ≥3 CNS-drug rule · lithium + ARB/ARNI · warfarin + SSRI · baclofen in renal impairment.

Anticoagulation — the synthesis box 4 agents
Drug2023 position
WarfarinAvoid starting for non-valvular AF or VTE unless DOACs are contraindicated or there are substantial access barriers. Continuing a long-term user may be reasonable, particularly with time in therapeutic range >70% and no adverse effects.
RivaroxabanMoved caution → avoid for long-term NVAF/VTE — more major and GI bleeding than other DOACs, particularly apixaban.
DabigatranRemains use with caution versus other DOACs long-term.
ApixabanIts renal criterion was removed — evidence supports safe use at lower renal function.
Other 2023 modifications 6
  • Aspirin moved Table 4 → Table 2: avoid initiating for primary prevention; consider deprescribing existing primary-prevention users. Still indicated for secondary prevention.
  • Sulfonylureas expanded from long-acting only to the whole class.
  • Estrogen: do not initiate oral or transdermal; vaginal estrogen remains appropriate for atrophy and recurrent-UTI prophylaxis.
  • Antidepressants in falls/fractures: evidence lowered high → moderate.
  • ≥3 CNS-active drugs: evidence raised to high.
  • Digoxin: caution added about discontinuing in long-term HFrEF users.

Table 5 — drug–drug interactions worth memorising 8
  • Opioid + benzodiazepine
  • Opioid + gabapentinoid — exception: cross-tapering off the opioid
  • Anticholinergic + anticholinergic
  • ≥3 CNS-active drugs from: antiepileptics including gabapentinoids, antidepressants, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids, skeletal muscle relaxants
  • Warfarin + amiodarone, ciprofloxacin, macrolides (not azithromycin), TMP-SMX, SSRIs

Table 4 — use with caution 6 entries

“Caution” means the concern does not reach the level of “avoid” — because the evidence is limited or inconsistent, the harm relative to alternatives is smaller, or extenuating circumstances are common.

Dabigatran long-term for NVAF or VTEMore GI bleeding than warfarin in head-to-head trials, and more GI and major bleeding than apixaban observationally
Prasugrel, ticagrelorMore major bleeding than clopidogrel, especially from 75 onward, though possibly offset by CV benefit in selected patients. If prasugrel is used, consider 5 mg from 75 onward
Hyponatraemia risk — mirtazapine, SNRIs, SSRIs, TCAs, carbamazepine, oxcarbazepine, antipsychotics, diuretics, tramadolMay cause or worsen SIADH. Monitor sodium closely when starting or changing dose
Dextromethorphan-quinidineLimited efficacy for behavioural symptoms of dementia (does not apply to pseudobulbar affect); falls risk; interactions; heart failure concerns
Trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazoleHyperkalaemia with an ACEi, ARB or ARNI when creatinine clearance is reduced
SGLT2 inhibitors — new 2023Urogenital infection, particularly in women in the first month; euglycaemic ketoacidosis. Monitor early. The panel notes it still recognises their value
Table 3 — disease-specific avoids 9 syndromes
Heart failurecilostazol, dextromethorphan-quinidine avoid · diltiazem and verapamil avoid in HFrEF · NSAIDs, COX-2, thiazolidinediones, dronedarone — caution if asymptomatic, avoid if symptomatic
Syncopechlorpromazine, olanzapine, AChEIs (bradycardia), non-selective alpha-1 blockers, tertiary TCAs
Deliriumanticholinergics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, corticosteroids, H2 blockers, opioids (new)
Dementiaanticholinergics, chronic or persistent PRN antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs
Falls or fracturesanticholinergics (new), SSRIs/SNRIs/TCAs, antiepileptics, antipsychotics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids. Shorter-acting benzodiazepines are not safer
Parkinson diseasemetoclopramide, prochlorperazine, promethazine, all antipsychotics except clozapine, pimavanserin, quetiapine
Ulcer historyaspirin, non-COX2 NSAIDs unless gastroprotection
Incontinence in womennon-selective alpha-1 blockers; oral and transdermal estrogen
BPH / LUTS in menstrongly anticholinergic drugs (except bladder antimuscarinics)

A prescription can be wrong in two directions. Beers only sees the drug that is present and shouldn’t be. STOPP/START adds the drug that should be there and isn’t.

STOPP — Screening Tool of Older People's Prescriptionspotentially inappropriate medications (PIMs)133
START — Screening Tool to Alert to Right Treatmentpotential prescribing omissions (PPOs)57

Version 3 (2023), by O’Mahony and colleagues; v1 2008, v2 2015 (80 + 34). 190 criteria in total. Organised by physiological system, not by drug — you work down the problem list. Each criterion carries its reason in-line, so it can be defended at the bedside rather than cited as authority. Both halves are applied as one review. 5 minutes for someone fluent, 20–30 otherwise.

STOPP — section by section

A · Indication 3 · the most productive three in the tool
  • Any drug with no clinical indication
  • Any drug beyond a well-defined recommended duration
  • Any duplicate class for regular daily use — two NSAIDs, SSRIs, loop diuretics, ACE inhibitors, anticoagulants, antipsychotics, opioids. Optimise monotherapy within a class before adding a second agent
B · Cardiovascular 21 · largest system section
  • Digoxin for HF with normal systolic function; digoxin first-line for long-term (>3 months) rate control in AF
  • Verapamil or diltiazem in NYHA III–IV; β-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem (heart block); any rate-limiter with bradycardia <50, type II or complete block
  • β-blocker as monotherapy for uncomplicated hypertension; amiodarone first-line for SVT
  • Loop diuretic first-line for hypertension unless there is concurrent heart failure requiring a diuretic — the exception is part of the criterion; loop diuretic for dependent ankle oedema with no cardiac, hepatic, nephrotic or renal cause — elevation and compression instead; loop diuretic for hypertension with incontinence
  • Thiazide with K⁺ <3.0, Na⁺ <130, corrected Ca²⁺ >2.65, or gout history
  • Centrally-acting antihypertensives as a class (methyldopa, clonidine, moxonidine, rilmenidine, guanfacine)
  • ACEi or ARB with K⁺ >5.5; aldosterone antagonist with K-sparing drugs and no K monitoring at least 6-monthly
  • QTc-prolonging drugs with demonstrable prolongation (>450 ms men, >470 ms women): quinolones, macrolides, ondansetron, citalopram >20 mg, escitalopram >10 mg, TCAs, lithium, haloperidol, digoxin, class IA and III antiarrhythmics, tizanidine, phenothiazines, mirabegron
  • Statin for primary prevention at age ≥85 with established frailty and life expectancy under 3 years
  • B19 — NSAIDs or systemic corticosteroids with heart failure requiring a loop diuretic. The corticosteroid limb is the half everyone forgets
  • Long-term systemic NSAIDs or antipsychotics with known vascular disease (thrombosis); antihypertensives in severe symptomatic aortic stenosis; PDE5 inhibitors with systolic BP <90 or nitrates
C · Coagulation 16 · dense with exam material
  • Long-term aspirin >100 mg/day; aspirin for primary prevention at all
  • Aspirin + clopidogrel beyond 4 weeks for secondary stroke prevention, unless stent within 12 months, ACS, or high-grade symptomatic carotid stenosis
  • Antiplatelet added to an anticoagulant in AF without a stent or >50% angiographic stenosis; dual therapy in stable vascular disease
  • Anticoagulant duration: beyond 6 months for a first DVT, beyond 12 months for a first PE, without continuing provoking factors
  • VKA as first-line for AF — inappropriate unless metallic valve, moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis, or eGFR <15
  • SSRI + anticoagulant with prior major haemorrhage; NSAID + anticoagulant; ticlopidine in any circumstance
  • C2 — any antiplatelet or anticoagulant where there is a significant current bleeding risk: uncontrolled severe hypertension, a bleeding diathesis, or recent non-trivial spontaneous bleeding
  • C7 — an antiplatelet used as a substitute for anticoagulation for stroke prevention in atrial fibrillation. No evidence of efficacy, and a common real-world compromise
  • C13 — dabigatran with diltiazem or verapamil
  • DOAC + P-gp inhibitors (amiodarone, verapamil, macrolides, itraconazole, ketoconazole, ticagrelor, carvedilol, ciclosporin, dronedarone, quinine, ranolazine, tamoxifen)
D · Central nervous system 25 · largest overall

The duration rules — learn the numbers:

  • Benzodiazepines ≥4 weeks (taper if over 4 weeks; abrupt stop risks withdrawal syndrome)
  • D10 benzodiazepines for insomnia ≥2 weeks; D11 Z-drugs — zolpidem, zopiclone, zaleplon — for insomnia ≥2 weeks. The general benzodiazepine criterion, D8, is the one at ≥4 weeks; the two are different rules and the pairing is exactly what a stem exploits
  • Antipsychotics for BPSD at unchanged dose >3 months without review; >12 weeks total unless severe and non-drug measures failed

The rest:

  • TCAs with dementia, narrow-angle glaucoma, conduction abnormality, prostatism, chronic constipation, recent falls, retention or orthostasis; TCAs first-line for major depression
  • SNRIs with severe hypertension (>180 systolic or >105 diastolic); SSRIs with Na⁺ <130 or current significant bleeding
  • Antipsychotics other than clozapine or quetiapine in parkinsonism or Lewy body dementia; antipsychotics as hypnotics; antipsychotics with dysphagia
  • Anticholinergics (biperiden, orphenadrine, procyclidine, trihexyphenidyl) to treat antipsychotic-induced extrapyramidal effects
  • D14 — drugs with potent anticholinergic effects in anyone with delirium or dementia. Stated as its own criterion, not merely as burden
  • D4 — antipsychotics with marked antimuscarinic effects (chlorpromazine, clozapine, olanzapine and the older phenothiazines) where there are lower urinary tract symptoms from BPH or previous retention
  • AChEIs with bradycardia <60, heart block or unexplained syncope; or alongside other bradycardia-inducing drugs; memantine with a seizure history
  • Two named prescribing cascades: levodopa or dopamine agonist for drug-induced parkinsonism; and for benign essential tremor
  • Nootropics in dementia dismissed wholesale — ginkgo, piracetam, phosphatidylserine, modafinil, L-theanine, omega-3, ginseng, rhodiola, creatine
  • First-generation antihistamines first-line for allergy or pruritus, and for insomnia
E · Renal 10 · differs from Beers
eGFRDrug
<30Digoxin maintenance ≥125 µg/day beyond 90 days · dabigatran · metformin · MRAs · bisphosphonates · methotrexate
<50NSAIDs
<45Nitrofurantoin
<15Factor Xa inhibitors (rivaroxaban, apixaban, edoxaban)
<10Colchicine
F · Gastrointestinal 8
  • Prochlorperazine or metoclopramide with parkinsonism
  • PPI at full therapeutic dose for uncomplicated peptic ulcer >8 weeks
  • Constipating drugs (antimuscarinics, oral iron, opioids, verapamil, aluminium antacids) in existing chronic constipation
  • Oral elemental iron >200 mg/day — no better absorption above that
  • Corticosteroids with ulcer or erosive oesophagitis history unless PPI co-prescribed; antiplatelet or anticoagulant with GAVE; antipsychotics with dysphagia; megestrol for appetite
G · Respiratory 4
  • Theophylline as COPD monotherapy (narrow therapeutic index)
  • Systemic instead of inhaled corticosteroids for maintenance in moderate-severe COPD
  • LAMAs (tiotropium, aclidinium, umeclidinium, glycopyrronium) with narrow-angle glaucoma or bladder outflow obstruction
  • Benzodiazepines with respiratory failure (pO₂ <8.0 kPa or pCO₂ >6.5 kPa)
H · Musculoskeletal 9
  • Non-COX2 NSAIDs with ulcer or GI bleed history unless PPI or H2 cover; NSAIDs with BP consistently >170/100; NSAID + corticosteroid; NSAID >3 months for OA where paracetamol untried
  • Corticosteroids >3 months as RA monotherapy; systemic steroids for OA other than periodic intra-articular injection for mono-articular pain
  • Long-term NSAID or colchicine >3 months for gout where a xanthine-oxidase inhibitor is not contraindicated
  • Oral bisphosphonates with current or recent upper GI disease; long-term opioids for OA
I · Urogenital 8
  • Systemic antimuscarinics (oxybutynin, tolterodine, trospium) with dementia or cognitive impairment, narrow-angle glaucoma, constipation, or BPH with post-void residual >200 mL
  • Alpha-1 blockers other than silodosin with symptomatic orthostatic hypotension or syncope history
  • Mirabegron in labile or severe hypertension; duloxetine for urge incontinence (it is for stress incontinence)
  • Antibiotics for asymptomatic bacteriuria
J · Endocrine 10
  • Long half-life sulphonylureas — glibenclamide, chlorpropamide, glimepiride — in T2DM
  • Thiazolidinediones with heart failure; non-selective β-blockers with frequent hypoglycaemia; SGLT2 inhibitors with symptomatic hypotension
  • Systemic oestrogens or androgens with prior VTE — the androgen limb matters for older men on testosterone; systemic oestrogens with breast cancer; MHT with stenotic arterial disease; unopposed oestrogen with an intact uterus
  • Levothyroxine in subclinical hypothyroidism — normal free T4, TSH raised but <10 mU/L
  • Desmopressin or vasopressin for incontinence or frequency (hyponatraemia)
K · Falls 12 · a syndrome, used as a cross-cutting index
  • Benzodiazepines · antipsychotics · Z-drugs · antiepileptics · first-generation antihistamines · opioids · antidepressants — all in recurrent falls
  • Vasodilators with a documented postural drop ≥20 systolic or ≥10 diastolic
  • Alpha blockers as antihypertensives, and for prostatic outflow other than silodosin; centrally-acting antihypertensives; antimuscarinics for overactive bladder
L · Analgesics 6
  • Strong opioids first-line for mild pain — WHO ladder skipped
  • Regular (non-PRN) opioids without a laxative
  • Long-acting opioids with no short-acting cover for breakthrough pain
  • Lidocaine patch for chronic osteoarthritis pain — no evidence
  • Gabapentinoids for non-neuropathic pain
  • Paracetamol ≥3 g/24h with BMI <18 or chronic liver disease
M · Anticholinergic burden 1

A single criterion: two or more drugs with antimuscarinic properties used concurrently. Beers handles this as a drug–drug interaction; STOPP gives it its own section, which is a reasonable way to remember that burden is additive.

START — the omissions

Governing caveat: unless the patient is end-of-life and therefore palliative in focus, these should be considered where omitted for no valid reason, with contraindications already checked. START is not a mandate to add drugs to a dying patient.

A–C · Indicated drugs, cardiovascular, coagulation 14
  • Antihypertensive above 140/90 — threshold relaxed to 150 systolic in established moderate-to-severe physical frailty
  • Three separate criteria, three different populations — do not merge them. B2 statin for documented coronary, cerebral or peripheral vascular disease, unless end-of-life or established moderate-to-severe frailty — and that exception belongs to the statin alone. B3 ACE inhibitor with coronary artery disease. B4 β-blocker with symptomatic coronary artery disease
  • HFrEF: ACE inhibitor · cardioselective β-blocker (bisoprolol, nebivolol, metoprolol, carvedilol) · MRA if eGFR >30 · SGLT2 inhibitor in symptomatic HF regardless of ejection fraction and regardless of diabetes (new in v3) · sacubitril/valsartan replacing the ACEi/ARB when symptoms persist on optimal dose · IV iron for HFrEF with iron deficiency
  • β-blocker for chronic AF with uncontrolled rate
  • Anticoagulant for chronic or paroxysmal AF; antiplatelet with documented vascular disease
D–E · CNS, renal 11
  • L-DOPA or dopamine agonist in idiopathic Parkinson's with functional disability; propranolol for disabling essential tremor
  • Non-TCA antidepressant for major depression; SSRI (or SNRI, or pregabalin if SSRI contraindicated) for persistent severe anxiety affecting function
  • AChEI for mild-to-moderate Alzheimer's; rivastigmine specifically for Lewy body or Parkinson's disease dementia
  • Dopamine agonist for restless legs once iron deficiency and severe CKD are excluded
  • CKD: alfacalcidol or calcitriol with hypocalcaemia and secondary hyperparathyroidism · phosphate binder if phosphate persistently >1.76 mmol/L · erythropoietin targeting Hb 10–12 g/dL · ACEi or ARB if proteinuria >300 mg/24h
F–G · Gastrointestinal, respiratory 10
  • PPI for severe GORD or peptic stricture; PPI when starting low-dose aspirin with prior ulcer or reflux oesophagitis; PPI with NSAID use of any duration
  • Fibre for diverticulosis with constipation; osmotic laxative for chronic constipation
  • Probiotics alongside antibiotics in non-immunocompromised patients to prevent C. difficile diarrhoea; H. pylori eradication in active ulcer
  • LAMA or LABA for symptomatic GOLD 1–2 COPD and chronic asthma; inhaled corticosteroid for GOLD 3–4 with FEV1 <50% and repeated exacerbations
  • Home oxygen for documented chronic hypoxaemia — pO₂ <8.0 kPa / 60 mmHg, or SaO₂ <89%
H–J · Musculoskeletal, urogenital, endocrine 15
  • DMARD for active disabling RA; folic acid with methotrexate; xanthine-oxidase inhibitor for recurrent gout
  • Bisphosphonate + vitamin D + calcium with long-term systemic steroids; anti-resorptive or anabolic therapy for documented osteoporosis unless one-year life expectancy is poor
  • Vitamin D with known osteoporosis, prior fragility fracture, or T-score below −2.5; and in confirmed deficiency (<20 µg/L, <50 nmol/L) if housebound, falling, or osteopenic
  • Anti-resorptive cover after discontinuing at least two doses of denosumab — the two-dose threshold is in the criterion — because of rebound bone turnover and vertebral fracture; and after stopping teriparatide or abaloparatide
  • Selective alpha-1 blocker (tamsulosin, silodosin) and 5-alpha reductase inhibitor for BPH symptoms where prostatectomy is not appropriate
  • Topical vaginal oestrogen for atrophic vaginitis, and for recurrent UTI in women; PDE5 inhibitor for distressing erectile dysfunction
  • ACEi or ARB in diabetes with proteinuria or microalbuminuria >30 mg/24h, unless eGFR <30
K–L · Analgesics, vaccines 7
  • High-potency opioids for moderate-severe non-arthritis pain where paracetamol, NSAIDs or weak opioids are inappropriate or have failed
  • Laxatives with regular opioids — the mirror image of the STOPP criterion, showing how the two halves interlock
  • Topical 5% lidocaine patch for localised neuropathic pain such as post-herpetic neuralgia — while STOPP rejects the same patch for chronic OA pain
  • Influenza annually · pneumococcal at least once · varicella-zoster · SARS-CoV-2

Limitations, stated honestly

190 criteria is a lot for a 15-minute clinic slot, and adoption suffers for it. The criteria are consensus-based, not individually evidence-graded, so they carry less transparency than Beers on how strong each recommendation is. And the evidence that applying them improves hard outcomes — mortality, hospitalisation — remains contested, even though they reliably reduce PIM counts. A question asking whether STOPP/START improves clinical outcomes has a nuanced answer, not a yes.

The 2025 Alternatives paper is organised as “if not this drug for this condition, then what” — which is the exact shape of a single-best-answer stem. Thirty of the 36 Table 2 criteria, covering 21 conditions, plus two drug–drug interactions (opioid + benzodiazepine, opioid + gabapentinoid).

Its five principles. Stopping a PIM is not the goal — the goal is management that helps the person feel better while reducing harm. Rather than swapping in a “better” drug, consider non-pharmacological strategies, which are often more effective and safer. Understand the underlying cause. PIMs should often be avoided but not always. Use the deprescribing supports that exist.

Two limits the panel states: it is guidance for ambulatory care primarily, built from a limited set of guidelines rather than a primary-literature review; and some listed alternatives are recommended for purposes or doses not in the manufacturer's label.

Insomnia benzodiazepines · Z-drugs · antihistamines · TCAs · barbiturates

Assess first for what is disrupting sleep: environment, pain, drugs or substances, obstructive sleep apnoea.

CBT-I is first-line for chronic insomnia in older adults, delivered by a trained provider or digitally — evidence supports both. Its components are sleep restriction, stimulus control, cognitive therapy, relaxation and sleep hygiene. Sleep hygiene alone is not effective for chronic insomnia; it is a component, not a treatment.

If CBT-I fails, with shared decision-making and short-term only: low-dose doxepin (3 or 6 mg), a dual orexin receptor antagonist (daridorexant, lemborexant, suvorexant), or ramelteon. The panel is explicit that formal guidelines on efficacy and safety of these in older adults are not available.

Insufficient evidence to recommend: trazodone, mirtazapine, melatonin. Guidelines do not recommend these for insomnia disorder at any age. Melatonin also has no FDA oversight, so content, purity and dose are not guaranteed.

Anxiety benzodiazepines · antihistamines · TCAs · barbiturates · meprobamate

Clarify the underlying disorder first, and evaluate contributors — comorbid medical illness, depression, substance misuse, medications. This matters especially for new-onset anxiety, because late-life onset of an anxiety disorder is uncommon. Some anxiety is an appropriate response to events and needs support, not a drug.

Non-pharmacological therapy is first-line: CBT, acceptance and commitment therapy, mindfulness-based stress reduction, imagery rehearsal therapy for nightmares.

Generalised anxietyescitalopram, sertraline, venlafaxine, duloxetine, buspirone, pregabalin
Panic disordersertraline, escitalopram, venlafaxine
Social anxietyescitalopram, sertraline, venlafaxine; propranolol for performance-only anxiety
PTSD, globalsertraline, venlafaxine
PTSD, nightmaresprazosin — but note this is contested since the PACT trial (NEJM 2018) found it no better than placebo for nightmares and sleep in veterans; guidelines have softened from recommending it to calling the evidence mixed. The Alternatives paper still lists it, so answer to the document the stem is written from

Note the internal tension: Beers cautions SSRIs and SNRIs in patients with a falls history, and pregabalin should not run alongside an opioid.

Delirium antipsychotics

First-line is multicomponent non-pharmacological care — the named programme is AGS CoCare: HELP. No drug is recommended as a routine response to delirium in any population.

Antipsychotics or sedatives may be considered for hours to days to address severe behavioural disturbance posing substantial risk to the patient or staff and refractory to non-pharmacological measures. Such use should come with documented discussion of risk and an explicit plan against prolongation.

Agitation and aggression in dementia antipsychotics

Evaluate contributors first: pain, constipation, urinary retention, acute illness, medication adverse effects, environmental stressors. Non-pharmacological strategies are first line and need revising as the disease progresses.

If they fail and the patient is at risk of harming themselves or others, and risks have been discussed with surrogate decision-makers: lowest dose, shortest time, combined with non-pharmacological strategies, with ongoing reassessment of the risk-benefit ratio.

Brexpiprazole is the only atypical FDA-approved for agitation in Alzheimer's dementia; pimavanserin the only one for Parkinson's disease psychosis. Both still carry the boxed warning for increased mortality in older adults with dementia.

A named framework for behaviour: DICE — Describe, Investigate, Create, Evaluate.

Overactive bladder, GSM, recurrent UTI antimuscarinics · systemic estrogen

Overactive bladder: behavioural interventions and pelvic floor muscle training; vaginal estrogen; and for drug therapy, β-3 agonists preferred over antimuscarinics on adverse-event profile in older adults. Refractory: percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, botulinum toxin, sacral nerve stimulation.

Vaginal atrophy or dyspareunia: non-hormonal lubricants and moisturisers, pelvic floor physical therapy, intravaginal estrogen, intravaginal DHEA (prasterone), hyaluronic acid, ospemifene.

Vasomotor symptoms: CBT or hypnosis; SSRIs (paroxetine, citalopram, escitalopram) or venlafaxine; gabapentin; fezolinetant (neurokinin-3 receptor antagonist). Only paroxetine and fezolinetant are FDA-approved for the indication.

Recurrent UTI in older women: vaginal estrogen is first-line prevention. Trial non-antibiotic measures first — increased fluid intake, behavioural modification, methenamine hippurate, cranberry products, D-mannose, glycosaminoglycans — evidence for these varies in extent and quality. Prophylactic trimethoprim or fosfomycin if necessary.

Nocturia desmopressin

Start with the non-urological causes of nocturnal polyuria: fluid timing, alcohol, caffeine, evening diuretic dosing; daytime oedema (treat the cause, compression stockings, leg elevation during the day); and the SCREeN conditions — Sleep (especially apnoea), Cardiovascular (congestive heart failure), Renal (CKD), Endocrine (diabetes), Neurological.

Then behavioural therapy for lower urinary tract symptoms: fluid adjustment, bladder retraining with pelvic floor exercises. For men with BPH-associated symptoms, uroselective alpha-1 blockers or 5-alpha reductase inhibitors.

GERD and gastroparesis PPI beyond 8 weeks · metoclopramide

GERD: first-line is non-pharmacological — stop smoking, avoid trigger foods, relaxation, weight management, no eating within 2–3 hours of bedtime, elevate the head of the bed. For breakthrough symptoms, alginate-containing therapy, which floats a low-density gel above the gastric contents as a physical barrier; avoid other medications within 2 hours either side because it affects absorption. For nocturnal symptoms, a nighttime H2 blocker. On twice-daily PPI, step down to once daily if not discontinuing.

For functional heartburn or reflux hypersensitivity: pharmacological neuromodulation, or referral for hypnotherapy, CBT, diaphragmatic breathing.

Gastroparesis: small-particle diet — soft, small, easy to chew; frequent small meals; avoid fatty, spicy, acidic and high-fibre meals; add soups and liquid meals. Ginger 1 mg twice daily or ondansetron for nausea. A short course of erythromycin 50–100 mg four times daily, 30–45 min before meals and at bedtime. Control glucose in diabetes.

Diabetes sulfonylureas · sliding-scale insulin

Sliding scale means variable short-acting insulin dosed on glucose values with no basal insulin. If it was started for unstable needs, adding basal insulin usually allows safe discontinuation; if glucose stays uncontrolled on basal, add pre-prandial bolus. If the sliding scale produces no insulin for 24–48 hours, stop it. For nearly all older adults with type 2 diabetes, up-titrating basal insulin and other agents allows safe discontinuation within weeks.

Instead of sulfonylureas: metformin remains first-line for most — ensure maximal tolerated dose given renal function before adding anything. Then SGLT2 inhibitors (heart failure, ASCVD, CKD), GLP1 receptor agonists (obesity, ASCVD, CKD), DPP4 inhibitors. Selection by comorbidity, goals and preference.

And the point the panel makes that is easy to miss: the need for drugs may fall with diet and exercise, and relaxed glycaemic targets are often appropriate in older adults with comorbid burden, functional impairment or cognitive decline.

Pain TCAs · NSAIDs · meperidine · muscle relaxants · gabapentinoid combinations

Use patient-reported outcomes before and after to identify clinically meaningful change. Improving function should be a key goal, not just score reduction.

Non-pharmacological approaches consistently recommended across chronic-pain guidelines: education; exercise therapy of any type (aerobic, aquatic, strengthening, yoga, tai chi); physical therapy; needling therapies including acupuncture; psychological interventions (CBT, operant therapy, multicomponent biopsychosocial care, mindfulness); peripheral electrical or magnetic stimulation and rTMS.

NociceptiveInstead of meperidine, a different opioid. Instead of muscle relaxants or long-term NSAIDs: short-term NSAIDs, topical NSAIDs (diclofenac gel), COX-2 selective agents, topical capsaicin, rubefacients, lidocaine, paracetamol, intra-articular corticosteroid
NeuropathicInstead of TCAs: SNRIs, gabapentinoids, topical agents including capsaicin and lidocaine

Two cautions worth memorising: methyl salicylate-containing topicals (BenGay, Icy Hot, Salonpas) risk systemic salicylate toxicity — limit to about 7 days of continuous use. And gabapentinoids must not run concurrently with opioids.

Allergy and pruritus first-generation antihistamines

Generalised pruritus is generally not responsive to antihistamines at all unless it is histamine-mediated, like urticaria. Tailor to the cause: dry skin, medications (opioids, CNS drugs, diuretics), or underlying disease.

Dry skin: hydrating emollient twice daily, short showers under 3 minutes in lukewarm water, humidifiers. Localised: topical anaesthetics (lidocaine, pramoxine), cooling agents (menthol), topical steroids, topical doxepin, capsaicin.

If an oral antihistamine is needed, second or third generation — loratadine, cetirizine, levocetirizine, fexofenadine. Fexofenadine is the least sedating even at high dose.

Allergic rhinitis: allergen avoidance; saline irrigation with distilled or sterilised water only, never unsterilised tap water; nasal antihistamine sprays (azelastine, olopatadine, absorbed less than oral agents); nasal corticosteroids; nasal mast cell stabilisers (cromolyn).

Involuntary weight loss megestrol

Non-pharmacological throughout: feeding assistance; identify and address contributing medications (those affecting taste, or causing dry mouth, nausea or anorexia); appealing foods; social support; ensure actual access to food — meal delivery, and lifting dietary restrictions where appropriate. Calorically dense supplements and dietitian referral. Evaluate dentition, chewing and swallowing, with swallow assessment if indicated.

Mirtazapine only for patients with depression — not as an appetite stimulant in its own right.

Cardiovascular warfarin · rivaroxaban · amiodarone · dronedarone · digoxin · alpha blockers · IR nifedipine

Anticoagulation in AF: other DOACs, apixaban or edoxaban. Attend to indication-specific dosing — full dose for most people with AF, reduced only for renal dysfunction and select situations; for long-term VTE treatment, guidelines suggest reducing after 6 months (apixaban to 2.5 mg twice daily). Where stroke risk is moderate-to-high but bleeding risk on oral anticoagulation is high: percutaneous left atrial appendage occlusion or surgical ligation.

Rhythm control: dofetilide and sotalol are the preferred antiarrhythmics for many older adults, both requiring hospitalisation for initiation and specialist referral. With normal LV function, no CAD or prior MI and no significant structural disease: dronedarone, flecainide, propafenone. Non-pharmacological: catheter ablation, or surgical Maze.

Rate control: β-blockers are the appropriate alternative to digoxin for most. With LVEF above 40%, diltiazem or verapamil may be used. Non-pharmacological: AV nodal ablation with a permanent pacemaker.

HFpEF is no longer “diuretics for symptoms”. After EMPEROR-Preserved and DELIVER, SGLT2 inhibitors are the first drug class with an outcome benefit in preserved ejection fraction. Be precise about how strong the recommendation is, because it differs: Class 2a in the 2022 ACC/AHA/HFSA guideline, Class I (A) in the 2023 ESC focused update, which also raised HFmrEF to Class I. In HFrEF they are Class 1 in both and one of the four foundational classes.

Heart failure: optimise guideline-directed therapy before considering digoxin at all — sacubitril/valsartan (or ACEi/ARB if not tolerated or unaffordable), β-blocker, MRA, SGLT2 inhibitor; hydralazine-nitrate for Black patients with NYHA III–IV HFrEF; diuretics as needed for congestion; cardiac resynchronisation as an advanced adjunct.

Hypertension: DASH diet, exercise, weight loss, treat obstructive sleep apnoea. First-line drugs are thiazides, CCBs, ACEi, ARBs; β-blockers only where separately indicated (recent MI or ACS, HFrEF, AF, angina). Instead of immediate-release nifedipine: amlodipine, felodipine or nifedipine ER. Resistant hypertension: spironolactone or hydralazine, after excluding non-adherence and hyperaldosteronism.

Parkinson's disease and tardive dyskinesia benztropine · trihexyphenidyl

Parkinson's: optimise exercise, strengthening, balance and physical therapy from diagnosis onward. First-line drug treatment is levodopa (usually with carbidopa) and dopamine agonists. For mild symptoms or where once-daily dosing is preferred, MAO-B inhibitors — rasagiline is the best tolerated. Amantadine helps levodopa-induced dyskinesia and “off” time in advanced disease but needs caution in older patients. Inadequate control: deep brain stimulation or focused ultrasound. Note that new psychosis may reflect disease progression, a treatment effect, or an intercurrent illness such as infection — assess before attributing.

Tardive dyskinesia: anticholinergics are not effective for it. Identify reversible causes and attempt deprescribing of the culprit (metoclopramide, haloperidol). If it persists after withdrawal and distresses the patient, consider valbenazine or deutetrabenazine.

Constipation and intestinal cramping mineral oil · GI antispasmodics

Constipation: identify the underlying cause. Lifestyle first — scheduled toileting after meals, fluid, fibre, exercise and ambulation. Then stimulant laxatives (senna) or osmotic laxatives (polyethylene glycol, magnesium-containing). Non-responders: secretagogues (lubiprostone, linaclotide, plecanatide) and the serotonin-4 agonist prucalopride.

Cramping and diarrhoea: address the aetiology; avoid gas-producing trigger foods; trial a low-FODMAP diet; gut-directed psychotherapies. Loperamide short-term for diarrhoea.

Four places the two tools give different answers. This is where questions live, because a stem can only have one right answer once it names the tool.

IssueBeers 2023STOPP/START v3
NitrofurantoinAvoid at CrCl <30, or for long-term suppressionAvoid at eGFR <45
Aspirin dose ceiling>325 mg/day treated as an NSAIDLong-term >100 mg/day
BenzodiazepinesAvoid the whole class, all durationsDuration-based — ≥4 weeks generally, ≥2 weeks for insomnia
SulfonylureasAvoid the whole class first- or second-line. If one is needed, short-acting glipizideOnly the long half-life agents — glibenclamide, chlorpropamide, glimepiride

Structural differences

Beers 2023STOPP/START v3
OriginUS, AGS-stewarded since 2010Europe, Ireland-led, Delphi consensus
Organised byDrug and drug classPhysiological system
Catches omissionsNoYes — START
Evidence gradingQuality of evidence + strength of recommendation on every criterionNot graded per criterion; reason stated in-line

Corrections to an earlier version of these notes

Three of these came from israeli_drug_database.js or geriatrics_research_library.js, which means those files encode one side of a disagreement as settled fact. Treat both as unverified until audited end to end.

Was writtenWhat the source says
“Gliclazide preferred” among sulfonylureasBeers lists all four including gliclazide; glipizide is the short-acting preference. The tools disagree — know both sides
Baclofen among muscle relaxants to avoidBeers' muscle-relaxant criterion explicitly excludes baclofen and tizanidine. Baclofen has its own criterion: avoid at eGFR <60
Trospium as a low-burden bladder alternativeBeers Table 7 lists trospium among the strongly anticholinergic antimuscarinics; the Alternatives paper's answer is β-3 agonists
“~190 STOPP and 70 START”133 + 57 = 190 total. Counted section by section from the source
SSRIs raise gastric acid secretion as a bleeding mechanismThat limb is weak — it appears in reviews with thin human data. The platelet serotonin mechanism is the established one
A Coupland anticholinergic citation with specific odds ratiosCannot be matched to any real paper. Coupland's anticholinergic–dementia work is JAMA Intern Med 2019. Do not memorise figures from that entry

Further disagreements worth holding

QuestionBeersSTOPP/START
Proton pump inhibitorsAvoid scheduled use beyond 8 weeks unless high risk — C. difficile, bone lossAvoid at full therapeutic dose beyond 8 weeks for uncomplicated disease; reduce or stop
Digoxin in heart failureAvoid as first-line; avoid doses above 0.125 mg/dayAvoid long-term above 125 micrograms/day in renal impairment; not first-line for rate control
NSAIDsAvoid chronic use; if unavoidable, add a PPI or misoprostolAvoid with hypertension, heart failure, CKD, or with an anticoagulant or corticosteroid without gastroprotection
MirabegronNot listed as a PIM — the cognitively safer choice for urge incontinenceFlagged in labile or severe hypertension, and among the QTc-prolonging drugs
Antipsychotics in dementiaAvoid except for schizophrenia, bipolar disorder, or short-term antiemetic use — increased mortality and strokeAvoid as hypnotics, and as first-line for behavioural symptoms; time-limited where used

The pattern across all five: Beers states a general prohibition with exceptions, STOPP states a conditional one tied to a comorbidity or a number. When a stem gives you a comorbidity or a renal figure, it is usually asking the STOPP question.
