Does the schedule still match the evidence?

Every chapter in the reading schedule carries its own question count, so the plan can be checked against the thing it was built from rather than taken on trust. Each point below is one chapter: how often it has been examined, against how many hours it is given.

Seven of 100 questions in the 2026 geriatrics block. The plan had it at 2.1% and scheduled for week 18. It is also the cheapest material on the paper: closed, factual, and asked as direct recall rather than through a vignette.

The recurring question shape is “which change is physiological in normal ageing?” — a list where three options are disease and one is normal ageing. What you need is the boundary between senescence and pathology, in each system.

Homeostenosis — the organising concept

Asked by name in 2026. Ageing narrows the reserve between resting function and maximal function in every system. Baseline performance is often preserved, so the older person looks well at rest; what is lost is the capacity to respond to a challenge. The consequence is the whole of geriatric medicine: a trivial insult produces a disproportionate failure, decompensation appears in the weakest system rather than the affected one, and recovery is slower and often incomplete.

Cognitive ageing — what is preserved and what declines

Preserved in normal ageingDeclines in normal ageing
Semantic memory — vocabulary, general knowledge, often improving into old age Speed of information processing — the earliest and most general change
Crystallised intelligence; procedural memory; language comprehension Working memory, divided attention, executive function
Recognition memory, and recall when cued Free recall and the speed of retrieval; complex visuospatial tasks

The examinable line: in normal ageing retrieval is slow but cueing helps; in Alzheimer's, encoding fails and cueing does not rescue recall. That single distinction separates benign forgetfulness from disease in most vignettes.

System by system

SystemPhysiological changeClinical consequence
CardiacMyocardial and vascular stiffening; impaired early diastolic filling with greater dependence on atrial contraction; reduced β-adrenergic responsiveness so maximal heart rate falls; sinoatrial pacemaker cell loss; increased afterload from arterial stiffening, producing widened pulse pressure and isolated systolic hypertension. Resting ejection fraction and resting cardiac output are preserved Loss of atrial contraction — new atrial fibrillation — is poorly tolerated. Output is raised by stroke volume rather than rate, so hypovolaemia is badly tolerated
RespiratoryLoss of elastic recoil with increased compliance; chest wall stiffens; small airways close at higher lung volumes so closing volume rises; residual volume and functional residual capacity increase while vital capacity falls; total lung capacity is roughly unchanged; ventilation–perfusion mismatch widens the A–a gradient and arterial PaO₂ falls modestly. Blunted ventilatory response to hypoxia and hypercapnia; weaker cough Less reserve for pneumonia; silent hypoxaemia; higher aspiration risk
AutonomicReduced baroreflex sensitivity; reduced β-receptor responsiveness with increased circulating noradrenaline; impaired thermoregulation and sweating; reduced thirst perception Orthostatic and postprandial hypotension; hypothermia; dehydration without complaint of thirst
RenalNephron loss and falling GFR with preserved serum creatinine because muscle mass falls; reduced concentrating and diluting capacity; blunted renin–aldosterone; impaired sodium conservation Dosing errors from a normal creatinine; hyponatraemia and hypernatraemia both easier to produce
Metabolic / endocrineIncreased insulin resistance with a progressive rise in post-prandial rather than fasting glucose; reduced growth hormone and IGF-1; reduced DHEA; oestrogen and, gradually, testosterone decline; vitamin D synthesis in skin falls Post-load hyperglycaemia is the earlier abnormality; a normal fasting glucose does not exclude it
SleepReduced slow-wave (N3) sleep, increased N1 and N2, more arousals, reduced sleep efficiency, phase advance — earlier sleep onset and earlier waking. Total REM is relatively preserved; total sleep requirement does not fall Complaints of fragmented, unrefreshing sleep are partly physiological. Treating them with hypnotics is the error the paper is looking for
Body compositionMuscle mass and strength fall — strength faster than mass — fat fraction rises and redistributes centrally, total body water falls, bone density falls The pharmacokinetic changes in the pharmacology section follow from this line alone
GastrointestinalImpaired oesophageal motility (presbyoesophagus); delayed gastric emptying; reduced gastric acid in some; colonic transit is not markedly slowed by age alone Constipation in an older person is drugs, immobility or disease — not ageing
ImmuneImmunosenescence with thymic involution, fewer naive T cells, poorer vaccine response, and low-grade chronic inflammation (“inflammageing”) Blunted fever, atypical infection presentation, reduced vaccine efficacy
SensoryPresbyopia, reduced pupil size and dark adaptation, lens yellowing; presbycusis — bilateral, symmetrical, high-frequency sensorineural loss with disproportionate loss of speech discrimination Why speech-in-noise fails before the audiogram looks bad

Four things that are never normal ageing, and each has been a distractor: a fall; confusion; a resting tremor; and a decline in activities of daily living. Each means disease until proven otherwise.

The mechanism layer the criteria papers do not give you. This is from Hazzard's and the general pharmacology literature, not from the three documents in Sources — flagged so you know which claims have a paper behind them in this file.

Definitions to have cold

Polypharmacy≥5 regular medications
Hyperpolypharmacy≥10 regular medications
PIMPotentially inappropriate medication — risk outweighs benefit in older adults, usually with a safer alternative
PPOPotential prescribing omission — an indicated drug that is missing. What START addresses
Prescribing cascadeAn adverse drug effect misread as a new disease, then treated with a second drug
Drug burden indexCumulative, dose-weighted anticholinergic and sedative exposure
Therapeutic competitionTreating disease A worsens disease B — a β-blocker for IHD worsening COPD or peripheral arterial disease

What changes with age, and the clinical consequence of each

ChangeEffectExample
↓ total body water, ↑ fat fraction↑ volume of distribution and half-life for lipophilic drugs; ↓ Vd and higher peaks per dose for hydrophilic onesLipophilic: diazepam, amiodarone. Hydrophilic: digoxin, lithium, aminoglycosides
↓ serum albumin↑ free (active) fraction of highly bound drugs at any measured total levelPhenytoin, warfarin, naproxen
↓ hepatic mass and blood flowPhase I (CYP oxidation, reduction, hydrolysis) declines; phase II (glucuronidation, conjugation) is relatively preservedThe reason lorazepam, oxazepam and temazepam are preferred over diazepam — they are conjugated, not oxidised
↓ GFR with preserved creatinine, because muscle mass is lowA normal creatinine does not mean normal clearance. Estimate clearance; do not read the creatinineEvery criterion in Beers Table 6 and STOPP Section E
Receptor and homeostatic changes↑ sensitivity to opioids, benzodiazepines, warfarin; ↓ β-receptor responsiveness; blunted baroreflexWhy orthostasis and sedation dominate the adverse-effect profile

Five prescribing cascades

Classic single-best-answer material, and two of them are named outright in STOPP.

DrugMisread asTreated with
Calcium channel blocker (amlodipine)Ankle oedemaFurosemide — STOPP B8 names this
Cholinesterase inhibitorUrinary urgencyOxybutynin — and the anticholinergic then cancels the ChEI
Metoclopramide or an antipsychoticParkinsonismLevodopa — STOPP D23 names this
NSAIDRaised blood pressureAn antihypertensive
ThiazideHyperuricaemia, goutAllopurinol or colchicine

Anticholinergic burden

The single mechanism that generates the most questions, because it links polypharmacy to delirium, falls, cognition, retention and constipation in one arc. Peripheral: dry mouth, blurred vision, constipation, urinary retention, tachycardia, anhidrosis. Central: confusion, delirium, sedation, impaired memory. Older adults are more susceptible because of reduced central cholinergic reserve and a more permeable blood–brain barrier.

Scoring tools — ACB (Anticholinergic Cognitive Burden), ADS, ARS — score each drug 0–3, with a total of 3 or more commonly taken as clinically significant. The tools disagree with each other, which is itself a valid exam point. None of these thresholds is in the three source documents; Beers gives a list (Table 7) rather than a score, and STOPP sets its threshold at two or more anticholinergic drugs concurrently.

Beers Table 7 — strong anticholinergics, by class

Antidepressantsamitriptyline, amoxapine, clomipramine, desipramine, doxepin >6 mg, imipramine, nortriptyline, paroxetine
Antiemeticsprochlorperazine, promethazine
Antihistamines, first generationbrompheniramine, chlorpheniramine, cyproheptadine, dimenhydrinate, diphenhydramine, doxylamine, hydroxyzine, meclizine, promethazine, triprolidine
Antimuscarinics for incontinencedarifenacin, fesoterodine, flavoxate, oxybutynin, solifenacin, tolterodine, trospium
Antiparkinsonianbenztropine, trihexyphenidyl
Antipsychoticschlorpromazine, clozapine, olanzapine, perphenazine
Antispasmodicsatropine, clidinium-chlordiazepoxide, dicyclomine, homatropine, hyoscyamine, scopolamine
Muscle relaxantscyclobenzaprine, orphenadrine

The panel's footnote: evidence on whether some bladder antimuscarinics are worse than others lacks consistent quality. Oxybutynin has the best evidence for adverse cognitive effects, but caution is warranted for all of them.

Two numbers that look like they disagree, and do not. STOPP B16 sets a life-expectancy threshold of under three years for withholding a primary-prevention statin. The time to benefit for a statin is about 2.5 years (Yourman and colleagues). One is the patient's remaining time, the other is how long the drug needs to work. They are different quantities and both belong in the same sentence: you withhold the statin when the first is shorter than the second.

Hyponatraemia, because half this file causes it

SSRIs, SNRIs, tramadol, carbamazepine, thiazides, mirtazapine and antipsychotics all appear above with a hyponatraemia warning attached, and none of them tells you how to work it out. Two numbers and the volume status do almost all of it.

StepWhat it separates
Serum osmolalityConfirms it is genuinely hypotonic. Normal or high means pseudohyponatraemia or an osmotic cause — hyperglycaemia, mannitol — and the sodium needs correcting for glucose, not treating
Urine osmolalityUnder about 100: the kidney is diluting properly, so the problem is intake or solute — primary polydipsia, beer potomania, the tea-and-toast diet that is common in exactly this population. Above 100: ADH is acting, appropriately or not
Urine sodiumWith ADH acting: under about 30 points to hypovolaemia or a low effective circulating volume — heart failure, cirrhosis. Above about 30 with clinical euvolaemia is SIADH, or a thiazide, or adrenal insufficiency, or hypothyroidism
Volume statusThe clinical half of the same question, and the least reliable part of it in an older patient — which is why the urine numbers matter more here than in a young one

Check thyroid and cortisol before settling on SIADH; stop the drug that is causing it; and correct slowly — the ceiling in common use is 8 mmol/L in 24 hours, less if the hyponatraemia is chronic, malnourished, alcoholic or hypokalaemic, because osmotic demyelination is the iatrogenic harm here. Acute symptomatic hyponatraemia with seizures or coma is the exception and is treated with hypertonic saline.

The deprescribing method

Have a named, ordered process you can write out.

  1. Ascertain what is actually taken, and why — including OTC, supplements, eye drops, inhalers, and the gap between the list and what gets swallowed
  2. Estimate the overall risk of drug-induced harm — number of drugs, high-risk agents, frailty, cognition, renal function — to set the intensity of intervention
  3. Assess each drug for eligibility to stop — no indication, indication expired, PIM, a preventive drug whose time-to-benefit exceeds life expectancy, harm outweighing benefit
  4. Prioritise — lowest benefit-to-harm ratio first, and the easiest withdrawals first, because early wins build trust
  5. Withdraw one at a time, with a monitoring plan and an agreed plan for what to do if symptoms return

Time-to-benefit is the concept that unlocks the topic. Statins for primary prevention, bisphosphonates, intensive glycaemic control and cancer screening all have a time-to-benefit measured in years. If life expectancy is shorter than that, the drug delivers only its harms. If you can argue a statin out of a frail 88-year-old in one sentence, you can answer most deprescribing stems. STOPP encodes exactly this at B16.

Tapering — what must not stop abruptly, and what happens if it does

DrugWithdrawal risk
BenzodiazepinesSeizures, delirium, rebound anxiety and insomnia. STOPP notes anything beyond 4 weeks needs gradual withdrawal. Roughly 25% every 2 weeks, slower at the end
β-blockersRebound tachycardia, angina, infarction
SSRIs and SNRIs, especially paroxetine and venlafaxineDiscontinuation syndrome — dizziness, electric-shock sensations, flu-like illness
Corticosteroids beyond 3 weeksAdrenal insufficiency
LevodopaNeuroleptic malignant-like syndrome
PPIsRebound acid hypersecretion — step down or alternate-day rather than stop
ClonidineRebound hypertensive crisis
OpioidsWithdrawal syndrome — reduce roughly 10–25% per week
AntiepilepticsSeizures
Digoxin in long-term HFrEF usersBeers added a specific caution in 2023: limited evidence suggests worse clinical outcomes after discontinuation

Can simply be stopped: most vitamins, laxatives, NSAIDs, most antihistamines, a short course of PPI, and most statins at end of life.

One worked mechanism: SSRIs and bleeding

Worth carrying because it explains a 2023 Beers addition (warfarin + SSRI, Table 5) and three separate STOPP criteria, and because the reasoning generalises.

Platelets have no ribosomes and cannot synthesise serotonin. They acquire all of it through SERT — the serotonin transporter, gene SLC6A4, the same protein the drug was designed to block in neurons — and store it in dense granules. Blocking SERT starves them over 1–2 weeks, the time the platelet pool takes to turn over. Serotonin is an amplifier in primary haemostasis: released on activation, it recruits passing platelets through 5-HT2A and constricts the injured vessel. A serotonin-poor platelet still adheres and aggregates, but recruitment is slower and the plug is looser.

So the coagulation cascade is untouched — INR and factor levels are normal — and the phenotype is mucosal ooze and bruising, never haemarthrosis. It is additive with aspirin rather than redundant: aspirin removes the thromboxane arm, the SSRI removes the serotonin arm, leaving ADP alone to recruit. Potency tracks SERT affinity, so paroxetine, sertraline and fluoxetine carry the most, and mirtazapine or bupropion the least. With warfarin there is a second mechanism: fluoxetine and fluvoxamine inhibit CYP2C9 and 2C19 and raise INR independently.

Three things that sound right and are not. The bleeding is not because SSRIs raise gastric acid — that limb has thin human data; the upper GI tract dominates because that is where older patients already have lesions. Stopping the SSRI does not help the bleed in front of you, because repletion needs platelet turnover. And co-prescribing a PPI rests on observational data only — there is no trial, and neither Beers nor START contains a criterion for it, so it is a defensible argument rather than a citable rule. If clopidogrel is involved, use pantoprazole: omeprazole and esomeprazole inhibit CYP2C19 and blunt clopidogrel activation.

The Israeli layer

Questions on גריאטריה בישראל frequently attach to polypharmacy. סל הבריאות coverage often decides what is realistically prescribable — DOACs for AF, SGLT2 inhibitors for defined cardiovascular and renal indications — so coverage rather than evidence is often the rate-limiting step. Kupot Holim run their own medication review and מרשם חוזר processes, and the geriatrician's letter is frequently what triggers a change. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines are covered annually from 65. Opioids require a special prescription. And the long-term-care settings (סיעודי, סיעודי מורכב, תשושי נפש) carry their own antipsychotic-oversight themes.

Note also that Beers itself says the criteria are not equally applicable across countries because of differences in drug availability — which is the formal basis for preferring STOPP/START where the two conflict on a drug that behaves differently in the Israeli formulary.

Hazzard ch 88, p1381 — 4 q, two of four sittings · deferred tier

Rank 2, 5.2% of past questions. The paper does not test oncology — it tests whether you can decide who should be treated, how hard, and when to stop looking.

The organising idea: chronological age is not a treatment decision. Undertreatment of fit older patients is as common an error as overtreatment of frail ones, and a stem describing an independent 82-year-old with good organ function is usually testing whether you will withhold standard therapy for no reason.

The decision framework

  1. Estimate life expectancy independent of the cancer — from comorbidity, function and frailty. Tools exist (ePrognosis aggregates the Lee and Schonberg indices), but the examinable point is that the estimate comes first
  2. Compare it with the time to benefit of the intervention — screening, adjuvant therapy and preventive drugs all pay out in years
  3. Establish the goal — cure, life prolongation, or symptom control — and say it out loud with the patient before choosing a regimen
  4. Assess for treatment tolerance, not just performance status. ECOG alone is insufficient in older adults; it misses cognition, nutrition, falls and social support

Screening: when to stop

CancerStopping logic
BreastBenefit accrues over roughly a decade; stop when life expectancy is under about 10 years rather than at a fixed age
ColorectalSame 10-year logic. A screening colonoscopy also carries procedural risk that rises with age and comorbidity
CervicalStop at 65 with adequate prior negative screening and no high-grade history
ProstateShared decision-making, and generally not beyond about 70 given indolent natural history and competing mortality
LungEligibility is by smoking history and age band, but the same life-expectancy logic applies at the upper end

The examinable generalisation: screening harms are immediate, benefits are delayed, so a shortening life expectancy inverts the balance. This is the same time-to-benefit reasoning that governs statins and bisphosphonates.

Geriatric assessment in oncology

Exam pearl

Performance status is not a geriatric assessment. If the stem gives you only an ECOG, the missing information is the answer.

The recommended sequence is screen, then assess. The G8 is the commonest screening instrument (a score of 14 or below is abnormal and prompts full assessment); VES-13 is an alternative. A positive screen leads to a full CGA, which changes the treatment plan in a substantial minority of cases.

Domains that independently predict chemotherapy toxicity and mortality: function (IADL before ADL), comorbidity (CIRS-G, Charlson), nutrition (MNA, unintentional weight loss), cognition, falls, polypharmacy, depression, and social support. A falls history and IADL dependence are among the strongest and the most often overlooked.

Toxicity prediction: the CARG score (Hurria) and the CRASH score both estimate severe chemotherapy toxicity in older adults using a mix of geriatric and laboratory variables, and both outperform performance status alone.

Treatment modification

  • Dose reduction is not the same as de-escalation. Starting lower with planned escalation preserves intent; abandoning a curative regimen does not
  • Primary G-CSF prophylaxis is generally recommended from 65 with regimens of intermediate febrile-neutropenia risk, where a younger patient would not receive it
  • Renal dosing matters more than in younger patients — carboplatin is dosed by target AUC from an estimated clearance, so an overestimated GFR overdoses directly
  • Agent-specific toxicities that fall hardest on older patients: anthracycline cardiotoxicity (cumulative, worse with existing cardiac disease); cisplatin nephrotoxicity, ototoxicity and peripheral neuropathy; taxane neuropathy compounding an existing falls risk; fluoropyrimidine mucositis and diarrhoea driving dehydration and AKI
  • Immune checkpoint inhibitors are relatively well tolerated with age, but immune-related adverse events — colitis, hepatitis, thyroiditis, hypophysitis, pneumonitis — present atypically and can be mistaken for infection or delirium
  • Radiotherapy is often the better-tolerated alternative where surgery is high risk, and hypofractionation reduces the transport burden, which is itself a geriatric consideration

Supportive care, and the crossover with the rest of the syllabus

  • Pain: the WHO ladder, and the Beers and STOPP rules still apply — no meperidine, no chronic NSAIDs, a laxative with every regular opioid
  • Delirium is a common presentation of hypercalcaemia, brain metastases, opioid initiation, infection and dehydration in this group
  • Anaemia, cachexia and sarcopenia overlap with frailty; megestrol is a Beers avoid
  • Oncological emergencies that present atypically: hypercalcaemia (confusion, constipation, dehydration), cord compression (back pain before weakness), febrile neutropenia (often afebrile), SVC obstruction, tumour lysis
  • Goals of care and advance directives — rank 12 on this syllabus, and almost always examined through an oncology vignette

The Israeli layer

Oncology drug access runs through סל הבריאות and the annual ועדת הסל, so an agent with good evidence may still not be available for a given indication — a real constraint on the honest answer to “what would you give?”. הוספיס בית and community palliative services are covered and are the usual route for symptom control at home. Cancer is a qualifying condition for מחלה קשה arrangements, which matters for the family conversation as much as for the chart.

Hazzard ch 61, p935 — 18 questions across four sittings. The single highest-yield chapter in the book for this exam, and the one the old topic plan had at rank 17.

Parkinsonism, defined the way the chapter defines it

Parkinsonism is the unifying term, not a diagnosis: a variable combination of six independent motor features. Learn them as six, because a stem listing three of them is testing whether you know the set.

The six
BradykinesiaThe central element — the one feature parkinsonism cannot be without. Appendicular when it affects the limbs; axial when it affects trunk, head and neck, oropharynx or eyes
Rest tremorAt rest, not on action
Rigidity
Loss of postural reflexesThe one that produces the falls
Flexed posture
Freezing of gaitFeet transiently glued to the ground

The lesion behind the bradykinesia is loss of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra pars compacta, which innervates the basal ganglia. Idiopathic Parkinson disease is the commonest cause, affecting roughly 1–2% of people over 60 — and nearly every other cause of parkinsonism also becomes commoner with age, which is why the differential below matters more in your clinic than in a neurologist's.

Parkinson disease versus parkinsonism

Asked directly in 2026: which clinical pattern supports PD rather than parkinsonism.

Supports idiopathic PDArgues against it
Unilateral onset with persistent asymmetrySymmetrical onset
Classic 4–6 Hz rest tremor, pill-rollingAbsent tremor, or postural/action tremor only
Excellent and sustained levodopa response, and later levodopa-induced dyskinesiaPoor or absent levodopa response
Slowly progressive over yearsRapid progression; wheelchair within 5 years
Hyposmia, REM sleep behaviour disorder, constipation preceding motor onsetEarly falls, early dementia, early autonomic failure

The atypical syndromes, by their giveaway

PSPEarly falls, backwards, within the first year · vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, slowed vertical saccades · axial rigidity · frontal features. Saccadic abnormality in a demented patient is this until proven otherwise
MSAEarly, severe autonomic failure — orthostatic hypotension, urinary retention or incontinence, erectile failure — plus either parkinsonism (MSA-P) or cerebellar ataxia (MSA-C). Cognition relatively spared early
Corticobasal degenerationMarkedly asymmetric apraxia, alien limb, cortical sensory loss, dystonia, myoclonus
Dementia with Lewy bodiesCognitive decline within a year of parkinsonism, fluctuation, visual hallucinations, neuroleptic sensitivity, RBD
Parkinson disease dementiaThe same pathology, but motor disease preceding cognition by more than a year — the one-year rule is the whole distinction. Ch 63's predictors of dementia in Parkinson disease, asked twice (2022, 2024): older age at motor onset, bradykinesia, non-tremor-predominant disease, bilateral onset, declining levodopa response, plus depression and visual hallucinations — tremor and young onset are the distractors
Drug-inducedSymmetrical, subacute, after metoclopramide, prochlorperazine or an antipsychotic. Resolves over weeks to months after withdrawal. STOPP D23: do not treat it with levodopa — that is a named prescribing cascade
VascularLower-body predominant, gait-led, stepwise, poor levodopa response, vascular burden on imaging
Normal-pressure hydrocephalusMagnetic gait, urinary urgency, cognitive slowing, ventriculomegaly

What levodopa actually fixes

Exam pearl

Falls, freezing and swallowing that do not improve on levodopa are not under-treatment. Raising the dose buys dyskinesia and nothing else.

Asked in 2026 as a direct question. Bradykinesia and rigidity respond best. Tremor responds variably and may not respond at all. Postural instability, freezing of gait, falls, dysphagia, autonomic failure and cognitive decline respond poorly or not at all — they are the non-dopaminergic features, and they are what determines disability late in the disease. A patient whose falls do not improve on levodopa is not under-dosed.

Treatment in the older patient

  • Levodopa/carbidopa is first-line in older adults — not dopamine agonists. Agonists (ropinirole, pramipexole, rotigotine) carry markedly more hallucinations, somnolence, impulse-control disorders and oedema with age, and the historical reason to delay levodopa does not survive contact with a frail 78-year-old
  • MAO-B inhibitors for mild disease or once-daily preference — rasagiline is the best tolerated. Watch the serotonergic interactions
  • Amantadine helps levodopa-induced dyskinesia and “off” time, but causes confusion, hallucinations, livedo reticularis and ankle oedema, and needs renal dose reduction
  • COMT inhibitors (entacapone) extend each levodopa dose for wearing-off
  • Anticholinergics are effectively contraindicated here — Beers Table 2 lists benztropine and trihexyphenidyl, and the cognitive cost outweighs any tremor benefit

Motor fluctuations

  • Wearing-off — benefit fading before the next dose, asked in 2026 at 30 minutes before the next dose. Shorten the dosing interval, or add a COMT or MAO-B inhibitor. Raising the individual dose worsens peak dyskinesia
  • Peak-dose dyskinesia — reduce the individual dose and give it more often, or add amantadine
  • Delayed on / dose failure — protein competition for absorption; take levodopa 30–60 min before meals, and redistribute protein to the evening
  • Freezing — poorly dopaminergic. Visual and auditory cueing, physiotherapy

Non-motor disease, which is where the questions live

  • Psychosis — withdraw in this order: anticholinergics, then amantadine, then MAO-B, then the dopamine agonist, and reduce levodopa last. Treat an intercurrent cause first. If a drug is needed: pimavanserin (FDA-approved for PD psychosis), or quetiapine or clozapine. Never haloperidol, risperidone or olanzapine
  • Dementia — rivastigmine, named in START D4 for PDD and DLB
  • Orthostatic hypotension — withdraw the offending drug, then non-pharmacological measures, then midodrine or fludrocortisone. Common enough in PD to be part of the diagnosis
  • Constipation often precedes motor onset by years; RBD by a decade or more
  • Depression and apathy are intrinsic, not reactive, and are under-treated

The hospital rules, which are examined and also kill people

Exam pearl

The most dangerous prescription on a Parkinson ward round is metoclopramide, and the second is a missed levodopa dose.

Levodopa is given on the patient's schedule, not the drug round's, and is never abruptly stopped — withdrawal can produce an akinetic crisis resembling neuroleptic malignant syndrome, with rigidity, fever and rhabdomyolysis. If the patient cannot swallow, convert: dispersible levodopa by nasogastric tube, or a rotigotine patch at an equivalent dose. “Nil by mouth for a scan” is not a reason to miss doses.

  • Contraindicated antiemetics: metoclopramide, prochlorperazine, and any typical antipsychotic. Use domperidone or ondansetron
  • Contraindicated for agitation: haloperidol and risperidone. If something is unavoidable, quetiapine or clozapine, and pimavanserin where available
  • Watch for the complications that end the admission: aspiration from dysphagia, constipation and ileus, orthostatic hypotension made worse by bed rest, urinary retention, and delirium

Device therapy

Deep brain stimulation and levodopa–carbidopa intestinal gel are for motor fluctuation in a patient who still responds to levodopa and whose cognition is intact. They do nothing for the non-dopaminergic features, and stimulation can worsen cognition and mood, which is why age and cognition are selection criteria rather than afterthoughts. A patient whose disability is falls, freezing and dementia is not a device candidate however severe the disease.

What motor fluctuation actually is

Early on, a levodopa dose produces benefit that outlasts the drug in the blood — the long-duration response — so the patient is smoothly “on” all day and dose timing barely matters. As dopaminergic terminals are lost, that buffering disappears: the striatal dopamine level starts to track the plasma level, and the therapeutic window between too little and too much narrows.

The examinable consequence. Wearing-off is a problem of the trough and dyskinesia a problem of the peak, so they are fixed in opposite directions — and the instinctive move, raising the dose, fixes the trough by worsening the peak. Shorten the interval or extend each dose pharmacologically (COMT, MAO-B) for wearing-off; lower the dose and give it more often, with amantadine, for dyskinesia.

Hazzard ch 46, p679 — 16 questions across four sittings. The second highest-yield chapter, and one the original topic plan put in the cheap-points lane.

Staging — NPIAP

Stage 1Intact skin with non-blanchable erythema. In darker skin tones the colour change may be subtle — look for temperature, firmness and pain
Stage 2Partial-thickness loss with exposed dermis. Shallow, pink-red, moist; may be an intact or ruptured blister. No slough, no granulation, no fat visible
Stage 3Full-thickness — subcutaneous fat visible. Slough or eschar may be present without obscuring depth. Undermining and tunnelling may occur. No fascia, muscle, tendon or bone
Stage 4Full-thickness with exposed fascia, muscle, tendon, ligament, cartilage or bone
UnstageableFull-thickness, but depth obscured by slough or eschar. Stage only once the base is visible
Deep tissue pressure injuryIntact or non-intact skin with persistent non-blanchable deep red, maroon or purple discolouration, or a blood-filled blister. May resolve or may declare as a full-thickness injury
Device-relatedConforms to the shape of the device. Staged as above
Mucosal membraneFrom a device at a mucosal site. Cannot be staged — mucosa has no keratinised layer

Do not reverse-stage. A healing stage 4 does not become a stage 2 — lost tissue is replaced by scar, not by the original structures. Describe it as a healing stage 4.

How common, and what they cost

  • About 70% of pressure injuries occur in people over 65, in 9–22% of nursing home residents and 5–32% of hospital patients
  • Healing is slow and stage-dependent: 75% of stage 2 wounds heal within 60 days, against only 17% of stage 3 or 4. A stage 2 should heal within 50 days; a full-thickness injury should at least show improvement every 2 to 4 weeks, and if it does not, the plan is wrong
  • Osteomyelitis is reported in 32% of stage 4 injuries — and the strongest clinical indicator is a probe reaching bone, not the swab
  • 60% of chronic wounds contain a biofilm, which is why debridement matters more than antiseptics

Pain is the part that gets missed: most patients with a pressure injury report pain at rest, a substantial minority at the highest level — and only a small fraction receive any analgesia for it. Give analgesia 30 minutes before a dressing change, not after.

Where they form, and what the definition actually says

A pressure injury is localised damage to skin and underlying soft tissue, usually over a bony prominence or related to a medical or other device, caused by intense or prolonged pressure, or pressure combined with shear. It may be intact skin or an open wound, and it may be painful.

  • The sites: sacrum, heels, ischial tuberosities, trochanters, lateral malleoli — sacrum and heels commonest. But a pressure injury can form on any soft tissue under pressure, so do not let location alone decide the aetiology
  • The NPIAP modifiers: tissue tolerance for pressure and shear is altered by microclimate — the heat and moisture at the skin surface — and by nutrition, perfusion, comorbidities and the condition of the soft tissue itself. That list is why two patients on the same mattress for the same hours do not fare the same
  • The name matters. Pressure ulcer, bedsore and decubitus ulcer all imply confinement to bed; these injuries form in chairs and under devices too, so pressure injury is the term the chapter uses throughout

Staging, as a depth

The staging system is not a severity scale — it is a statement about which tissue plane has been lost. Reading it that way makes the whole table fall out, including why you cannot reverse-stage and why an obscured base cannot be staged at all.

  • Stage 1 blanches? Then it is reactive hyperaemia, not a pressure injury. The test is whether it fails to blanch. In darker skin the colour change is unreliable — use temperature, firmness and pain instead
  • Stage 2 has no slough and no granulation. If either is present it is deeper than stage 2 by definition, whatever it looks like
  • Deep tissue injury reflects intense pressure about 48 hours earlier, and the damage starts in muscle, deep, before the skin shows it. Stage 1 changes are reversible but may take 1 to 3 weeks to settle; stage 2 heals in 2 to 4 weeks
  • Deep tissue injury can declare either way — it may resolve without breaking, or open into a full-thickness injury within days. Documenting it early protects the patient and you
  • Mucosal injuries cannot be staged at all, because mucosa has no keratinised layer to stage through

Risk assessment

Exam pearl

If the wound base cannot be seen, no stage can be assigned — and that is the correct answer, not a cop-out. “Unstageable” is a finding.

Braden is the instrument to know: six subscales — sensory perception, moisture, activity, mobility, nutrition, and friction and shear. The first five score 1–4, friction and shear scores 1–3, giving 6–23, with lower being worse and 18 or below commonly taken as at risk. Norton is the older alternative. Clinical judgement plus a documented scale beats either alone.

Prevention

  • Repositioning on a schedule matched to the support surface and the patient, not a fixed two hours for everyone — ch 46 cites a trial randomising residents to turning every 2, 3 or 4 hours on a viscoelastic mattress that found no significant difference in pressure-injury incidence — 942 residents, and the rates were 2.5% at two-hourly, 0.6% at three-hourly and 3.1% at four-hourly, with no significant difference between them. Limit head-of-bed elevation to 30° where possible — higher generates shear at the sacrum
  • Seated patients need weight shifted every 15 minutes where they can do it themselves, and repositioning at least hourly in a chair — sitting concentrates more pressure over a smaller area than lying does
  • Prophylactic multilayer foam at the sacrum and heels in critical care cut injuries at the heel (3% vs 12%) and sacrum (1% vs 5%), number needed to treat 10
  • Offload heels completely, floating them off the bed; heel devices rather than pillows that slip
  • Support surfaces — reactive or alternating-pressure, selected by risk and by whether the patient can reposition themselves
  • Skin and moisture — incontinence-associated dermatitis is a separate diagnosis from a pressure injury and is treated with barrier products, not repositioning
  • Nutrition — adequate protein and calories. Routine high-dose vitamin C or zinc is not supported in the absence of deficiency
  • Prophylactic multilayer foam dressings over sacrum and heels in high-risk patients

Dressings, chosen by the wound

WoundChoice
Dry, minimal exudateHydrogel or transparent film — donates moisture
Moderate to heavy exudateFoam, alginate or hydrofibre — absorbs
Painful woundHydrogel, hydrocolloid, or soft-silicone non-adherent contact layers. Asked in 2026: the dressing that relieves pain is the one that keeps the bed moist and does not adhere on removal. Avoid gauze that dries onto the surface
Cavity, underminingLoosely packed filler; never tight packing
Critical colonisationShort-course topical antiseptic or silver; reassess at two weeks

Dressing changes are the main source of pressure-injury pain. Analgesia before the change, soak adherent dressings off, and consider topical lidocaine.

Debridement and infection

Exam pearl

A surface swab from an open pressure injury answers a question you should not have asked — every one of them is colonised. Deep tissue or bone culture is a different matter, and is the right move when you suspect spreading infection or osteomyelitis.

  • Sharp, enzymatic, autolytic or larval, according to urgency and setting
  • Do not debride stable, dry, adherent eschar on an ischaemic heel — it is acting as a biological cover. Assess perfusion first. Debride it if it becomes fluctuant, draining, erythematous or malodorous
  • Infection is a clinical diagnosis. All open pressure injuries are colonised, so a surface swab answers a question you should not be asking. Deep tissue or bone culture if needed
  • If it probes to bone, suspect osteomyelitis — MRI, and a plan that involves surgery, not another antibiotic course

Odour, when the patient cannot be debrided — the palliative stage-4 wound the 2024 paper described — is managed by ground metronidazole applied to the wound bed; for infection needing parenteral therapy the chapter's empiric choices are cefazolin, ceftriaxone or clindamycin, vancomycin for MRSA, and metronidazole, a carbapenem or a beta-lactamase inhibitor where anaerobes are suspected. Antiseptics belong on full-thickness wounds: cadexomer iodine, silver, honey or PHMB.

When healing is not the goal

In advanced illness the aim shifts to comfort: odour control, exudate management, pain relief at dressing changes, and repositioning only as far as the patient tolerates. A Kennedy terminal ulcer — sudden, pear-shaped, purple, sacral, in the last days — is a sign of dying, not of failed care, and naming it to the family matters.

Israeli layer: pressure-injury prevalence is a reported quality indicator in Israeli long-term care, which is why a grade 4 ulcer that will not heal turns up in questions about תום שיקום and placement rather than only in wound care.

Nutrition, and what the evidence actually supports

The targets ch 46 gives: 30–35 kcal/kg and 1.3–1.5 g/kg of protein daily, which has been shown to improve healing significantly. Supplements produced a relative reduction in incidence of about 25%.

Malnutrition is a risk factor and an impediment to healing, so screen (MNA-SF) and correct energy and protein intake, with a higher protein target while a wound is open. What is not supported is reflexive supplementation of vitamin C or zinc in the absence of deficiency — a recurrent distractor — and neither albumin nor prealbumin is a nutritional marker in an inflamed patient; they fall as acute-phase reactants and tell you about the illness, not the diet.

The ones that are not pressure injuries

Looks likeActuallyGiveaway
Stage 2 over the sacrumIncontinence-associated dermatitisDiffuse, in the skin folds rather than over the bone, no depth; treated with barrier products, not repositioning
Unstageable heel woundArterial ulcerAbsent pulses, punched-out, painful, dry base; assess perfusion before debriding anything
Deep tissue injurySkin failure at the end of life — Kennedy terminal lesionRapid appearance, pear-shaped, in the actively dying patient; comfort is the goal, not healing
Chronic non-healing edgeMalignant change, or osteomyelitisRolled edges, or probes to bone; biopsy or MRI, not another dressing

Hazzard ch 59 p893 — 6 q · plus the four named 2024 papers

The diagnostic half. With ch 60 and 63 this block ranks 3rd at 4.8%; on its own, ch 59 sits below the behavioural and movement chapters. Questions here cluster on telling the subtypes apart from a vignette, the biomarker papers, the genetics, and capacity. Behaviour, the drug tables and the non-Alzheimer discriminators are in .

Diagnosis

Major neurocognitive disorder requires decline from a previous level in one or more cognitive domains, sufficient to interfere with independence in everyday activities, not occurring exclusively during delirium and not better explained by another mental disorder. Mild neurocognitive disorder (MCI) is the same decline without loss of independence — the functional criterion is what separates them, not the test score.

Subtypes — the discriminating features

TypePoints towards itPoints away
Alzheimer'sInsidious onset, gradual progression, prominent episodic memory loss with impaired recall not helped by cueing, medial temporal atrophy Early gait disorder, early hallucinations, stepwise course
VascularStepwise decline, focal neurological signs, executive and processing-speed deficits early, vascular burden on imaging, temporal relation to stroke Pure amnestic presentation with clean imaging
Lewy bodyFluctuating cognition and attention, recurrent well-formed visual hallucinations, REM sleep behaviour disorder, spontaneous parkinsonism, severe neuroleptic sensitivity, autonomic failure. Reduced dopamine transporter uptake on DaT imaging Parkinsonism preceding cognitive decline by more than a year — that is Parkinson's disease dementia
FrontotemporalYounger onset, behavioural change first — disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsivity, hyperorality — or progressive language failure, with memory relatively spared early Early amnesia; late onset
Normal-pressure hydrocephalusThe triad — magnetic gait first, then urinary urgency, then cognitive slowing — with ventriculomegaly out of proportion to atrophy. Gait improvement after high-volume lumbar drainage predicts shunt response Cognitive decline preceding gait disorder

Mixed pathology is the rule at post-mortem, not the exception, and a vignette with both vascular burden and an amnestic profile is usually testing whether you say so.

What to exclude before settling on a label

B12 deficiency, hypothyroidism, depression (the classic pseudodementia, though the distinction is less clean than teaching suggests — depression is also a prodrome), hyponatraemia, hypercalcaemia, obstructive sleep apnoea, chronic subdural haematoma, NPH, and — the one you can actually fix that day — drugs. Anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids and antiepileptics. Cross-reference Beers Table 7 and STOPP Section M before ordering an MRI.

Cognitive testing

MMSEWidely known, insensitive to MCI and to executive dysfunction, heavily affected by education and language. In Israel, the validated Hebrew, Arabic and Russian versions are not interchangeable with a live translation by a family member
MoCAMore sensitive for MCI and executive function. Conventional cut-off 26, with one point added for 12 or fewer years of education
Mini-CogThree-word recall plus clock draw. Fast, useful as a screen, relatively education-resistant
Clock drawingExecutive and visuospatial in one task
Informant historyIQCODE or a structured collateral. In practice the single most informative item in the assessment, and the one most often skipped

The numbers behind the diagnosis

  • Alzheimer disease is 50–90% of all dementia in the United States. Prevalence by age: about 3% at 65–74, 17% at 75–84, and 32% at 85 and over
  • Median survival from diagnosis to death is 7 to 10 years
  • 12–15% of people with MCI progress each year to Alzheimer disease or another dementia — the annual rate, distinct from the 5-to-8-year figure in 57 Cognitive change
  • Familial Alzheimer disease is only 1–5% of cases, linked to APP, PSEN1 and PSEN2. Everything else is sporadic, whatever the family history suggests

APOE, in numbers you can quote

Risk multiplierDeveloped AD by 85 (Framingham)
Two ε4 alleles12-fold55%
One ε4 allelefourfold27%
No ε4—9%

Read the right-hand column before quoting the left: a 12-fold relative risk sounds deterministic, and yet 45% of ε4 homozygotes had not developed Alzheimer disease by 85. That gap is why the chapter treats APOE as a risk factor and not a diagnostic test, and why the Lancet Commission's finding that risk is modifiable irrespective of APOE status is the clinically useful half of the genetics.

The 2024–25 diagnostic criteria papers

Five of 100 questions in the 2026 geriatrics block came from four named journal papers, all on dementia diagnosis. They are cited by title in the question stem. No textbook contains them, and they are the single highest-yield reading outside Hazzard. Obtain all four; what follows orients you, and is not a substitute for the papers.

Revised Alzheimer's Association criteria (2024)

Shifts diagnosis from syndrome to biology: Alzheimer's disease is defined by its biomarkers, whether or not symptoms are present. Biomarkers are grouped by when they become abnormal, which is what the exam asked.

  • Core 1 — the early-changing markers, and abnormality here is sufficient to establish the diagnosis: amyloid markers (amyloid PET, CSF Aβ42/40) together with the phosphorylated and secreted tau markers that track alongside amyloid (p-tau217, p-tau181, p-tau231)
  • Core 2 — markers that turn abnormal later and are used for staging rather than diagnosis: tau PET, and CSF MTBR-tau243 and p-tau205
  • Non-specific — neurodegeneration (NfL, MRI atrophy, FDG-PET) and inflammation (GFAP), which support but do not define

IWG recommendation, JAMA Neurology 2024

The counter-position, and the axis the exam tests. The International Working Group argues against calling biomarker-positive asymptomatic people “Alzheimer's disease”, because most will not progress within their lifetime. It reserves presymptomatic for those with a deterministic cause — autosomal dominant mutation, or Down syndrome — and calls everyone else biomarker-positive but asymptomatic at risk. Know both positions and which one the stem is citing.

VasCog-2 / WSO criteria, JAMA Neurology 2024

Revised criteria for vascular cognitive impairment and vascular dementia, asked twice in 2026 — once as “who meets the criteria” and once applied to a patient with lacunar infarcts who was also CSF-tau positive and APOE ε4 positive. The examinable tension is mixed pathology: vascular burden and Alzheimer biology commonly coexist, and the criteria have to say what to call that.

Dementia prevention narrative review

Asked as risk reduction advice to a worried 68-year-old with an affected parent. The modifiable risk factors are the examinable content — hearing loss, hypertension, physical inactivity, diabetes, smoking, obesity, depression, low education, social isolation, excess alcohol, head injury, air pollution, and more recently untreated vision loss and high LDL.

Verify every biomarker detail above against the papers themselves before relying on it. This is orientation written from the question stems and general knowledge, not extracted from the primary sources.

Staging, and why it is asked

Because almost every management decision — driving, capacity, tube feeding, hospice eligibility, which drug — is a function of stage rather than diagnosis. The two systems in use are the Clinical Dementia Rating (0, 0.5, 1, 2, 3 — none, questionable, mild, moderate, severe, scored across six domains) and the FAST scale of seven stages with substages through 7f. Advanced dementia in the sense used by the palliative literature means profound memory loss, minimal verbal output, inability to walk independently, total ADL dependence and incontinence — FAST 7. That is the population in which the tube-feeding evidence applies.

The anti-amyloid antibodies, in proportion

Lecanemab and donanemab slow decline modestly in early symptomatic Alzheimer disease with confirmed amyloid, and the effect size is small relative to the demands they make. Know the shape of the argument rather than the trial numbers:

  • Eligibility is narrow: MCI or mild dementia, biomarker-confirmed, with the cognitive and imaging infrastructure to run it — which excludes most of the patients a geriatrician sees
  • ARIA — amyloid-related imaging abnormalities, oedema and haemorrhage — is the characteristic harm, commoner in APOE ε4 homozygotes, requiring serial MRI
  • Anticoagulation and these drugs together raise the haemorrhage question sharply
  • They do not apply to moderate or severe disease, to non-Alzheimer dementias, or to prevention

Meanwhile the things with the best evidence for the patient in front of you remain unglamorous: treat the reversible contributors, deprescribe the anticholinergics, treat pain, support the carer, plan while capacity remains, and use cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine where they are indicated — which the Lancet Commission restates for Alzheimer and Lewy body disease.

One number on prevention

SPRINT-MIND: intensive blood-pressure lowering against a standard target of 140 mmHg produced a statistically significant 19% reduction in the incidence of MCI. It is the closest thing to a positive prevention trial in this chapter, it is a vascular intervention, and it sits directly behind the Lancet Commission's instruction to hold systolic pressure at or below 130 from the age of 40.

Capacity, autonomy and the Israeli legal layer

  • Capacity is decision-specific and time-specific, not global. The four abilities: understand the information, retain it long enough to decide, weigh it against alternatives, and communicate a choice. A diagnosis of dementia does not itself remove capacity
  • ייפוי כוח מתמשך — the durable power of attorney, executed while capacity is retained, and now the preferred route over guardianship
  • אפוטרופסות — guardianship, a court appointment and a more restrictive instrument; מקבל החלטות זמני and supported decision-making are the less restrictive alternatives
  • Driving. Fitness to drive is a defined medical reporting question in Israel, routed through המכון הרפואי לבטיחות בדרכים. Dementia is not automatically disqualifying at the mild stage, but moderate dementia is, and the assessment is not a cognitive score alone
  • Caregiver burden is examinable in its own right — depression, physical morbidity, financial strain, and the point at which home care becomes unsafe. In Israel this is where חוק ביטוח סיעוד entitlement and the תשושי נפש versus סיעודי classification enter

Hazzard ch 60 p919 · 63 p981 — 17 q combined

The treatment half. Ch 60 and 63 both appear in every sitting and between them outscore the diagnostic chapter. Questions cluster on what not to prescribe, the starting doses, and separating the non-Alzheimer dementias from a vignette. Diagnosis, biomarkers, APOE and the anti-amyloid antibodies are in .

Behavioural and psychological symptoms

Look for the cause before reaching for a drug: pain, constipation, urinary retention, infection, a new medication, sensory deprivation, an over- or under-stimulating environment, or a caregiver interaction that is being experienced as a threat. The named framework is DICE — Describe, Investigate, Create, Evaluate.

Antipsychotics increase stroke and mortality in dementia. Beers permits them only when documented non-pharmacological options have failed or the patient is threatening substantial harm to self or others, with periodic attempts at deprescribing. STOPP adds duration limits: review by 3 months at an unchanged dose, and not beyond 12 weeks unless symptoms are severe and non-drug measures have failed. In Lewy body dementia, avoid antipsychotics other than quetiapine or clozapine — neuroleptic sensitivity can be catastrophic; pimavanserin is the agent approved for Parkinson's disease psychosis.

How universal the behavioural symptoms are

  • Neuropsychiatric symptoms affect almost everyone with dementia at some point — ch 60 puts it at 98% of people with Alzheimer disease across the course of illness. Cognitive deficit is the hallmark; behaviour is the near-universal accompaniment
  • The commonest three are depression, apathy and anxiety — not agitation, which is merely the one that generates referrals
  • They appear before dementia does. Depression and irritability are common even prior to MCI and are the first symptoms in well over half of those who later develop dementia
  • Mild behavioural impairment (MBI) is the term for late-life onset of neuropsychiatric symptoms of any severity, in someone without dementia, lasting over six months, not attributable to another psychiatric disorder. It is a prodromal category, and the six-month duration is the examinable part
  • Severity rises with cognitive decline, in the community and in nursing homes alike, and the symptoms carry worse quality of life, increased mortality, accelerated progression, higher costs and greater carer burden

The carer is the second patient

Carer burden predicts institutionalisation more strongly than the patient's cognitive score does. What has evidence: multicomponent interventions combining education, skills training, support and respite — not education alone, which reliably fails. Screen the carer for depression, ask about their sleep and their own health, and name the eligibility for services rather than mentioning that services exist. This is examinable as a management answer, not as a courtesy.

The five that matter, side by side

Exam pearl

Hallucinations plus fluctuation plus parkinsonism within a year means you may not give haloperidol or risperidone. This single sentence answers more dementia questions than any criterion set.

Opening pictureDiscriminatorImagingPrescribing trap
AlzheimerEpisodic memory, storage failure — cueing does not helpGradual, years; insight lost lateMedial temporal and parietal atrophyNone specific; treat vascular risk
Vascular (VCID)Processing speed and executive function; gait earlyStepwise, or a temporal link to stroke; vascular burden on imagingInfarcts, white-matter disease, microbleedsAnticoagulation decisions where there is amyloid angiopathy
Lewy bodyFluctuation, formed visual hallucinations, RBD, parkinsonism within a year of cognitive onsetThe one-year rule against Parkinson disease dementiaOccipital hypometabolism; abnormal DaTSevere neuroleptic sensitivity. Quetiapine or clozapine only; pimavanserin where available. Rivastigmine is named by START
FrontotemporalBehavioural change, disinhibition, apathy, loss of empathy, compulsions, hyperorality — or progressive aphasiaYounger onset, memory relatively spared early, family history in a thirdFrontal and anterior temporal atrophyCholinesterase inhibitors do not help and may worsen behaviour. SSRIs for the behaviour
Parkinson disease dementiaMotor disease first, cognition more than a year laterThe interval, and nothing elseAs Parkinson diseaseAs Lewy body — same pathology, same sensitivity

The discriminators ch 63 states outright

  • Mixed pathology is the norm in old age. The chapter says plainly that with advancing age it becomes increasingly common for more than one pathology to be producing the dementia syndrome. A clean single-diagnosis answer is often the wrong instinct
  • Lewy body dementia: cognitive impairment with profound fluctuation, spontaneous parkinsonism, REM sleep behaviour disorder, and visual hallucinations
  • Parkinson disease dementia: about 30% of people with Parkinson disease develop dementia, and — unlike Alzheimer disease — the motor symptoms predate the dementia by many years
  • Behavioural-variant FTD: behavioural and personality change dominant, in the relative absence of memory and perceptual symptoms. Behaviour appears in advanced dementia of any cause; it is its prominence as the presenting feature that points to FTD
  • Progressive supranuclear palsy: falls and dysphagia with abnormal vertical gaze but a preserved oculocephalic reflex — the doll's-eye manoeuvre overcomes the gaze palsy, which places the lesion above the brainstem nuclei. That triad is the exam's PSP question; the imaging answer the 2025 committee wanted (Table 63-5) was atrophy of the dorsal midbrain
  • The proteins, since the exam asks them: FTLD pathology is tau in nearly half (including Pick bodies and corticobasal degeneration) and TDP-43 in a similar share (semantic-variant PPA is TDP-43 type C, tau-negative), FUS under 10%. The 2024 stem — a 60-year-old with disinhibition, sweet cravings, MMSE 28 and a failed clock — wanted tau. Many FTD patients are misdiagnosed as Alzheimer disease in life

The chapter also insists the cognitive history be comprehensive — memory, language, visuospatial function, executive function, behaviour and attention — because a history that only asks about memory finds only Alzheimer disease.

Pharmacological treatment

  • Cholinesterase inhibitors — donepezil, rivastigmine, galantamine — for mild to moderate Alzheimer's. Rivastigmine is the named agent for Lewy body and Parkinson's disease dementia (START D4)
  • Memantine for moderate to severe disease, alone or added to a cholinesterase inhibitor
  • Their adverse effects generate the exam questions: bradycardia and syncope (STOPP D17 and D18 — avoid with bradycardia under 60, heart block, unexplained syncope, or alongside other rate-limiting drugs), nausea and weight loss, vivid dreams, and urinary urgency — which is the start of the classic prescribing cascade when it is met with oxybutynin
  • Memantine with a seizure history is a STOPP criterion (D19)
  • Nootropics are dismissed wholesale by STOPP D20 — ginkgo, piracetam, phosphatidylserine, modafinil, omega-3, ginseng, creatine
  • Anti-amyloid monoclonals (lecanemab, donanemab) are covered with the biomarker criteria in

The drugs, at the doses actually used

Exam pearl

A cholinesterase inhibitor in frontotemporal dementia is the wrong answer twice: it does not help and it can worsen the behaviour.

Table 59-7 and tables 60-8 and 60-9 are all cited in recent papers, and they are cited because they contain numbers.

AgentStageTitrationNote
DonepezilAll stages5 mg daily, to 10 mg after about 4 weeksBradycardia and syncope, vivid dreams, GI upset, weight loss, urinary frequency
Rivastigmine capsuleMild to moderate1.5 mg twice daily, up by 1.5 mg twice daily at intervals of at least 2 weeksThe one named by START for Parkinson disease dementia and Lewy body dementia
Rivastigmine patchMild to severe4.6 mg/24 h for at least 4 weeks, then 9.5 mg/24 h; maximum 13.3 mg/24 hFewer GI effects than the capsule; rotate sites. Low body weight, under about 50 kg, is the warning that matters — these patients get markedly more adverse effects, so titrate slowly, watch closely, and think hard before the 13.3 mg/24 h patch. Dose down in hepatic impairment
GalantamineMild to moderate4 mg twice daily, up at 4-week intervalsAvoid in severe renal or hepatic impairment
MemantineModerate to severe5 mg daily, up by 5 mg weekly to 10 mg twice dailyCrCl 5–29: target 5 mg twice daily. Dizziness, headache, confusion, constipation

Cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine are both restated by the Lancet Commission for Alzheimer and Lewy body disease. They do not modify the disease; they buy months of function. Stopping them is a legitimate decision at the point where there is no function left to protect, and it is taken with the family rather than announced to them.

If an antipsychotic is unavoidable: the doses

Everything in 60 Behavioural symptoms says to exhaust the non-drug route first — DICE, analgesic trial, environment, the contributing causes. When a drug is genuinely required, the starting doses are far below the psychiatric ones, and every agent here carries the boxed warning for increased mortality in dementia and can prolong the QT.

AgentDaily dose in dementiaWhat limits it
Risperidone0.25–1 mgDose-dependent extrapyramidal effects, hyperprolactinaemia, orthostasis, stroke risk

Quetiapine12.5–150 mgSedation and orthostasis — but the choice in Lewy body disease and Parkinson disease

Long-acting injectables are not used for neuropsychiatric symptoms in dementia. Start low, review at days rather than months, and document the plan for stopping at the same visit you start.

Antidepressants, starting doses

Hazzard ch 58, p879 — 15 q, in all four sittings

Rank 5, 4.6%. The highest-yield single fact on the topic: the commonest subtype is the one that gets missed.

The four numbers this chapter is built on

  • Delirium affects as many as half of all hospitalised people aged 65 and over
  • It is preventable in up to 50% of cases — the single most important fact on the topic, and the reason prevention outranks treatment everywhere below
  • It goes unrecognised in up to 70% of older patients. Not missed at the margin: missed as the rule, mostly because the hypoactive form does not announce itself
  • People aged 65 and over account for nearly 40% of all days of hospital care, which is why a condition of hospitalised elders is a system-level problem

Why the chapter calls it a marker of care quality. Delirium is common, frequently iatrogenic, and tightly linked to the processes of care — so its incidence measures the ward as much as the patient. It also initiates a cascade: functional and cognitive decline, loss of independence, institutionalisation, death. Costs exceed $60,000 per patient across the hospital and post-hospital period. During COVID-19, patients presenting with delirium had worse hospital outcomes than those who did not — the same pattern the chapter describes for any severe illness.

Definition and what each element means

  • Acute onset and fluctuating course — hours to days, waxing and waning within a day. Collateral history is how you establish this; the patient cannot
  • Inattention — the cardinal feature. Test it: months of the year backwards, serial sevens, digit span. If attention is intact, it is probably not delirium
  • Disorganised thinking or altered level of consciousness
  • Evidence of a medical cause — an illness, an intoxication, a withdrawal, a drug

The three subtypes

HyperactiveAgitation, hallucinations, pulling at lines. The most recognised and the least common
HypoactiveThe commonest. Withdrawn, drowsy, slow, apathetic. Routinely mislabelled as depression, fatigue or “just their dementia”, and carries the worst prognosis. If a stem describes a quiet, sleepy, inattentive patient, this is the answer
MixedFluctuation between the two, which is why a single calm assessment does not exclude delirium

Screening instruments

Exam pearl

Attention is the discriminator. If attention is genuinely intact, whatever else is wrong, it is not delirium.

CAM requires feature 1 (acute onset and fluctuation) and feature 2 (inattention), plus either feature 3 (disorganised thinking) or feature 4 (altered consciousness). The and/or structure is itself examinable. CAM-ICU for ventilated patients, 3D-CAM for a structured three-minute version, and 4AT as a rapid bedside tool needing no special training, which also functions when the patient is too unwell to complete cognitive testing.

Inouye's model: vulnerability multiplied by insult

The practical consequence is that a highly vulnerable patient needs only a trivial insult — a catheter, a night of poor sleep — while a robust patient needs a major one. That is why the same operation causes delirium in one 80-year-old and not another, and why prevention works by lowering both sides.

Predisposing (baseline vulnerability)Precipitating (the insult)
Dementia or any cognitive impairment — the single strongestDrugs — benzodiazepines, anticholinergics, opioids, corticosteroids, H2 blockers, Z-drugs (Table 58-2 — zolpidem was the 2023 answer over memantine, omeprazole and ceftriaxone)
Age, frailty, functional dependenceInfection, particularly urinary and respiratory
Sensory impairment — absent glasses and hearing aids countSurgery and anaesthesia; hip fracture especially
Multimorbidity, renal or hepatic impairmentUncontrolled pain — and, separately, the opioid used to treat it
Depression, alcohol useUrinary retention, faecal impaction
Prior deliriumDehydration, electrolyte disturbance, hypoxia, hypoglycaemia
MalnutritionRestraints, catheters, sleep deprivation, ward transfers

Risk, in multiples

FactorIncrease in delirium risk
Dementiatwo- to fivefold — and up to two-thirds of delirious patients have underlying dementia
Sedative-hypnotics3- to 12-fold
Two committee rulings the chapter supports by structure rather than by sentence: a CAM that cannot be completed — the drowsy patient who fails the three words and the months backwards but cannot be assessed for fluctuation — does not diagnose delirium; it says the assessment is incomplete (2024). And an acutely inattentive, fluctuating patient is delirious even when no cause has yet been found — the diagnosis is clinical, the search for the cause comes after it (2026)
Anticholinergics5- to 12-fold
Opioidsthreefold
Any one or more culprit drugsup to fivefold

Two-thirds is the number to carry: a first episode of delirium should prompt cognitive follow-up once the illness has settled, because the odds are the dementia was already there.

What it costs, in outcomes

  • Delirium in the ICU carries a fourfold increase in in-hospital mortality and a sixfold increase at six months
  • In the emergency department, a sevenfold increase in mortality at six months
  • It does not clear on discharge: symptoms generally persist a month or more, and as few as 20% have complete symptom resolution at six months
  • Prevalence at admission ranges 7–80% and incidence during admission 8–82% across studies; up to 48% in nursing homes and post-acute care, and up to 83% at the end of life

Those wide ranges reflect the setting and the detection method, not real disagreement — which is itself the point about a condition missed in 70% of cases.

Prevention beats treatment

Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention cut delirium by 40% against standard care, and proactive geriatric consultation reduced delirium after hip fracture by 40% in a randomised trial — two separate 40% figures, both worth quoting. Multicomponent non-pharmacological prevention is the intervention with the best evidence on this entire topic. The named programme is HELP (Hospital Elder Life Program), cited by name in the Beers Alternatives paper as AGS CoCare: HELP. Its components map directly onto the precipitants: repeated orientation, therapeutic activity, early mobilisation, sleep protocols without drugs, vision and hearing aids restored, hydration, and pain control.

No drug is recommended as routine prophylaxis or as a routine response to delirium in any population. Prophylactic haloperidol does not prevent it. Antipsychotics do not shorten it. They are for severe distress or danger that has not responded to non-drug measures — hours to days, lowest dose, documented, with a plan against continuation.

If a drug is genuinely unavoidable: the chapter's doses

Only for severe symptoms threatening the patient's safety or the medical treatment itself — never for disturbance.

Olanzapine2.5 mg10 mg
Risperidone0.25–0.5 mg1.5 mg
Lorazepam — end-of-life sedation0.5–1.0 mg PO, IV or SCtitrate to effect

The end point is an awake but manageable patient, not a sedated one, and the patient is reassessed continually with a view to tapering. Note the benzodiazepine position, which is narrower than usual but not as narrow as “withdrawal only”: alcohol and benzodiazepine withdrawal, and terminal sedation at the end of life, where ch 58 names lorazepam as the agent of choice. Outside those, benzodiazepines cause delirium rather than treat it.

Management

Exam pearl

Every stem offering haloperidol has a better answer above it in the list. The drug is for danger, not for disturbance.

  1. Find and treat the cause, and expect more than one. Review every drug started in the preceding days — a medication chart is the highest-yield investigation on the round
  2. Non-pharmacological measures first, every time: glasses, hearing aids, light, family presence, mobilisation, bladder and bowel, remove the catheter and the restraint
  3. If a drug is unavoidable: low-dose antipsychotic short-term. Avoid entirely in Lewy body dementia and Parkinson's — quetiapine or clozapine if truly unavoidable. Benzodiazepines are only first-line for alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, and otherwise make delirium worse
  4. Follow up. Delirium is not a transient event that resolves at discharge in this population — it predicts mortality, institutionalisation and persistent cognitive decline, and it both unmasks and accelerates dementia. Document it, tell the family what it means, and arrange cognitive review after recovery

Cross-reference: Beers Table 3 lists the delirium precipitants to avoid, with opioids added in 2023. STOPP D14 covers anticholinergics in delirium, and the Beers ≥3 CNS-active drug rule catches the combination that produces most hospital delirium.

What happens afterwards

Delirium is not a self-limiting episode with no sequel. It is independently associated with longer stay, institutionalisation, functional decline and death, and it accelerates the trajectory of cognitive decline in patients with dementia. In a third or more it persists for weeks to months, so a patient still muddled at discharge is not evidence that the diagnosis was wrong. Document it, tell the family what it was, arrange cognitive follow-up at a distance from the illness, and do not diagnose a dementia during it.

Delirium, dementia, depression, psychosis — the grid

Table 58-4, reduced to the discriminators. The stem will give you two or three of these features and expect the diagnosis.

DeliriumDementiaDepressionAcute psychosis
OnsetHours to daysInsidious, weeks to monthsEitherAcute
CourseWaxing and waningUnrelentingVariableEpisodic
AttentionImpaired — the hallmarkIntact until end-stageReduced concentrationVariable
ConsciousnessAltered, lethargic to hyperalertNormal until end-stageNormalNormal
OrientationDisorientedNormal until end-stageUsually normalUsually normal
SpeechDisorganised, incoherentSparse, anomic, aphasicSlowedOften disorganised
HallucinationsUsually visualSometimesRareUsually auditory, more complex
Organic causeYesYesNoNo

Perceptual disturbance occurs in only about 15% of delirium, so its absence proves nothing: acute onset, inattention, altered consciousness and global cognitive impairment are what identify it. The reason to separate these carefully is pharmacological — treating the “depression” or the “psychosis” with an anticholinergic drug makes an unrecognised delirium worse.

Why the same insult spares one patient and floors the next

The model that organises the whole chapter: delirium is what happens when an acute stressor meets an already vulnerable brain. The two trade off against each other, so there is no fixed amount of insult that causes delirium — only an amount relative to the reserve of the person receiving it.

Two consequences worth holding. Prevention works on both axes: you cannot undo the dementia, but you can remove the catheter, restore the glasses, fix the sleep and stop the anticholinergic — each of which moves the patient left along the insult axis. And delirium in response to a trivial insult is itself diagnostic information: it tells you the baseline vulnerability was already high, which is why a first episode of delirium earns cognitive follow-up at a distance from the illness.

What sits underneath vulnerability, per the chapter: structural lesions, vascular change, altered connectivity, neuroinflammation, neurodegeneration and the other changes of age. The EEG shows global slowing of the dominant posterior alpha rhythm — asked in 2024 twice — with a false-negative rate of 17% and false-positive of 22% against non-delirious patients, so it is reserved for suspected subclinical seizures and for separating delirium from psychiatric illness; imaging is for focal signs, head trauma or no other cause. Imaging and EEG point to dysfunction in the prefrontal cortex, thalamus, basal ganglia and the temporoparietal and fusiform cortex of the non-dominant hemisphere. No single pathway explains it; the final common picture is a large-scale network failure. The neurotransmitter picture ch 58 gives, and the 2025 committee asked: raised dopaminergic activity, reduced cholinergic activity, or an imbalance of the two, with serotonin either way; cholinergic deficiency has the most evidence, alongside inflammation and abnormal glucose metabolism. The validated precipitating factors in hospital, each conferring a two- to fourfold risk and cumulative: physical restraints, malnutrition (low albumin), more than three drugs added in a day, an indwelling catheter, and any iatrogenic event — the 2023 question wanted the albumin, not the depression, disability or severe illness, which are predisposing.

Hazzard ch 65 p1007 — 12 q across the three 8th-edition sittings

The chapter with the most questions and no section until today. Ch 65 is unusual: it is less a pharmacology chapter than an argument about what antidepressants do and do not do in the old, and the committee has asked that argument directly — twice with the same question. The drug tables are in .

The PHQ-9, and what “minor” means

  • The chapter's instrument is the PHQ-9, built on DSM-5 major-depression criteria, and it insists on symptom frequency — depression is not a bad day. 0–4 no or clinically insignificant symptoms; 5–9 mild, generally subsyndromal (“minor”); 10 or higher correlates with major depression and warrants evaluation and intervention. It doubles as the measurement-based-care tool, and item 9 asks about death wishes and suicidal ideation. Both the 2024 and 2025 papers built a stem on the 5–9 band
  • Subsyndromal depression has about the same effect on health and quality of life as major depression, but antidepressants do not help it. The chapter's answer is not “you do not merit treatment” but non-pharmacological approaches and, where symptoms are mild, watch and wait with check-ins — never a first choice if there is any safety concern. The 2025 committee answer for the active 90-year-old with new low mood was exactly this: minor depression, follow up, no drug
  • Real-world care: about 5% of older adults in primary care have clinically significant depression, half are recognised, a fifth of those get guideline-concordant care — about 10% treated adequately. And adequate care does not guarantee remission: in collaborative care, under a third remit at six months

What the chapter says about antidepressants — and the exam has asked twice

Exam pearl

“Principles of recommending an antidepressant” was asked in 2025 and again in 2026 with the same keyed answer: the placebo effect is large. Know the five findings, because any of them could be the next stem.

  • The placebo effect is powerful. In many studies antidepressants offered no significant benefit over placebo and placebo response rates were large, especially in less severe cases; some meta-analyses find the drug's own effect only in more severe depression. Telling the patient that believing in the drug increases its chance of working is honest. Most antidepressants take 6 to 8 weeks to show a measurable effect
  • They treat major, not minor, depression. “A little antidepressant for a little depression” does not hold up, and starting one for a condition that may resolve on its own commits the patient to a drug and to the problem of stopping it
  • They do not generally work in dementia. A large number of negative studies; consensus is that their usefulness is questionable, and patients with dementia cannot usually engage in psychotherapy either. Carer support and behavioural interventions lift mood; an antidepressant is continued only if it yields a measurable benefit. The 2024 (“efficacy in dementia is doubtful”) and 2026 (“avoid the antidepressant, use behavioural approaches”) answers both come from this paragraph
  • Slow up-titration improves adherence — patients started low and titrated over visits adhered far better than those started at the full dose, reaching the same dose; probably the attention, and fewer side effects
  • There is no standard effective dose. The dose–response relationship is small, placebo is substantial at every dose, and the right dose is the one that works for that patient, capped by safety
  • Patients do not volunteer side effects, sexual ones above all; they stop the drug instead. Name them and ask. The chapter's stated risks: falls, SIADH and mortality

Stopping, and what discontinuation looks like

  • Withdrawal from SSRIs and SNRIs: sweating, chills, dizziness, flu-like symptoms, GI upset, insomnia, vivid and excessive dreaming, low mood, vertigo, numbness, shock-like sensations — the 2024 answer was the dreams and sleep disturbance. The danger is mistaking withdrawal for relapse
  • The risks of stopping are “surprisingly low”: relapse trajectories on drug and on placebo look alike, and continued treatment offers only modest protection. Indefinite continuation is reasonable only where depression returned on stopping (not merely during withdrawal) or after multiple prior episodes; otherwise consider a deliberate, monitored taper — SSRIs, SNRIs and mirtazapine over 2 to 4 weeks, tricyclics over months; fluoxetine needs no taper and can smooth the last step. Decide the end game when you start

ECT, collaborative care, psychotherapy

  • ECT remains by far the most effective treatment: response over 80%, remission over 60%; no trial has found a drug more effective; older patients respond even better than younger ones; in its current form it is safe with few side effects, and the short-term memory loss almost always resolves within a few weeks.
