Three to six treatments a week for 2 to 4 weeks; the benefit decays, so maintenance ECT is sometimes needed. Early option for severe or psychotic depression and for poor medication response. Asked in 2024 (remission in more than half) and 2025 (safe, few side effects)
  • Collaborative care — care manager, primary care prescriber, mental-health consultant, measured symptoms — is the most effective system-level approach; still, fewer than a third remit at six months in real clinics
  • Psychotherapy: CBT, interpersonal therapy, behavioural activation, reminiscence groups all work; structured and short, about 3 months at most, and if nothing has moved in 1 to 2 months change modality. In the largest geriatric trial 51% preferred counselling and 38% medication. Exercise is not a treatment for depression but the active have less onset and recurrence. Carers of a spouse with dementia may need permission to look after themselves

Suicide

Every depressed older patient is assessed for suicide risk: thoughts, intent to act, plans, and access to means. Suicidal ideation may be a communication of suffering or a genuine wish to die; the chapter's stance is a problem-solving one, keeping the patient engaged and focused on what can be changed. Risk and protective factors are Figure 65-3. In Israel the practical routes and the reporting layer are in Ethics & EOL law.

Hazzard ch 104 p1667 · 105 p1679 · 106 p1699 — 9 q

Rank 4, 4.7%. Two themes carry most of the marks: infection presents differently, and most positive urine cultures should not be treated.

Atypical presentation

The febrile response is blunted with age, so a normal temperature does not exclude infection. In long-term care the thresholds come from a document worth naming, because a stem may name it: the revised McGeer surveillance criteria (Stone et al., Infect Control Hosp Epidemiol 2012;33(10):965–977). Fever is a single oral temperature above 37.8°C, or repeated oral readings above 37.2°C, or a rise of more than 1.1°C above the patient's own baseline — the last being the point, because the baseline is often low.

Presentation is frequently through one of the geriatric syndromes instead: delirium, a fall, functional decline, anorexia, incontinence that is new, or simply “off legs”. Hypothermia and a normal white count are consistent with severe sepsis in this group, and qSOFA is insensitive here.

Asymptomatic bacteriuria — the single highest-yield item

Exam pearl

Confusion plus a positive urine culture is not a urinary tract infection. Treating it is the commonest antibiotic error in geriatrics.

Do not screen for it and do not treat it, with two exceptions: pregnancy, and before a urological procedure expected to breach the mucosa. Treating it does not prevent symptomatic infection, does not improve mortality or function, and does cause C. difficile and resistance. STOPP I8 states it outright.

  • Pyuria is not infection. It is near-universal in bacteriuric older adults and tells you nothing about whether to treat
  • Catheterised patients are bacteriuric by definition within days. A culture from a long-standing catheter answers a question you should not be asking
  • Cloudy or malodorous urine is not an indication. Neither is a positive dipstick in an asymptomatic patient
  • The hard case: a patient with dementia, delirium, and a positive culture but no localising urinary symptoms. Delirium alone does not establish UTI. Evaluate for other causes first; treat empirically only if the patient is systemically unwell or no alternative explanation emerges. This is what the Loeb and McGeer minimum criteria exist to discipline

Pneumonia

Distinguish community-acquired from aspiration, which is the one the geriatric vignette is usually describing: dysphagia after stroke, Parkinson's disease, advanced dementia, sedating drugs, poor dentition. Severity scores such as CURB-65 were not built for frailty and tend to understate risk in this group. The healthcare-associated pneumonia (HCAP) category has been abandoned — it drove broad-spectrum overtreatment without benefit. Assess swallowing before the first oral dose in anyone with a plausible aspiration story.

C. difficile

  • Risk factors that are yours to control: antibiotic exposure — particularly fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, broad-spectrum cephalosporins — and proton pump inhibitors, which is why Beers caps scheduled PPI use at eight weeks
  • Treatment has moved: oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin are first-line; metronidazole is no longer preferred except where neither is available
  • Do not test formed stool, and do not re-test to prove cure — carriage persists
  • Recurrent disease is where faecal microbiota transplantation and bezlotoxumab enter

The rest of the ground

  • Skin and soft tissue: cellulitis is over-diagnosed — venous stasis, lipodermato- sclerosis and dependent oedema mimic it, and bilateral lower-limb “cellulitis” is usually neither. Pressure ulcers are colonised by definition; infection is a clinical diagnosis, and a swab of an open ulcer is not one. Suspect underlying osteomyelitis when an ulcer probes to bone
  • Herpes zoster and post-herpetic neuralgia — hence the START criterion for zoster vaccination, and the topical lidocaine patch for established post-herpetic pain
  • Endocarditis presents as weight loss, anaemia and confusion rather than fever and murmur; degenerative valve disease and intracardiac devices raise the base rate
  • Tuberculosis reactivates with age and immunosenescence, and presents non-specifically. Relevant to the Israeli population mix
  • Antimicrobial dosing by renal function — cross-reference Beers Table 6 and STOPP Section E. Nitrofurantoin is the criterion the two tools disagree about; ciprofloxacin needs reduction under 30 and carries CNS effects, tendon rupture and QTc prolongation; trimethoprim- sulfamethoxazole causes hyperkalaemia with an ACE inhibitor, ARB or ARNI
  • Vaccination is a START section in its own right: influenza annually, pneumococcal at least once, varicella-zoster, SARS-CoV-2

The Israeli layer

Local resistance patterns drive empirical choice and differ from the American texts — ESBL-producing Enterobacterales are common in Israeli long-term care, which changes what “empirical cover for urosepsis” means. Use the institutional antimicrobial guidelines (at SZMC, the DAG guidelines) over a textbook regimen. Influenza and pneumococcal vaccines are covered from 65.

Two things that are not what they look like

  • Bilateral “cellulitis” is almost never cellulitis. Bilateral erythema is venous stasis dermatitis, lymphoedema or contact dermatitis; cellulitis is unilateral, tender and acute. This is the commonest infectious-disease misdiagnosis on the general ward
  • A swollen, red, warm calf in a patient who has been in bed is a deep vein thrombosis until imaged. Cellulitis and DVT are treated in opposite directions, and the one that kills is the one without the fever

Herpes zoster

Incidence and severity both rise with age, as does post-herpetic neuralgia. Antivirals within 72 hours of rash onset reduce acute pain and shorten the course; they reduce but do not abolish the neuralgia. For established post-herpetic neuralgia the options are a gabapentinoid, a tricyclic (with the anticholinergic cost, so nortriptyline over amitriptyline), and the topical 5% lidocaine patch, which is START K2 for localised neuropathic pain. The recombinant zoster vaccine is the one that works in this age group, is not live, and is a START criterion.

Hazzard ch 43, p633 — 5 q, in all four sittings · Lord & Menant. Tables 43-1, 43-2 and 43-3 read from the page.

Rank 6, 3.7%. It is also the syndrome that most other topics feed into — medication review, cognition, vision, sarcopenia and bone health all arrive here. The chapter is written by two balance physiologists, and it reads that way: falls are what happens when balance control fails, and everything else is a route to that failure.

What a fall is, and how big the problem is

Ch 43 opens with the WHO definition — an event which results in a person coming to rest inadvertently on the ground or floor or other lower level — and it is the definition a stem will use. It says nothing about cause, so a syncopal collapse, a trip on a kerb and a slow slide off a chair are all falls; and it says nothing about injury, so the fall that hurt nobody still counts and still predicts the next one. The incidence figures come straight from the first paragraph and from the Key Clinical Points, which is where this paper draws from.

SettingAnnual fall incidence
Community, 65 and over32–40%
Community, beyond 7540–50%
Residential aged care (RACF)30–56%
General hospital2%
Acute hospital geriatric ward27%

The pattern to understand rather than memorise: the rate rises with age and with the frailty of the setting. The hospital pair is the counter-intuitive one and the one to hold — 27% on an acute geriatric ward against 2% in a general hospital. The general-hospital figure is diluted by every young surgical and obstetric patient in the denominator; the geriatric-ward figure is what happens when delirium, new drugs, unfamiliar rooms and weak legs are concentrated in one place. Your ward is the highest-incidence setting in the chapter, and a stem contrasting settings is asking whether you know that.

Most falls do not cause serious harm — 37–56% cause a minor injury and 10–15% a major one — but because falls are so common, the small injurious fraction adds up to falls being the leading cause of injury-related hospitalisation in people 65 and over, 14% of emergency admissions and 4% of all hospital admissions in that age group. The chapter is explicit that a fall without physical injury still has serious consequences: significant fear of falling, which leads to reduced mobility and frailty through the avoidance of daily activities, and falls are a key predisposing factor for needing institutional care.

Why older people fall: the balance system, and what erodes it

The chapter's organising idea is that staying upright needs the continuous integration of sensory information about where the body is (vision, the vestibular system, peripheral sensation from the feet), central processing to work out what to do about it, and a motor system fast and strong enough to do it. Any of these can be damaged by a specific disease or worn down by ageing itself, and older people usually have several marginal at once. That is why a fall is a symptom, not a diagnosis; why the causes are typically multiple and additive in the same patient; and why single-factor fixes disappoint in the frailest.

Vision. It supplies a continually updated reference frame for where the body is relative to the surroundings. The two components that matter for falls are contrast sensitivity and depth perception — not acuity as such — because they are what let you see a kerb edge or a pavement misalignment. Table 43-1 rates contrast sensitivity strong evidence and acuity only moderate.

Muscle strength and reaction time. Reduced knee extension strength raises fall risk in large community studies; in residential care, knee extension and ankle dorsiflexor weakness are the major risk factors. Strength is what corrects a perturbation once it is sensed; reaction time is how quickly the correction starts, and both are strong-evidence factors.

Gait. The older gait is slower, with shorter steps, more step-time variability, a wider base and more time in double support. Some of this is adaptation for safety, but these patterns still predict falls, and high-risk older people are worse at adapting gait on short notice to an obstacle, at recovering from a trip or slip, and at controlling the accelerations of the trunk and head while walking, which unsettles the gaze.

Cognition. Walking is not fully automatic in old age; it draws on attention and executive function. A substantial fraction of residential-care residents cannot answer a simple question while continuing to walk, and those who cannot are at higher risk. Fallers do badly on tests of executive function and attention, and imaging during stepping shows increased reliance on the prefrontal cortex with task complexity, with older people showing neural inefficiency — more cortical activity for no better performance. This is the mechanism behind the dual-task stems and behind cognitive impairment undermining every intervention that requires remembering to do something.

Fear and mood. Fear of falling and depression are both strong-evidence risk factors. They restrict daily activity and pastimes, which leads to inactivity and social isolation, and high fear or generalised anxiety produces inadequate postural strategies — excessive stiffening in threatening conditions such as standing at height. Fear, in other words, is not just a consequence of falling; it changes the way the person stands.

Environment. Extrinsic factors are involved in 35–45% of injurious falls. The chapter's point is the interaction: a person with good physical ability copes with most hazards but can still fall on an icy footpath, and a person with very poor ability falls in a hazard-free room. Depending on the population, a quarter to a half of falls occur away from home, where stairs, slips and trips, and temporary unanticipated hazards are more often involved; a fall on stairs doubles the risk of injury.

The risk factors, graded — Table 43-1

The table is a stem-writer's list, because each row carries a strength-of-evidence grade and the surprises are examinable. The strong-evidence (***) rows are the ones to know cold; the rows that are weaker than you would expect are the ones the committee has asked about.

DomainRisk factors, graded — *** strong · ** moderate · * weak · – none
Psychosocial and demographic*** advanced age · history of falls · ADL limitations · ** female gender · living alone · inactivity · – Alcohol consumption
Medical*** stroke · Parkinson disease · dementia · ** incontinence · acute illness · arthritis · foot problems · dizziness · * vestibular disorders · * orthostatic hypotension
Medication*** psychoactive medication · 4 or more medications · ** antihypertensive use (acute effects) · – NSAIDs
Balance and mobility*** inadequate responses to perturbation · slow voluntary stepping · impaired gait and mobility · impaired standing up · impaired transfers · ** impaired stability standing, leaning and reaching
Sensory and neuromuscular*** visual contrast sensitivity · reduced peripheral sensation · muscle weakness · poor reaction time · ** visual acuity · visual field loss · * reduced vestibular function
Neuropsychological*** impaired cognition · depression · fear of falling
Environmental** home hazards · * poor footwear · * inappropriate spectacles · – external hazards

Three rows are traps. Orthostatic hypotension and vestibular disorders are commonly thought to be strong fall-risk factors; the chapter says the community cohorts have not found them to be, though they may matter in clinical populations — its example is orthostatic hypotension in Parkinson disease. Alcohol has not been shown to be a fall-risk factor in several large cohorts; the chapter suspects under-reporting and selection bias rather than safety, notes that long-term heavy intake causes osteoporosis, cerebellar atrophy and neuropathy, and that traumatic brain injury is twice as prevalent among fall presentations with an indication of alcohol use. And NSAIDs, in the most recent comprehensive review, do not raise fall risk in adjusted analysis.

Two demographic points are worth a line. Women fall more than men in the community — attributed to living alone, being underweight, more psychotropic use and less muscle strength, and they fracture more because of osteoporosis — but in hospitals and institutions the rates are similar, or higher in men. And being physically active does not always prevent falls, because active people are exposed to more fall-risk situations and frail people starting exercise overestimate their balance early on; the chapter's answer is that exposure risk is outweighed by the gains in function and independence.

Medications, in the chapter's own terms

The consistent association is with psychoactive medication — benzodiazepines, antidepressants, antipsychotics — and with multiple medication use. Psychoactive drugs carry a two- to threefold increase in falls and a twofold increase in hip fracture. Two points the committee could turn into a stem:

  • Antihypertensives must be examined by class, not lumped. Some classes — the chapter names angiotensin-system blockers — appear protective against falls, mechanism unclear. What raises risk is the 24 hours after starting an antihypertensive or changing its dose: an acute effect, hence the “acute effects” grading in Table 43-1.
  • The FRID list used on the ward is STOPP Section K in full — benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, antipsychotics, antidepressants, antiepileptics, opioids, first-generation antihistamines, vasodilators with a postural drop, alpha blockers, centrally-acting antihypertensives, antimuscarinics — and Beers Table 3 adds anticholinergics as a class, new in 2023. That list is from the prescribing tools, not from ch 43, which sticks to the psychoactive classes.

Screening and assessment

The chapter's screen is simpler than the guideline one you may know. Ask about falls in the past 12 months and assess balance and mobility; previous falls are among the strongest predictors of falling again in the following year, so every older person should be asked. (The three-question screen used in practice — fallen in the past year, feel unsteady, worry about falling — comes from the CDC STEADI and World Falls Guidelines, not from ch 43; a single yes triggers assessment.) Whoever screens positive — a fall in the past year and poor performance on a simple balance or gait test — gets a full assessment to build an individualised care plan, using either a multifactorial tool covering the range of risk factors or functional mobility assessments of vision, strength, coordination, balance and gait.

The setting changes the rule. In hospital, NICE says patients aged 65 and over, and those aged 50–64 with a predisposing condition such as recent stroke, are assumed to be at risk and go straight to multifactorial assessment, targeting what can be fixed during the stay: postural instability, cognition, vision, continence, medications. In residential care most residents are at risk, so it is pragmatic to skip screening and assess everyone regularly; the CaHFRiS screen (MMSE below 17, impulsivity, reduced standing balance, reliance on a frame, a fall in the previous year, antidepressants or hypnotics/anxiolytics) takes six-month fall probability from zero with no factors to 100% with six or more, and doubles as a list of things to fix.

The bedside measures — Table 43-2, and what each one tests

Best-practice guidelines recommend the Timed Up and Go — rise from a chair, walk 3 m at normal pace with the usual aid, turn, return, sit — as the screen for who needs a fuller balance and gait assessment, recording the quality of the walk and transfers as well as the time. But the chapter then reports a systematic review of 25 studies finding its predictive value for falls in community-dwellers limited, with no cut-point that could be recommended. The alternatives it endorses as simple and predictive are the Alternate Step Test, the Sit to Stand Test and the SPPB.

TestWhat it isThreshold
Timed Up and GoChair, 3 m, turn, back, sit; usual aid; record quality toonone recommended by ch 43; 12 s (STEADI convention)
Alternate Step TestAlternately place left and right foot on an 18-cm step, eight steps, as fast as possible>10 s impaired
Sit to Stand TestFive chair rises as fast as possible>12 s impaired
SPPBStanding balance, chair rise, gait; each 0–4total 0–12 (ch 43 gives no cut-point)
Gait speedUsual pace over a short course<0.8 m/s impaired; <0.6 m/s unlikely to cross a road safely (ch 42 / sarcopenia, not ch 43)

The TUG cut-point is a convention, and the exam's own textbook says so. Twelve seconds is what most services use. On a stem sourced to Hazzard, a slow TUG triggers assessment; it does not establish risk. If the stem wants a test with a number attached, the chapter's numbers are the Alternate Step Test over 10 seconds and five sit-to-stands over 12.

What works: the single interventions, as listed in Key Clinical Point 4

Exam pearl

If the stem lists four drugs and one recent fall, the answer is still stopping one, not adding one — but know what ch 43 actually says: withdrawal trials did not reduce falls, so the evidence-based move is not starting the psychoactive drug in the first place. An Epley for BPPV and the right walking aid remain the interventions that work the same day.

The chapter's own list of single interventions proven in RCTs is the list to reproduce: exercise, enhanced podiatry, occupational-therapy home interventions, expedited cataract extraction, single-lens glasses for regular multifocal wearers, cardiac pacing for carotid sinus hypersensitivity, and vitamin D in people with low levels living in residential care. Each has a figure and a caveat.

Exercise has the strongest evidence, and the reason is mechanical: what stops a stumble becoming a fall is a fast, strong corrective step, and that is trainable. Across 64 RCTs, community-dwellers allocated to well-designed programmes had 23% fewer falls. The effect is larger with a high challenge to balance and three or more hours a week; it holds at 75 and older, in groups or individually, delivered by a health professional or a trained leader. Walking alone is not balance training. Programmes aimed specifically at rapid stepping — the key balance-recovery response — cut falls by 52% in a meta-analysis of seven RCTs. Table 43-3's four exemplars are individually prescribed home exercise three times a week (tandem stance, heel and toe walking, stepping over objects, chair rises, stair climbing, ankle-weight strengthening plus walking — the Otago pattern), the LiFE programme (balance and strength folded into daily activity rather than a set of exercises), a hybrid group-plus-home programme, and tai chi. Exergames on step mats or balance boards match traditional exercise on risk factors; whether they prevent falls is still under study.

The caveat is the examinable part. Exercise alone works in Parkinson disease and cognitive impairment but not in long-term stroke survivors or people recently discharged from hospital — one home-based programme after discharge increased falls by 43%. In those groups it has to sit inside a multifactorial plan. In subacute hospitals three RCTs show balance and mobility training prevents falls; in acute hospitals the effect of exercise alone is not known. In residential care the single-intervention evidence is mixed, but twice-weekly progressive resistance and balance training for 25 weeks (Sunbeam) cut falls by 55%, and a multifaceted programme with staff training, resident education, environmental changes, hip protectors and twice-weekly group exercise cut them by 45%. The 2023 committee answer to “single most effective” was exercise.

Vision. Cataract surgery for the first eye cut falls by 34%; the second eye by 32%, not significant. A cohort study adds that the benefit holds when the lens-power update after surgery is cautious (under ±0.75 dioptres). Simply updating glasses is a different story: one RCT of vision correction did not reduce falls and another increased them by about 50% — new lenses change the visual world the person has adapted to. The intervention that worked was single-lens distance glasses for people who regularly wore multifocals outdoors, with counselling to show how the lower lens blurs ground-level hazards: 40% fewer falls, fewer outdoor and injurious falls, in those who regularly went out. For uncorrectable low vision, a targeted home-safety programme cut falls by 41%.

Medication management. The chapter is uncomfortable reading for deprescribers. Early trials found withdrawing centrally acting drugs reduced falls, but a recent systematic review of five trials and 1309 participants found FRID withdrawal strategies did not significantly reduce falls (rate ratio 0.98, 95% CI 0.63–1.51) over 6–12 months. The chapter's conclusion is that the effort belongs in preventing initial uptake: benzodiazepines, Z-drugs and other psychotropics for insomnia should be avoided unless there is established dependence or a failed withdrawal, and insomnia managed non-pharmacologically. Vitamin D is the same shape: current mega-trials show supplementation does not improve physical function or prevent falls in community-dwelling older adults, even when deficient; it may reduce falls in residential care, which is the only setting the chapter endorses it for. Two sittings have asked exactly this (2023, 2024).

Home safety. Effective in high-risk groups and when delivered by an occupational therapist: 21% fewer falls overall, 39% in high-risk groups. The mechanism the chapter emphasises is not the grab rail but the behaviour change and safe-mobility advice that comes with it — successful programmes reduced outdoor falls too, which no rug removal can explain. Home modification also cuts fall injuries (26% overall in a cluster RCT of 842 households).

Feet and footwear. Multifaceted podiatry — orthoses or safe footwear, footwear advice, foot and ankle exercises, routine podiatry — cuts falls by 23% in community-dwellers, and multifactorial programmes that include podiatry by 27%. In residential care a pilot showed a small effect at 3 months that was gone by 6.

Psychological. CBT programmes as sole interventions have not prevented falls in people with fear of falling; adding CBT principles to a multifactorial programme with exercise may beat exercise alone. Depression, anxiety and sleep disorders are risk factors and CBT treats them, but that has not been tested as fall prevention.

Cardiovascular. Not all falls are balance failures. Recurrent falls with no obvious gait or balance problem earn a specialist assessment and specific investigation. Three studies of pacemakers for cardioinhibitory carotid sinus hypersensitivity — an abnormal haemodynamic response to carotid sinus massage, presenting as unexplained dizziness or syncope — show fewer drop attacks, less syncope and fewer falls. (The orthostatic-hypotension definition, 20/10 mmHg within 3 minutes, and its work-up belong with syncope, ch 45, not ch 43.)

Multifactorial interventions, and the two big trials that failed

A multifactorial intervention assesses the individual's risk factors and intervenes on the ones found; common components are medication adjustment, home safety, exercise and education. A Cochrane review of 43 community trials found 23% fewer falls — the same size as exercise alone. In residential care, where frailty and cognitive impairment are the norm, single interventions have generally not worked, and multifactorial programmes delivered by multidisciplinary teams with staff education are what reduce falls. In hospital, the successful combinations include supervised exercise and balance training, patient and staff education, medication review, vitamin D, environmental review, walking aids and hip protectors.

Then the two very large trials. Two recent general-practice trials tested multifactorial prevention on fractures (n = 5451) and on serious fall injuries (n = 9803) — Bhasin's STRIDE trial (NEJM 2020) is the one the further reading names, both implemented through existing services with existing resources — and neither reduced falls or fractures. The chapter's reading: multifactorial programmes are hard to implement, demand more of participants and clinicians than single interventions, and work when the interventions are delivered directly rather than by referral to routine services. A stem asking why a well-designed programme failed in practice is asking for that sentence.

After the fall

Exam pearl

“Found on the floor, cannot say how long” is a long lie until proven otherwise: check creatine kinase, creatinine, temperature and the sacrum before anything else.

Ch 43 is a prevention chapter and does not cover the post-fall work-up; what follows is ward practice, not chapter-sourced. The post-fall assessment is a search for the injuries that hide. Head injury on an anticoagulant needs a low threshold for CT, and a subdural can present weeks later. A long lie causes rhabdomyolysis from muscle compressed under body weight, acute kidney injury from the myoglobin, pressure injury over the same bony points, hypothermia and dehydration; ask how long they were down and whether they could get up. An occult fracture is the hip fracture with a normal radiograph: if the patient cannot weight-bear, MRI or CT; the pubic rami, vertebrae and proximal humerus break the same way. Then bone health: a fragility fracture is itself the indication for osteoporosis treatment, and START H4 covers it. And fear of falling, addressed explicitly, or the exercise programme will not be done.

Restraints, bedrails and alarms

Also not in ch 43, but examined. All three increase injury rather than reducing it. Physical restraints cause pressure injury, delirium, deconditioning, incontinence, aspiration and strangulation, and do not prevent falls, because a restrained patient who wants to get up still tries. Bedrails convert a low fall into a high one. Bed and chair alarms have been tested in randomised trials and do not reduce falls. What the chapter endorses in hospital is the multifactorial programme above — supervised exercise, education, medication review, environment, walking aids.

The Israeli layer

Inpatient falls-risk scoring is routine on Israeli wards and drives documentation as much as care. Community fall-prevention and physiotherapy run through the kupot; home adaptation and personal-care hours come through חוק ביטוח סיעוד via ביטוח לאומי, which is often the practical answer to “what would you actually arrange for this patient?”. Recurrent unexplained falls also bear on fitness to drive.

Hazzard ch 67–70, p1045 — low yield as a source; the law section carries the EOL questions

Rank 7, 3.1%. The one topic where the rest of this file stops applying — the Beers Criteria explicitly exclude hospice and end-of-life care, and saying so is often the answer.

Illness trajectories

Knowing which curve a patient is on tells you when to have the conversation.

TrajectoryShapeImplication
CancerFunction preserved, then a short steep decline over weeks to monthsPrognostication is relatively tractable; the window for planning is narrow but identifiable
Organ failure (heart failure, COPD)Sawtooth — acute exacerbations with incomplete recovery, any of which may be terminalDeath often arrives during an admission that looked like the previous three. Plan early, because there is no obvious moment
Frailty and dementiaSlow dwindle from a low baseline over yearsNo transition point at all. Recurrent infection, weight loss, pressure injury and aspiration are the terminal phase

The surprise question — would you be surprised if this patient died in the next twelve months? — is crude but outperforms clinician gestalt at identifying who needs planning. For dementia, functional staging (FAST) is the conventional instrument.

Symptom control

SymptomApproach
BreathlessnessTreat reversible causes, then low-dose opioids are the first-line pharmacological treatment — they reduce the sensation without hastening death at appropriate doses. Oxygen helps only if the patient is hypoxaemic; in non-hypoxaemic breathlessness it performs no better than air. A handheld fan to the face works through trigeminal afferents and is genuinely effective. Benzodiazepines are an adjunct for the anxiety component, not a primary treatment
PainSee the pain section. At end of life the ceiling comes off pure agonists, but watch for opioid-induced neurotoxicity — myoclonus, hyperalgesia, delirium — which is a signal to rotate or reduce, not to escalate
NauseaChoose by mechanism. Chemoreceptor trigger zone (drugs, uraemia, hypercalcaemia) → haloperidol. Gastric stasis → metoclopramide. Raised intracranial pressure → dexamethasone. Vestibular → antihistamine or antimuscarinic. Bowel obstruction → octreotide, steroid, antisecretory
ConstipationProphylactic laxative with every regular opioid, always. Methylnaltrexone for refractory opioid-induced constipation with a patent gut
Respiratory secretionsReposition, stop artificial hydration, explain to the family. Antimuscarinics — glycopyrronium is preferred because it does not cross the blood–brain barrier — have weak evidence and treat the family's distress more than the patient's
Terminal deliriumLook for the reversible causes first — retention, impaction, opioid toxicity, hypercalcaemia, drug withdrawal. If irreversible and distressing: low-dose haloperidol; midazolam for refractory agitation. Avoid restraints
Dry mouthMouth care is not a nursing afterthought — it is the commonest source of discomfort in the last days and the thing families can do

Artificial nutrition and hydration in advanced dementia

Exam pearl

Nothing a feeding tube is used for in advanced dementia survives contact with the evidence. The alternative is careful hand feeding, offered as a choice.

PEG feeding in advanced dementia does not prolong survival, does not prevent aspiration pneumonia, does not heal or prevent pressure ulcers, and does not improve function or comfort. It does add restraint, agitation, tube complications and loss of the pleasure of eating. The alternative is careful hand feeding — comfort feeding only — and it should be offered as an active choice, not as doing nothing. This is among the most reliably examined facts in geriatrics, and it collides directly with family and institutional expectation in Israel, which is part of why it is examined.

Deprescribing at the end of life

The Beers Criteria do not apply here, and preventive drugs whose time-to-benefit exceeds the remaining life expectancy are now pure burden.

  • Stop: statins (discontinuation in advanced illness is safe and improves quality of life), bisphosphonates, vitamins and supplements, antihypertensives as blood pressure falls, tight glycaemic control — relax targets and accept hyperglycaemia over hypoglycaemia, antiplatelets and anticoagulants once bleeding risk dominates, AChEIs and memantine when no longer meaningful
  • Keep and optimise: analgesia, antiemetics, laxatives, anxiolytics, antisecretories, and anything treating a symptom the patient can feel
  • Change the route: when swallowing fails, convert to subcutaneous rather than abandoning symptom control

Palliative sedation

Proportionate sedation for a refractory symptom — one that cannot be relieved by any tolerable means — titrated to comfort rather than to unconsciousness as an end in itself. The distinguishing feature from euthanasia is intent and proportionality: the aim is symptom relief, the dose is the lowest that achieves it, and death is not the goal or the measure of success. It requires multidisciplinary agreement, documentation, and family discussion. The doctrine of double effect covers giving opioids sufficient to relieve suffering even if a foreseen but unintended consequence is a shortened life.

The Israeli layer

See the ethics section for חוק החולה הנוטה למות in full — it is the legal frame for everything above, and the withholding versus withdrawing distinction it draws is stricter than the bioethics textbooks. הוספיס בית and community palliative services are covered through the kupot and are the usual route for dying at home; הוספיס אשפוזי exists but capacity is limited. Cultural and religious expectations around disclosure and around withdrawing treatment vary sharply across the populations you will treat in Jerusalem, and the examinable skill is asking rather than assuming.

Hazzard ch 47, p699 — 12 q, in all four sittings

Rank 8, 3.1%. Under-reported by patients, under-asked by doctors, and a direct driver of falls, pressure injury, social isolation and institutionalisation.

How common, and in whom

Defined as the complaint of any involuntary leakage of urine. Prevalence rises with age and with frailty, and is 1.3 to 2.0 times greater in older women than older men.

WomenMen
Any incontinence, community-dwelling~35%~22%
Daily incontinence, community-dwelling~12%~5%
Nursing home residentsapproaching 60%
  • Severity runs from rare dribbling to continuous leakage with concurrent faecal incontinence
  • Many older people who do not leak at all have bothersome lower urinary tract symptoms — urgency, frequency, nocturia — that affect their lives. Absence of leakage is not absence of a problem
  • Incontinence can be cured or greatly improved, particularly where mobility and cognition are adequate; and where it cannot, it can always be managed to improve comfort, reduce carer burden and cut the cost of care
  • Patients are embarrassed and often unaware treatment exists, so the clinician has to ask, periodically, and record it as a problem. That is a chapter instruction, not a courtesy

The neural control, asked in 2023: during filling, sympathetic tone closes the bladder neck and inhibits the parasympathetic supply, relaxing the dome, while somatic tone holds the pelvic floor; voluntary pelvic-floor contraction also inhibits the parasympathetic. For emptying, sympathetic and somatic tone fall and parasympathetic cholinergic impulses contract the detrusor. That is why an antimuscarinic quiets urgency and an alpha-blocker opens the outlet.

Reversible causes first — DIAPPERS

DDelirium — new incontinence in a confused patient is often the confusion, not the bladder
IInfection — symptomatic UTI only; asymptomatic bacteriuria does not cause chronic incontinence. One nuance from ch 47: in an institutionalised patient with chronic stable incontinence, do not treat it. In a non-institutionalised patient being evaluated for the first time, the chapter considers it reasonable to eradicate the bacteriuria once and watch the effect on the incontinence. Narrower than “never treat”, and the version a stem sourced to this chapter will use
AAtrophic vaginitis and urethritis
PPharmaceuticals — diuretics, alpha blockers, anticholinergics causing retention with overflow, sedatives, opioids, calcium channel blockers
PPsychological — particularly depression
EExcess urine output — hyperglycaemia, hypercalcaemia, heart failure, peripheral oedema mobilising at night, excess caffeine or fluid
RRestricted mobility — the commonest cause of functional incontinence, and the one fixed by a commode rather than a drug
SStool impaction

The types, and how the vignette signals each

TypeMechanismSignal in the stem
UrgeDetrusor overactivitySudden urgency, moderate-to-large volume leak, nocturia, cannot reach the toilet in time
StressUrethral hypermobility or sphincter deficiencySmall-volume leak on cough, laugh, lift. Multiparous women; men after prostatectomy
MixedBothThe commonest picture in older women. Treat the more bothersome component first
OverflowOutlet obstruction or detrusor underactivityDribbling, hesitancy, poor stream, palpable bladder, high post-void residual. BPH, diabetic neuropathy, anticholinergics, opioids
FunctionalCannot reach or use the toiletNormal bladder, impaired mobility, cognition, vision or dexterity, or a bed rail in the way
DHICDetrusor hyperactivity with impaired contractilityUrgency and a raised residual in the same frail patient. The trap: an antimuscarinic worsens the retention half

Assessment

History with a bladder diary over three days — volumes, times, leaks, fluid intake — which is the single most informative investigation. Then urinalysis, post-void residual, a cough stress test with a full bladder, pelvic examination for atrophy and prolapse, and rectal examination for impaction and prostate. Urodynamics only when the diagnosis is unclear or surgery is contemplated.

Treatment

  • Behavioural measures are first-line for both urge and stress, and outperform drugs in trials. Pelvic floor muscle training with proper instruction; bladder retraining with progressively spaced voiding for urge; timed and prompted voiding for the cognitively impaired, which works through the carer rather than the patient; weight loss; caffeine reduction; treating constipation
  • Urge, pharmacological: the whole antimuscarinic class is a Beers PIM and STOPP flags it in dementia, glaucoma, constipation and BPH with a residual over 200 mL. β-3 agonists (mirabegron) are preferred on cognitive grounds — but STOPP flags mirabegron in labile or severe hypertension and lists it among the QTc-prolonging drugs, so it is not free
  • Refractory urge: intradetrusor onabotulinumtoxinA (with a risk of retention and the need to self-catheterise), percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, sacral neuromodulation
  • Stress: pelvic floor training, then pessary or surgery (midurethral sling). Duloxetine is for stress, not urge — STOPP I7 — and is avoided below eGFR 30
  • Atrophy-related: topical vaginal estrogen, which is also first-line prevention for recurrent UTI. Systemic oral or transdermal estrogen worsens incontinence and is a Beers avoid in women with incontinence of any type
  • Overflow from BPH: alpha-1 blocker, 5-alpha reductase inhibitor, or both — both are START criteria where prostatectomy is not appropriate. Prefer silodosin or tamsulosin; STOPP flags the less selective alpha blockers with orthostatic hypotension or syncope, and Beers bans doxazosin, prazosin and terazosin as antihypertensives outright
  • Catheters are for retention that cannot be managed otherwise, sacral wound healing, accurate output measurement in critical illness, and comfort at the end of life. Not for convenience, not for incontinence, not to save nursing time. Every catheter day adds bacteriuria, and a long-standing catheter makes urine culture uninterpretable

Two interaction traps. Beers Table 5 lists a non-selective alpha-1 blocker combined with a loop diuretic as an avoidable interaction in older women, precisely because it produces incontinence. And an anticholinergic given for urgency in a man with BPH, or in a patient on a cholinesterase inhibitor, is the classic cascade running in both directions at once.

Israeli practical layer: incontinence products are funded through the kupot subject to eligibility criteria, and the entitlement assessment is often what the family actually needs from the consultation. Severity of incontinence also feeds the ביטוח סיעוד dependency assessment.

The assessment, in order

  1. History that establishes the type — leak with cough or effort, leak preceded by urgency, constant dribble, or inability to reach the toilet — plus duration, volume, pad use, fluid and caffeine, bowels, and the drug list
  2. A bladder diary for three days: times, volumes, leaks and their triggers. It is the single most informative investigation in the chapter and it costs nothing
  3. Examination: abdominal for a palpable bladder, pelvic for atrophy, prolapse and pelvic floor contraction, rectal for tone, impaction and prostate, plus a neurological screen and a functional assessment — can they walk to the toilet, undress, and see it at night
  4. Urinalysis to exclude haematuria, glycosuria and symptomatic infection — not to hunt asymptomatic bacteriuria
  5. Post-void residual, because retention with overflow and DHIC both change the management completely. A cough stress test where stress incontinence is suspected

Urodynamics is not routine. It belongs where surgery is planned, where the diagnosis remains unclear after the above, or where empirical treatment has failed — and its findings in the frail often do not change what can actually be offered.

The post-void residual, in three numbers

  • Under 100 mL, in the absence of straining to void, reflects adequate emptying
  • Over 200 mL is abnormal. Between 100 and 200 is indeterminate and has to be interpreted against the patient rather than the number
  • Where catheterisation is being used to manage retention, the goal is to keep residual under about 300–400 mL
  • Measure it within a few minutes of a spontaneous void, or the number means nothing. Gross distension — 500 mL or more — should be detectable on examination

Two physiological numbers that make the diary interpretable: the first urge to void comes at 150–350 mL, and normal bladder capacity is 300–600 mL, with voiding every three to four hours while awake.

Drug doses, from ch 47 Table 47-12

AgentDose
Mirabegron25–50 mg daily — max 25 mg/day in renal impairment
Vibegron75 mg daily
Solifenacin5–10 mg daily
Darifenacin7.5–15 mg daily
Fesoterodine4–8 mg daily
Tolterodine1–2 mg BD, or 4 mg daily long-acting
Trospium20 mg BD, or 60 mg each morning
Oxybutynin, immediate release2.5–5 mg TDS — the Beers item; patch 3.9 mg twice weekly is gentler
Duloxetine30–60 mg daily
Tamsulosin · silodosin0.4–0.8 mg daily · 4–8 mg daily
Alfuzosin · doxazosin · terazosin10 mg nocte · 1–8 mg nocte · 1–10 mg nocte
Finasteride · dutasteride5 mg daily · 0.5 mg daily
Vaginal oestrogencream 0.5–1.0 g per application; ring every 3 months

Expect a 60–70% reduction in incontinence episodes from drug therapy in selected older adults — a reduction, not continence. And the signal worth weighing before you start: bladder antimuscarinic therapy is associated with a 50% relative increase in the odds of developing dementia, which is the argument for mirabegron.

The drugs, with their costs

AgentPlace in an older patient
Mirabegron (beta-3 agonist)Preferred for urgency on cognitive grounds — no anticholinergic burden. STOPP flags it in labile or severe hypertension and among the QTc-prolonging drugs
Antimuscarinics — oxybutynin, tolterodine, solifenacin, darifenacin, trospiumModest benefit, roughly one fewer leak a day. Immediate-release oxybutynin is the worst of them and is a Beers item; trospium and darifenacin cross the blood–brain barrier least. Dry mouth, constipation, retention, delirium, and a cumulative dementia signal with long exposure
Vaginal oestrogenAtrophy-related symptoms and recurrent UTI prevention. Systemic oestrogen worsens incontinence and is a Beers avoid — the route is the whole distinction
DuloxetineStress incontinence; nausea and hyponatraemia limit it here
Alpha blockers for male outflow symptomsEffective; orthostatic hypotension and falls, and STOPP names them as fall-risk drugs other than silodosin. 5-alpha-reductase inhibitors work slowly and shrink the gland — and halve the PSA within about six months, so double the measured value before deciding it is reassuring
DesmopressinBeers avoid for nocturia — hyponatraemia

Behavioural therapy, with the actual protocols

  • Pelvic floor exercises: three sets daily of 15 contractions, building from 3 seconds to 10 seconds each
  • Prompted voiding: prompt the patient to try to void up to three times, every two hours during the day. 25–40% of nursing home residents respond very well, and responders are identified by a three-day trial — so the trial is the test, not a guess
  • At night, do not prompt on a schedule. Check every hour or two and toilet only if the patient is found awake — waking someone to keep them dry costs more sleep than it saves laundry
  • The cough stress test: at a comfortably full bladder, about half capacity (200 mL). Immediate leakage is stress incontinence; delayed leakage, after about three seconds, suggests a cough-provoked bladder contraction instead

When drugs are not the answer

Exam pearl

The fastest fix for functional incontinence is a commode by the bed. If the stem mentions a walking frame and a toilet down the corridor, that is the finding.

  • Refractory urgency: intravesical botulinum toxin — effective, with a real rate of retention needing intermittent catheterisation, which must be a realistic option for that patient — percutaneous tibial nerve stimulation, or sacral neuromodulation
  • Stress incontinence: supervised pelvic floor training first and for at least three months; then a midurethral sling or urethral bulking, weighed against life expectancy and anaesthetic risk
  • Male outflow obstruction: medical therapy, then TURP or a minimally invasive alternative. Chronic retention with a rising creatinine is a urological referral, not a catheter and a review in six weeks
  • Containment done well is a legitimate goal in advanced dementia or at the end of life: the right absorbent product, skin barrier protection, a scheduled toileting routine, and a commode in the room. Incontinence-associated dermatitis is a separate diagnosis from a pressure injury and is treated with barriers, not repositioning

The drug list, which is where the fix usually is

Exam pearl

Urgency that began after a cholinesterase inhibitor was started is a prescribing cascade, not overactive bladder. Do not answer with an antimuscarinic.

Table 47-4 is cited three times in the recent sittings, alongside the reversible-causes table. Between them they say the same thing: before typing the incontinence, look at what the patient is taking.

Drug classHow it causes incontinence
DiureticsPolyuria, frequency, urgency — and the timing of the dose is usually the whole story
AnticholinergicsRetention with overflow, and stool impaction
Antidepressants, antipsychoticsAnticholinergic action plus sedation and, with antipsychotics, immobility
Sedative–hypnoticsSedation, delirium, immobility, urethral relaxation
OpioidsRetention, faecal impaction, sedation, delirium
Alpha blockersUrethral relaxation — stress incontinence in women
Alpha agonistsThe opposite: retention
Cholinesterase inhibitorsFrequency and urgency — the first half of the classic prescribing cascade
ACE inhibitorsCough, and therefore stress incontinence
Calcium-channel blockersRetention, and oedema causing nocturia
Gabapentinoids, glitazonesOedema causing nocturia
Alcohol · caffeinePolyuria, urgency, bladder irritation — and alcohol adds sedation and immobility

The chapter frames continence itself as a set of requirements, all of which must hold: a bladder that stores at low pressure and empties, an outlet that closes at rest and opens on command, the cognition to recognise and interpret the sensation, the mobility and dexterity to reach a toilet and undress, and the motivation and environment to do so. Incontinence is a failure of any one of them, which is why the drug list and the walking aid matter as much as the urology.

Mechanistically there are only two faults: failure to store — an overactive or poorly compliant bladder, or too little outflow resistance — and failure to empty — a poorly contractile bladder, or too much outflow resistance. Every type maps onto one or both, and one patient often has two at once.

Hazzard ch 73–79 — mostly deferred tier; ch 75 Valvular carries 5 q

Rank 9, 3.0%. Two examinable themes: it does not present the way the textbook says, and age alone is not a reason to withhold treatment.

Presentation

Dyspnoea is the commonest anginal equivalent in older adults — more common than chest pain in the very old. Other presentations: confusion or delirium, syncope or near-syncope, fatigue, weakness, epigastric or shoulder pain, nausea, a fall, or new heart failure. Silent infarction is more frequent with age and with diabetic neuropathy.

The diagnostic trap: troponin is chronically elevated in chronic kidney disease, heart failure, atrial fibrillation, sepsis and pulmonary embolism. In this population the absolute value is often abnormal at baseline, so interpret the delta across serial samples against the clinical picture, not the single number against the reference range.

Acute coronary syndrome: strategy

  • Older patients have more to gain in absolute terms because their event rate is higher — and more to lose, because their bleeding rate is higher too. That tension, not age, is the decision
  • An invasive strategy in NSTEMI reduces recurrent infarction and revascularisation; the mortality signal in the very old and frail is less clear and the evidence continues to evolve. Frailty, cognition, life expectancy and the patient's own goals should drive the choice, and a frailty assessment before catheterisation is the geriatrician's actual contribution
  • Radial access materially reduces access-site bleeding and is preferred
  • Contrast nephropathy risk rises with age and CKD — hydrate, minimise contrast volume, and hold nephrotoxins

Antithrombotics — where most of the iatrogenic harm happens

P2Y12 choicePrasugrel and ticagrelor both cause more major bleeding than clopidogrel, particularly from 75 onward — Beers Table 4 caution. If prasugrel is used from 75, consider the reduced 5 mg dose. Clopidogrel is often the right answer in the frail older patient
DAPT durationShorter durations are increasingly favoured at high bleeding risk; the duration is a bleeding-risk decision, not a default
Triple therapyAnticoagulant plus DAPT in a patient with AF and a stent should be as short as possible. STOPP flags antiplatelets added to an anticoagulant in chronic AF unless there is a stent or angiographically proven stenosis over 50%
GastroprotectionSTART F2: a PPI when starting low-dose aspirin in someone with prior ulcer or reflux oesophagitis
Dosing errorsExcess dosing of enoxaparin and glycoprotein IIb/IIIa inhibitors in older patients is a documented and preventable driver of major bleeding — because weight and renal function are both overestimated. Calculate, do not assume
Aspirin doseSTOPP C1 flags long-term aspirin above 100 mg/day; Beers treats aspirin above 325 mg/day as an NSAID. Neither supports a high maintenance dose

Secondary prevention, and what START demands

The omissions are as examinable as the excesses. START requires, in documented coronary disease: a statin unless end-of-life or moderate-to-severe frailty, an ACE inhibitor, a β-blocker for symptomatic disease, and antiplatelet therapy. Add cardiac rehabilitation, which is effective and systematically under-referred in this age group. Blood pressure and lipid targets are relaxed with frailty, not abandoned.

Where it collides with the rest of the syllabus

  • β-blocker with verapamil or diltiazem — STOPP B3, risk of complete heart block; and any rate-limiting drug with bradycardia under 50
  • Severe symptomatic aortic stenosis coexists often; STOPP B20 warns against antihypertensives there, and the answer to symptomatic severe AS is valve intervention, with TAVI having changed what is offerable at 85
  • Anaemia and CKD both worsen ischaemia and both complicate antithrombotic choice
  • Nitrates plus a PDE5 inhibitor — STOPP B14, cardiovascular collapse
  • Digoxin, amiodarone and dronedarone all carry Beers and STOPP restrictions; see the Alternatives section for the rate and rhythm control alternatives

Israeli layer: catheterisation is widely and rapidly available, which makes the restraint question — should this frail 92-year-old go to the lab — a live one rather than theoretical. שיקום לב is covered and under-used.

Atrial fibrillation and the anticoagulation decision

Exam pearl

A falls history is not a reason to withhold anticoagulation. The stroke you prevent is larger than the bleed you fear.

The commonest sustained arrhythmia in this population, frequently asymptomatic, and the stroke it causes is larger and more disabling than other strokes. Score with CHA2DS2-VASc — age 75 or over scores 2, age 65–74 scores 1, so essentially every geriatric patient reaches the treatment threshold on age alone. Anticoagulate at 2 or more in men, 3 or more in women.

  • A DOAC, not warfarin, unless there is a mechanical valve or moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis. Dose by the licensed criteria, not by instinct: apixaban is reduced when two of three are present — age 80 or over, weight 60 kg or less, creatinine 1.5 mg/dL or more. Under-dosing a DOAC to feel safer is common, is not safer, and loses the benefit
  • Aspirin is not an alternative. It provides little stroke protection in AF at nearly the same bleeding cost
  • Falls are not a contraindication. The modelling behind that statement is worth remembering: a patient would need to fall an implausible number of times a year for the haemorrhage risk to outweigh the stroke prevented. Recurrent head injury on anticoagulation is a real problem; a falls history on its own is not a reason to withhold
  • HAS-BLED identifies modifiable bleeding risk — blood pressure, alcohol, aspirin and NSAIDs alongside, labile INR — and is not a tool for declining treatment
  • Rate control is enough for most; beta-blocker first, digoxin as an adjunct with the Beers dose cap. Rhythm control for symptoms, and remember that amiodarone brings a thyroid, lung, liver and interaction burden that lasts for months after it is stopped

Hazzard ch 76 p1165 — 12 q across the three 8th-edition sittings

Split out of the cardiac block because the committee keeps returning to it: HFpEF pharmacology, device criteria, high-output failure and the newer drugs. Coronary disease, valves and the Beers/STOPP cardiac criteria stay in .

What it is in the old, and what precipitates it

  • More than half of older patients with heart failure have preserved ejection fraction; 70–80% of them are hypertensive, and cardiac amyloid is an increasingly recognised cause. Age-related diastolic dysfunction — impaired active relaxation and reduced compliance — explains the failure when nothing else is found; the 2024 vignette with a soft late-diastolic sound at the apex and pulmonary congestion wanted a relaxation problem, not contractility
  • High-output failure is overlooked: chronic anaemia, hyperthyroidism, thiamine deficiency, arteriovenous shunting (dialysis fistula, AV malformation), morbid obesity. Asked in 2024 with B1 as the answer
  • The commonest precipitant of decompensation is non-adherence to drugs or diet — up to two-thirds of exacerbations (64% in one study), with emotional and environmental factors behind 26% of readmissions. Cognitive impairment, depression, poor mobility and thin social support make complex regimens fail; the 2023 committee answer for “commonest cause of worsening” was non-adherence. Atypical presentations (Table 76-5) are often the only sign after 80
  • BNP is the single most useful test but rises with age (especially in women), renal impairment and anaemia, and is lower with obesity, so its specificity falls with age: over 500 pg/mL strongly suggests active failure; under 100 in a non-obese older adult makes it unlikely. Echocardiography for every new diagnosis, because HFrEF and HFpEF cannot be separated clinically

HFrEF drugs — the ones the exam has asked

AgentWhat ch 76 says
Sacubitril–valsartanPARADIGM-HF: 20% fewer cardiovascular deaths or HF admissions than enalapril, consistent below and above 75. More hypotension and angioedema, but less rise in creatinine and potassium than an ACE inhibitor — the 2024 answer. First line for stable HFrEF and after decompensation (PIONEER); 36-hour ACE-inhibitor washout; start low, 24/26 mg twice daily, unless converting from a high-dose ACEi/ARB
SGLT2 inhibitorsDAPA-HF and EMPEROR-Reduced in HFrEF with or without diabetes. In HFpEF, EMPEROR-Preserved (5,988 patients, EF over 40%, empagliflozin 10 mg): death or HF hospitalisation HR 0.79, driven by fewer admissions, consistent with and without diabetes — the 2024 HFpEF answer
Spironolactone / MRAsRALES: spironolactone 12.5–50 mg in NYHA III–IV on top of ACEi, digoxin and loop diuretic, benefit at least as great in the old; EMPHASIS-HF for class II. Hyperkalaemia and gynaecomastia are the costs
Hydralazine–nitrateFor patients who cannot take an ACE inhibitor or ARB — the 2024 answer — and, after A-HeFT, approved in Black patients with NYHA II–IV. Hydralazine 12.5–25 mg three to four times daily with isosorbide dinitrate 10 mg; headache, hypotension, and hydralazine-induced lupus
CandesartanCHARM: ARB where ACEi is not tolerated, 30% reduction in the composite; 4–8 mg titrated to 32 mg
DigoxinNo benefit in HFpEF; in HFrEF a symptomatic drug, not a survival one — see 73–79 Cardiac for the dose and toxicity rules

Devices — the criteria, and the age caveats

  • ICD: primary prevention in NYHA II–III HFrEF with EF 35% or less, and secondary prevention after resuscitated ventricular arrhythmia. Guidelines ignore age, but few trial patients were over 75, benefit declines with age from competing mortality, life expectancy under 12–18 months means no benefit, and the over-80s have twice the implantation complications. Shared decision; and agree in advance when the shocks are switched off, and whether the generator gets replaced
  • CRT: improves symptoms, exercise tolerance, quality of life and survival — including in octogenarians — where ICDs only prevent sudden death. Criteria: NYHA II–IV HFrEF, EF 35% or less, QRS 150 ms or more; greatest benefit with left bundle branch block (present in 20–30% of HFrEF) and in women. The 2024 answer was “HFrEF, NYHA III”; the QRS distractor was 120
  • MitraClip (COAPT): fewer admissions and deaths in HFrEF with severe secondary mitral regurgitation despite maximal therapy — but only after optimisation, because much regurgitation is load-dependent and disappears with diuretics and afterload reduction. Heart-team decision with a geriatrician on it
  • LVAD: the recurring stem (2020, 2025) is the woman in her seventies with EF 20% and six admissions in six months — the keyed answer is the left-ventricular assist device as the intervention that can both lengthen and improve life, not inotropes, not transplant, and not palliation alone

HFpEF: what actually has evidence

Treatment begins with aggressive blood-pressure control — SPRINT-derived targets under 130/90 for ambulatory community-dwelling older adults, personalised for falls risk — and diuretics for congestion. Beta-blockers may worsen the chronotropic incompetence that limits exercise in HFpEF; nitrates are not recommended after a negative crossover trial; digoxin is not beneficial; ACE inhibitors and ARBs are reasonable, especially with hypertension; spironolactone (TOPCAT) may help and the FDA has considered it. The one drug with a positive outcome trial is the SGLT2 inhibitor above.

The non-drug programme, which is where the readmissions are

Disease-management programmes in a meta-analysis of 33 trials: heart-failure readmissions down 42%, all-cause readmissions down 24%, mortality down 20%. In one cohort of over-70s, 47% were readmitted within 90 days, and the reasons were social: non-adherence (drugs 15%, diet 18%), inadequate support (21%), poor discharge planning (15%), inadequate follow-up (20%), and patients not seeking help when symptoms returned (20%). Influenza and pneumococcal vaccination reduce the pneumonia and viral decompensations, and influenza vaccination is associated with lower mortality — the 2023 committee answer for HFrEF (Table 76-8). Exercise training is safe and improves function in both HFrEF and HFpEF (Tables 76-9, 76-10). Heart failure often worsens after discharge — ch 53's warning for the hip-fracture patient sent to subacute care — and the geriatrician's job is the transition.

Hazzard ch 68, p1055 — 11 q, three of four sittings

Rank 10, 2.9%. Older adults are systematically under-treated for pain, and patients with dementia most of all — because they do not report it, not because they do not feel it.

Definitions and scale, before anything else

Nociceptive pain comes from stimulation of pain receptors by tissue injury, inflammation or mechanical distortion — trauma, burns, infection, arthritis, ischaemia, tissue distortion — and responds to analgesics; neuropathic pain is a lesion or disease of the somatosensory system, peripheral or central. The 2026 pairing question keyed angina as nociceptive.

  • Acute pain runs with the tissue healing, roughly 3 months or less. Chronic pain persists or recurs beyond 3 months, and the IASP updated its chronic-pain classification in 2019 — that date and that threshold are both examinable
  • Chronic pain in older adults: 25–75%, and higher in residential care
  • High-impact chronic pain — pain limiting life or work activities on most days — affects 11% at 65–84 and 16% at 85 and over
  • Neuropathic pain affects 7–10% of the population
  • Complexity is the norm: most older adults with chronic pain report multisite pain, and a majority report more than one type of pain at once

Assessment, including in the non-verbal patient

Self-report remains the standard wherever it is obtainable. Ch 68 asks for simple, transparent questions — “does this hurt?” beats “how are you doing?” — and points out that in chronic pain the impact on mobility, mood and fatigue is more meaningful than the intensity score. Unidimensional scales are Table 68-3, multidimensional Table 68-4. Where the patient cannot self-report, ask the family or carer and use a nonverbal observational instrument — PAINAD (the one the committee asked for, from Table 68-3), Abbey or DOLOPLUS-2 — which score breathing, vocalisation, facial expression, body language and consolability.

Agitation in advanced dementia is pain until proven otherwise. An analgesic trial is a legitimate diagnostic step and frequently more effective than the antipsychotic that would otherwise be reached for. This connects the pain, dementia and BPSD questions into one answer.

The ladder, adapted

  • Paracetamol first-line for persistent musculoskeletal pain. STOPP L6 caps it at under 3 g/24h where BMI is under 18 or there is chronic liver disease
  • NSAIDs: avoid chronic oral use — GI bleeding, AKI, hypertension, heart failure decompensation — and avoid entirely below CrCl 30 (Beers) or eGFR 50 (STOPP). Topical NSAIDs are the geriatric answer for localised osteoarthritis, with a far better systemic profile
  • Avoid the combinations: NSAID with an anticoagulant or antiplatelet; NSAID with a corticosteroid; two NSAIDs

Starting doses, from ch 68 Table 68-6

The chapter gives starting doses for an opioid-naive older adult. These are starting points to titrate from, not targets.

DrugStarting dose
Morphine, immediate release10 mg every 4–6 h
Morphine, extended releasetablet 15 mg BD–TDS; capsule 30 mg daily or 15 mg BD
Oxycodone, immediate release5–10 mg every 4–6 h
Oxycodone, extended release10 mg BD (capsule 9 mg BD)
Hydromorphone1–2 mg every 3–4 h
Oxymorphone, immediate release5–10 mg every 4–6 h
Hydrocodone–paracetamol2.5–10 mg every 4–6 h
Codeine15–60 mg every 4 h PRN; max 360 mg/day
Tramadol25–50 mg every 4–6 h; max 300 mg/day
Tapentadol50 mg every 4–6 h
Methadone2.5–10 mg daily
Fentanyl, transdermal25 microgram patch, 72-hourly — never in the opioid-naive; the dose follows the previous 24-hour MME
Buprenorphinebuccal 75–150 mcg BD (max 900 BD); patch 5 mcg/h weekly (max 20); IV/IM 0.3 mg 6-hourly

The two MME numbers. Evaluate benefits and risks carefully beyond 50 morphine milligram equivalents a day, and avoid exceeding 90 MME/day. Follow up within 1 to 4 weeks of starting an opioid, then at least every 3 months; a bowel regimen, a falls assessment and the prescription-monitoring database go with the first script. Opioid overdose deaths in the over-65s rose 7.7% in a single year, 2013 to 2014, and older adults with opioid use disorder die more than younger ones.

Opioid-induced hyperalgesia — asked in 2025. A sensitisation in which the opioid itself raises pain sensitivity: pain rises with dose, and allodynia spreads beyond the original site. Risk is highest with a history of opioid use disorder, chronic-pain patients on opioids, and high doses of potent opioids — not the opioid-naive patient being titrated, which is the distractor. It is distinguished from tolerance by that dose–pain paradox. Management is gradual reduction or withdrawal, non-opioid co-analgesia, buprenorphine, or an NMDA antagonist.

Opioids

Exam pearl

Agitation in advanced dementia is pain until proven otherwise, and a scheduled analgesic trial is a diagnostic step, not a concession.

AgentWhat to know
Morphine(The renal pharmacology in this table is standard teaching and Beers, not spelled out in ch 68, which says only that renally cleared drugs and metabolites accumulate.) Active metabolites M3G and M6G accumulate in renal impairment, causing sedation, myoclonus, hyperalgesia and delirium. Avoid or reduce substantially in CKD
Oxycodone, hydromorphoneGenerally better tolerated than morphine in renal impairment, though not risk-free
Fentanyl, buprenorphineThe usual choices in significant renal impairment. Transdermal fentanyl is not for opioid-naive patients and not for titrating acute pain — slow onset, long offset, and fever or an external heat source increases absorption
Codeine, tramadolBoth are CYP2D6 prodrugs with unpredictable conversion. Tramadol additionally: serotonergic (serotonin syndrome with SSRIs, SNRIs), lowers the seizure threshold, and causes hyponatraemia and SIADH — added to the Beers caution list in 2023. Below CrCl 30, reduce the immediate release and avoid the extended release
Meperidine (pethidine)Avoid. Normeperidine is neurotoxic and accumulates; ineffective at usual oral doses
  • Start low, go slow, but do start. Roughly 25–50% of the usual adult starting dose, with unhurried titration and a short-acting agent for breakthrough
  • Every regular opioid gets a laxative — STOPP L2 — and an antiemetic for the first days if needed
  • Do not use a long-acting opioid without short-acting cover for breakthrough (STOPP L3); do not use a strong opioid first-line for mild pain (STOPP L1); do not use long-term opioids for osteoarthritis (STOPP H9)
  • Beers Table 5 combinations to avoid: opioid with a benzodiazepine, and opioid with a gabapentinoid — both risk profound sedation and respiratory depression. Opioids were added to the delirium-precipitant list in 2023, and appear in the falls criteria of both tools

Co-analgesic doses, from Table 68-8

AgentDose
Gabapentin100 mg at night, up to 900 mg TDS
Pregabalin25 mg at night, up to 75 mg TDS
Duloxetine20–60 mg daily
Venlafaxine37.5–75 mg daily — less sedating than a TCA
Amitriptyline or nortriptyline10–50 mg at night — both Beers items; nortriptyline is the lesser evil
Carbamazepine200–400 mg BD, max 1200 mg/day. HLA-B*1502 and HLA-A*3101 (South Asian ancestry) predict Stevens–Johnson; sodium, drug level, blood count, liver and renal tests at initiation; a potent CYP450 inducer; have a carer watch for sedation at the start
Oxcarbazepine150–300 mg BD, max 2400 mg/day — watch the sodium

Neuropathic pain

  • Gabapentinoids — effective but sedating and ataxic; reduce the dose below eGFR 60 for both gabapentin and pregabalin, and never alongside an opioid
  • Duloxetine — useful, but avoid below eGFR 30 and note the hyponatraemia caution
  • TCAs — effective and essentially unusable here: strongly anticholinergic, orthostatic, cardiotoxic. Beers avoid, STOPP D1
  • Topical 5% lidocaine patch — START K2 for localised neuropathic pain such as post-herpetic neuralgia. STOPP L4 rejects the same patch for chronic osteoarthritis pain, which is exactly the kind of paired criterion a stem is built on
  • Capsaicin and other topicals; diclofenac 1% gel is the one ch 68 names as the safe NSAID form. The methyl-salicylate one-week caution is label advice, not in the chapter
  • Gabapentinoids for non-neuropathic pain lack evidence — STOPP L5

Paracetamol: two ceilings that are not the same

Ch 68 sets the maximum total daily dose at 4000 mg, falling to 2000–3000 mg with hepatic impairment or a history of alcohol use. STOPP L6 flags paracetamol at 3 g/24 h or more where BMI is under 18 or there is chronic liver disease. The chapter gives a drug ceiling; STOPP gives a patient-specific flag. They do not conflict, and a stem may cite either.

Non-pharmacological, which is not an afterthought

Exercise therapy of any type, physical therapy, needling therapies, psychological approaches including CBT, heat and cold, and education. The Alternatives paper lists these ahead of drugs for chronic pain and makes function, not the pain score, the target of treatment.

Israeli layer: strong opioids require a special prescription form, which is a real friction on discharge planning and a common source of gaps in continuity. Pain clinics (מרפאות כאב) exist through the kupot with waiting times that matter for planning.

Ranks 11 and 12 combined, 5.6% — which makes this the second heaviest subject on the paper after polypharmacy, and the one where Israeli law diverges most from the international textbooks.

Capacity

Covered in the dementia section: decision-specific, time-specific, and defined by four abilities — understand, retain, weigh, communicate. Three additions that get examined on their own:

  • Capacity is presumed until demonstrated otherwise, and the demonstration must be specific to the decision at hand
  • Refusing recommended treatment is not evidence of incapacity. A capacitous patient may make a choice the team considers unwise
  • Fluctuating capacity obliges you to assess at the best moment, not the most convenient one, and to optimise the conditions — hearing aids, interpreter, time of day, absence of delirium

Surrogate decision-making

Exam pearl

A family member saying “we want everything done” is answered by asking what the patient would have wanted, not by agreeing or refusing.

Where capacity is absent, decisions follow, in order of preference: the patient's prior expressed wishes; then substituted judgement — what would this patient have chosen, which is a question about their values, not the surrogate's; then best interests, as a last resort. A common error in vignettes is a family member asserting their own preference; the correct move is to redirect to what the patient would have wanted.

Withholding versus withdrawing

In mainstream bioethics these are held to be morally equivalent — if it would be permissible not to start a treatment, it is permissible to stop it when it proves ineffective. Israeli law does not accept that equivalence. Know both positions and which one you are being asked about.

חוק החולה הנוטה למות — the Dying Patient Act, 2005

The governing statute, and the single most Israel-specific thing on this syllabus.

Who it coversA חולה נוטה למות — an incurable patient whose life expectancy is under six months. A separate, stricter category applies in the שלב סופי, the final stage, where several vital systems have failed and life expectancy is under two weeks
PresumptionThe law presumes a person wishes to go on living unless the contrary is proven to the standard the statute sets
WithholdingPermitted. Life-prolonging treatment need not be started — including resuscitation, dialysis, surgery, chemotherapy and ventilation
WithdrawingProhibited where the treatment is continuous. Discontinuing an already-running continuous treatment is treated differently from not starting it
The timer mechanismThe practical consequence of that distinction: continuous treatments can be converted to cyclical ones with a timer, so that continuation becomes an affirmative decision at each interval rather than withdrawal. This is a genuinely distinctive feature of Israeli practice
Symptom reliefPermitted, including where it may foreseeably shorten life, provided the intent is relief of suffering — the doctrine of double effect
Nutrition and hydrationTreated separately and more protectively than other interventions; the law is more restrictive here than most Western frameworks
Advance directivesWritten on the statutory form, lodged in the Ministry of Health registry, and valid for five years, renewable. A patient may also appoint a proxy
DisputesReferred to an institutional ethics committee; national-level questions go to the national committee
Euthanasia and assisted suicideIllegal. Active shortening of life is outside the statute entirely and is not a grey area

Verify the current wording and any amendments before you rely on a specific clause in an answer — this is a statute, not a guideline, and the detail is what is examined.

The other Israeli instruments

  • ייפוי כוח מתמשך — durable power of attorney, executed while the person has capacity, covering health, property or personal matters. Now the preferred route, and the thing to recommend at the time of a mild dementia diagnosis rather than later
  • אפוטרופסות — guardianship, court-appointed, restrictive, and increasingly a last resort. מקבל החלטות זמני and supported decision-making are the less restrictive alternatives the reformed law prefers
  • Mandatory reporting — suspected abuse or neglect of a helpless person carries a legal duty to report. This is a legal obligation, not a clinical judgement call
  • Fitness to drive — a defined medical reporting pathway through המכון הרפואי לבטיחות בדרכים

Communication, and what the stems actually test

  • Truth-telling. Western bioethics defaults to full disclosure to the patient; several communities you will treat expect disclosure to the family first. The examinable answer is to ask the patient how much they want to know and whom they want told, which respects autonomy without imposing a disclosure norm
  • Goals-of-care conversations should start from values and function, not from a menu of interventions. “Would you want CPR?” asked cold is a badly formed question
  • DNR is not do-not-treat. A resuscitation decision says nothing about antibiotics, admission, or surgery, and conflating them is a recognised error
  • Futility is contested territory: physiological futility is a medical judgement, while qualitative futility is a values judgement and cannot be declared unilaterally
  • Religious consultation is legitimate and often requested — rabbinic, and the equivalents in the Muslim and Christian communities. Facilitating it is part of the job; deferring the medical facts to it is not

Eight real sittings, every question with the committee's own answer key and its מראה מקום reference. This is the exam itself rather than anything written about it, and it is the best material in this file.
