Where the misses are

Grouped by chapter, from the cards you have marked missed. Four or five in one place is a chapter to re-read, not a set of cards to re-drill.

Hazzard ch 44, p643 — 6 questions across four sittings, and one of the nine that appear every time. The examinable core is what ageing does to sleep, what it does not do, and why almost every drug answer here is wrong.

What ageing actually changes

  • Less slow-wave sleep, more arousals, lower sleep efficiency
  • A phase advance — sleepy early, awake early. This is circadian, not insomnia
  • Sleep need falls little; the ability to consolidate it falls a lot

What is not normal ageing: daytime sleepiness heavy enough to impair function. That sends you looking for sleep apnoea, restless legs, nocturia, pain, depression or drugs — not to a hypnotic.

The vocabulary, before the picture

  • Sleep cycles roughly every 90 minutes through a fixed progression of stages
  • Two states: REM — brain activity resembling wake, rapid eye movements, complete loss of skeletal muscle tone, and the vivid dreaming people report on waking from it — and NREM, divided into N1, N2 and N3
  • N3 is slow-wave sleep. Arousal gets harder from N1 through N3, so N1 is light sleep and N3 deep sleep
  • Sleep efficiency is time actually asleep divided by time spent in bed. It falls with age, and it is the number that makes sense of the patient who is in bed ten hours for six hours of sleep
  • What changes with age: longer to fall asleep, more fragmentation, and less N3 from early adulthood onward — more markedly in men. Whether REM changes with age is less clear, which is the honest answer if a stem asks

Two framings from the chapter worth carrying: poor sleep in older adults is more closely associated with comorbidity than with chronological age, and healthy older adults actually show a lower propensity to fall asleep when offered naps — a lower sleep drive — even though unplanned napping is commoner. Sleepiness in an older patient is a finding, not an expectation.

The architecture, in one picture

Two clinical consequences. A patient who is in bed for ten hours to get six hours of sleep does not need a hypnotic — they need sleep restriction, which is the component of CBT-I that works and the one patients resist. And because the falls in slow-wave sleep and the rise in fragmentation happen to everyone, neither is by itself a disease; what makes it a disorder is daytime consequence.

Chronic insomnia

CBT-I is first-line, by a trained provider or digitally. Its active ingredients are sleep restriction and stimulus control — the two patients find hardest. Sleep hygiene alone is not effective for chronic insomnia and is the classic distractor.

If a drug is unavoidableStanding
Doxepin 3–6 mgSafety comparable to placebo at this dose; above 6 mg it becomes a strongly anticholinergic PIM
RamelteonMelatonin-receptor agonist, no dependence
DORAs — daridorexant, lemborexant, suvorexantShort-term, listed in the 2025 Alternatives paper
Trazodone, mirtazapine, melatoninInsufficient evidence — widely used, not supported
Prolonged-release melatonin 2 mg (Circadin)A regulatory split worth knowing here: in the US melatonin is an unregulated supplement, which is what the AGS statement above is about. In the EU and Israel, prolonged-release melatonin has held a marketing authorisation since 2007, indicated as monotherapy for short-term primary insomnia in patients aged 55 or over, 2 mg one to two hours before bed, for up to 13 weeks. Licensed is not the same as strongly evidenced — the effect sizes are modest — but a stem written locally may treat it as a legitimate option where the AGS paper would not
Benzodiazepines, Z-drugsBeers avoid. STOPP: two weeks or more for insomnia is a criterion in itself
Diphenhydramine and other first-generation antihistaminesAnticholinergic; tolerance to the sedation within days, none to the delirium risk

Obstructive sleep apnoea

Exam pearl

Nocturia plus new cognitive complaints plus refractory hypertension in an older man is sleep apnoea in disguise. Nobody in the vignette will mention snoring.

Prevalence rises with age and the presentation is less typical — nocturia, cognitive complaints, falls and refractory hypertension rather than a bed partner's complaint about snoring. STOP-BANG screens; polysomnography or home testing confirms; the apnoea–hypopnoea index grades it. CPAP remains the treatment and adherence, not age, is the limiting factor. Untreated OSA is a reversible contributor on every dementia workup list.

Restless legs and periodic limb movements

Exam pearl

Ferritin before dopamine. A normal haemoglobin does not exclude the iron deficiency that is driving the legs.

Diagnosis is clinical and five-part: an urge to move, worse at rest, relieved by movement, worse in the evening, and not better explained by something else. Check ferritin — ch 44 gives the numbers: oral iron when ferritin is under 75 µg/L, and IV iron in moderate-to-severe RLS with ferritin under 300 — a far higher bar than the anaemia threshold. Review the drugs that provoke it: antidepressants, antipsychotics, antihistamines, metoclopramide.

The examinable reversal. Dopamine agonists used to be first-line and are now avoided where possible because of augmentation — symptoms starting earlier in the day, spreading to the arms, and worsening on dose escalation. Alpha-2-delta ligands (gabapentin enacarbil, pregabalin) are preferred first, with their own sedation and falls cost.

REM sleep behaviour disorder

Loss of REM atonia — the patient acts out dreams, often violently. It is a strong prodromal marker of the synucleinopathies: Parkinson disease, dementia with Lewy bodies, multiple system atrophy, often by years. Manage the bedroom first — clear the bedside, lower the mattress, protect the partner. Melatonin is the usual first drug; clonazepam works but is a benzodiazepine in a patient who already has a falls and cognition problem coming.

Circadian and institutional sleep

Advanced sleep phase responds to timed bright light in the evening and to keeping the patient out of bed during the day. In long-term care the usual cause of broken sleep is the institution: night-time noise, light, observations and toileting rounds. Sundowning is an evening behavioural disturbance in dementia, not an insomnia diagnosis, and it is managed as behaviour — light, routine, activity, pain — not as a sleep disorder.

Sleep in hospital, which is where you will be asked about it

Inpatients are woken for observations, drugs and blood tests, in light and noise, on a ward with no daytime activity. The result is fragmented sleep, then a hypnotic, then delirium and a fall. The answer to the three-in-the-morning bleep is almost never a drug.

  • Cluster observations and bloods; stop the four-hourly set that nobody is acting on
  • Light and activity by day, dark and quiet at night; earplugs and eye masks have trial evidence in the intensive care unit
  • Warm drink, orientation, pain and bladder attended to; no caffeine after the afternoon
  • Review the drugs that fragment sleep: diuretics late, steroids late, beta-blockers with nightmares, SSRIs and SNRIs, donepezil, levodopa, theophylline, and alcohol, which shortens sleep latency and wrecks the second half of the night

A newly-started hypnotic in hospital is the drug most likely to still be on the discharge list for no reason — and once it is home, it will be there in a year.

Hazzard ch 55, p817 — 7 questions across four sittings, in every sitting. It is also the chapter with the highest density of numbers you either know or do not: FIM, Barthel, and the thresholds that decide where a patient goes after the acute bed.

The instruments

ScaleStructureWhat it measures
FIM18 items — 13 motor, 5 cognitive · each 1–7 · total 18–126Burden of care: how much another person must do. Admission score and the gain over the stay are what services are judged on
Barthel10 items · 0–100 in steps of 5Basic ADL independence. Ceiling effect — 100 does not mean independent living
IADL (Lawton)8 itemsInstrumental function — telephone, shopping, finance, medication. Falls before BADL and is the earlier signal
Rankin0–6Global disability after stroke, 6 being death

FIM measures assistance, not impairment and not diagnosis. A hemiplegic patient who has adapted may score better than a frailer patient with milder impairment — which is the point of the instrument, not a flaw in it.

Who benefits

  • A new and potentially reversible functional loss, not a long-standing plateau
  • Enough cognition to participate, or a deficit that rehabilitation itself can work around — dementia is not an automatic exclusion, and short repetitive task-specific practice works
  • Medical stability enough to tolerate the sessions
  • A realistic discharge destination, which is a question about the home and the family as much as about the patient

Hip fracture

Outcome is predicted, in order, by pre-fracture function, cognition and delirium, comorbidity, nutrition, depression, pain control, and the home going back to. Delirium in the first days is both a predictor and a target — it is the one on the list you can still change. Orthogeriatric co-management, surgery within about 48 hours where the patient is fit, early mobilisation, and bone-health follow-through: a fragility fracture is itself the indication to treat osteoporosis, and it is missed in the majority of cases.

Stroke

  • Timing. Early mobilisation, but very early high-dose out-of-bed activity within 24 hours reduced favourable outcomes at three months in the AVERT trial. Early, frequent, short and graded — dose matters as much as timing
  • Intensity and repetition drive motor recovery; constraint-induced movement therapy for a partially useful arm
  • Most recovery occurs in the first three months, but gains continue and a plateau in one domain does not close the others
  • Screen swallow before the first oral anything; screen for post-stroke depression, shoulder subluxation and pain, spasticity, and neglect, which is the deficit that most often defeats rehabilitation

Complications that end a rehabilitation admission

Delirium, falls, pressure injury, deconditioning from a weekend without therapy, deep vein thrombosis, constipation and urinary retention, malnutrition, and undertreated pain — which looks like refusal to participate and is treated as motivation when it should be treated as pain.

Israeli context worth having. The endpoint of the funded rehabilitation period (תום שיקום) and the criteria for complex nursing care (סיעוד מורכב) are part of the law-and-procedure block, which is the most reliable five questions on the paper. They are set out in Ethics & EOL law.

Hospital-associated disability

A substantial share of older patients leave hospital less able than when the illness started, and much of that is the admission rather than the disease. Muscle strength falls measurably within days of bed rest, and the losses are fastest in the already weak. The examinable countermeasures are unglamorous and mostly not drugs.

  • Out of bed and dressed daily; walk to the toilet rather than being taken to it
  • Remove the tethers: catheters, infusion lines, telemetry, continuous oxygen — each is a reason to stay in the chair
  • Delirium prevention, sleep protection, hearing aids and glasses within reach
  • Eat sitting up, with help if needed; nil-by-mouth orders reviewed daily
  • Plan the discharge from day one and measure function on admission, or you will not know that it has fallen

Spasticity, contracture and the team

Spasticity is treated when it interferes with function, hygiene or comfort — positioning and stretching first, then focal botulinum toxin, which is preferred to oral agents because baclofen and tizanidine sedate and both appear in the prescribing criteria. Contractures are prevented, not treated. The multidisciplinary team is examined as a structure: physiotherapy, occupational therapy, speech and language therapy, dietetics, social work, nursing and medicine, with goals set jointly, written down, and reviewed against a date.

What is different about rehabilitating an older adult

The purpose is to restore what disease or injury took away and reach the highest attainable function, independence and quality of life. The techniques do not differ by age. The outcomes and the approach do, and the chapter is organised around why.

  • A younger adult usually has one acute event. An older adult more often has multiple comorbidities that produce disability over time — and where there is an acute event, a hip fracture or a stroke, the comorbidities still shape the outcome
  • Subclinical impairment surfaces under challenge. Mild cognitive impairment is often first recognised during rehabilitation, when the patient cannot learn to use a new walking aid. Difficulty learning the frame is a cognitive finding, not a motivational one
  • Recovery takes longer and the functional outcome is usually worse than in a younger patient. Saying so at the outset is part of goal-setting, not pessimism
  • The goals differ in kind. Younger patients aim at work or study; older patients at self-care and mobility — and at whatever they actually value. The chapter's own examples are golf and fishing. A patient who has never cooked will not be served by kitchen practice

Stroke recovery, from the handbook the exam cites

The EBRSR Stroke Rehabilitation Clinician Handbook is named directly in the מראה מקום tables, so this is source material rather than commentary. Its first distinction is the one everything else hangs on.

Neurological recoveryFunctional recovery
What recoversThe impairment itself — the normal movement pattern returningThe task, often through learned compensation — a new movement pattern
Determined bySite and extent of the lesion. Severity of the initial deficit is inversely proportional to prognosisMotivation, ability to learn, family support, and the quality and intensity of therapy
Measured withFugl-MeyerBarthel, FIM, ARAT
Rehabilitation changes it?Largely not — it is spontaneousYes. This is what rehabilitation is for

Functional improvement can occur with no neurological recovery at all, and can continue for months after neurological recovery has finished. A patient who is walking better without a better Fugl-Meyer is not a paradox.

The time course, in weeks

Exam pearl

The best predictor of where a stroke patient will end up is what they could do a fortnight before the stroke. Ask it explicitly; it is the number the vignette buries.

Peak neurological recovery falls in the first one to three months, slowing thereafter, with about 5% still recovering at a year. From the Copenhagen Stroke Study of 1,197 patients, which is where the numbers in this chapter come from:

  • Neurological recovery precedes functional recovery by about two weeks
  • 80% reach their best neurological recovery by 4.5 weeks, and their best ADL function by 6 weeks
  • 95% reach best neurological recovery by 11 weeks and best ADL by 12.5 weeks
  • Best walking function: 4 weeks with mild paresis, 6 weeks moderate, 11 weeks severe
  • Two-thirds of survivors have mild-to-moderate strokes and achieve ADL independence. Only about 10% of moderate-to-severe strokes reach “full recovery”
Severity bandEarly FIMMotor FIMExpected course
Mild>80>62Few deficits; rehabilitation gains limited by a ceiling effect
Moderately severe40–8038–62Marked gains; about 85% discharged to the community — the group rehabilitation helps most
Severe<40<37Slower, unlikely to reach independence unless young; least likely to go home. Here rehabilitation reduces mortality more than it restores function

The best single predictor of outcome is the initial clinical severity, and it predicts the time to maximal recovery as well as its extent. Three mechanisms account for the early improvement and none of them is therapy: resolution of peri-lesional oedema, reperfusion of the ischaemic penumbra, and resolution of diaschisis.

Swallowing and the complications that follow it

  • Aspiration occurs in 16–52% of acute strokes, and silent aspiration in 8–27% — passage below the vocal cords with no cough and no outward sign. That is the whole argument for a formal swallow screen before the first oral anything, and for videofluoroscopy, the gold standard, when clinical assessment is not enough
  • Malnutrition is reported in 6–62% after stroke, the range reflecting that there is no agreed definition, and it worsens during the admission. Albumin is a marker of inflammation here, not of diet
  • Encourage self-feeding where it is safe — being fed carries its own aspiration risk

Stairs, canes and the hip precautions — ch 55 verbatim

  • “Up with the good, down with the bad.” Ascending: the uninvolved leg goes up first while the involved leg and the cane stay on the lower step. Descending: the involved leg and the cane go down first, then the uninvolved leg joins them. The 2024 answer for a healed right-ankle fracture was “descend right foot first”. The cane is held in the hand opposite the affected leg, and the elbow is 15–20° flexed — the 2026 answer for a left-sided weakness was a single-point cane in the right hand
  • After a total hip replacement by the posterolateral approach, for the first months: no crossing the legs, no hip flexion beyond 90°, no rolling the leg in and out, and a raised toilet seat. The 2024 “forbidden action” was crossing the legs; a high chair and full weight-bearing are allowed

Choosing the walking aid

Exam pearl

A patient who needs a wheeled walker to stay upright will not manage its brakes on a slope. Stability and usability trade against each other, and the exam tests the trade.

Table 55-5 is cited three times across the recent sittings, which makes it one of the highest-yield tables in the book, and it is the sort of thing that is never taught explicitly. The logic is a ladder: more support means less freedom, more weight on the arms and, past a point, more risk rather than less.

DeviceSupportGainsCostsTypical patient
Straight caneUnilateralBalance and proprioceptive cue; unloads the opposite side a littleOften not enough support; falls over when set down, so doors and parcels are a problemKnee or hip osteoarthritis; peripheral neuropathy
Quad (4-point) caneUnilateralMore stable, takes more weightHeavier; the wide base is itself a trip hazardStroke with hemiparesis
Standard pick-up walkerBilateralThe most stable of the walkers; permits genuine non-weight-bearingMust be lifted each step — needs strength and coordination; gait and turns are broken upHip fracture where non-weight-bearing is required; amputation before a prosthesis
Two-wheeled rolling walkerBilateralSmoother, faster gait than a pick-up walkerLess stable; fixed wheels turn awkwardlyDeconditioning; Parkinson disease
Rollator (4-wheeled)BilateralSmoothest gait, turns easily, large wheels for outdoors, and a seat to rest onLeast stable of the walkers; brakes demand coordination; costs moreCardiopulmonary disease; neuropathy with balance difficulty
Manual wheelchairWhole bodyMobility for a patient who cannot walk, or for a carer to pushSelf-propulsion needs arms and enduranceNon-ambulatory with cognitive impairment
Power chair or scooterWhole bodyCommunity mobility where walking is not possibleRequires the cognition to drive it safely; home modifications; a scooter still needs working armsAdvanced neurological disease; multiple amputations

Two examinable inversions. The rollator is the least stable walker despite looking like the most substantial — and in a patient with poor braking coordination it runs away downhill. And a power chair is refused not for physical reasons but for cognitive ones. Height-set the aid to the wrist crease with the arm at the side, elbow about 15–20° flexed; a cane goes in the hand opposite the affected leg.

Hazzard ch 42, p615 — 9 questions across four sittings. Two competing definitions, and the exam wants you to know that they are different constructs, not rival measurements of one thing.

The two models

Phenotype (Fried)Deficit accumulation (Rockwood)
What it isA physical syndromeA count of accumulated deficits
ItemsWeight loss (about 5% or 4.5 kg in a year), exhaustion, weakness by grip, slow gait, low activityUsually 30 or more — diseases, symptoms, signs, abnormal tests, disabilities
OutputCategorical: 3 or more frail, 1–2 pre-frailContinuous 0–1 — deficits present divided by deficits counted
StrengthSpecific about mechanism; deliberately excludes disability and comorbidity so it can predict themSensitive to change, grades severity, predicts across the whole range

The Clinical Frailty Scale is the judgement-based 1–9 ordinal scale used at the bedside — quick, reproducible enough, and the one that actually gets recorded. It is scored on the baseline two weeks before the acute event, not on the patient in front of you.

Sarcopenia is not frailty

Sarcopenia is loss of muscle mass and function. The examinable point is the order: low strength raises the suspicion, low muscle quantity or quality confirms it, and low physical performance marks it as severe. SARC-F is the screening questionnaire; grip dynamometry and the chair-stand test are the bedside measures; gait speed under 0.8 m/s is the usual performance cut-off. Frailty is broader — a state of reduced reserve across systems, of which sarcopenia is the muscular component.

How common, and in which populations

Setting or groupPrevalence
Community-dwelling, 65 and over11% average (reported range 4–59%)
Same population, broader definition vs Fried14% vs 10%
Aged 80–8416%
Aged 85 and over26%
Women vs menFried 9.6% vs 5.2%; deficit index 39% vs 37%
Hospitalised older patients27–80%
Institutionalised older adults30–70%
With cardiovascular diseaseabout 3× the prevalence of those without

The wide community range — 4% to 59% for the same construct — is itself the examinable point: it reflects which definition was used, not which population. And frailty is not a one-way state: using the Fried definition, nearly 60% of people over 70 make at least one transition between frailty states over 4.5 years, though transitions toward greater frailty outnumber those away from it.

What to do about it

Exam pearl

Only two interventions have consistent evidence: resistance exercise and taking drugs away. Everything else in the answer options is plausible and unproven.

  • Progressive resistance exercise is the only intervention with consistent benefit, and it works in the tenth decade and in nursing homes. Multicomponent programmes add balance and gait
  • Protein of roughly 1.0–1.2 g/kg/day for healthy older adults and more in acute illness — above the 0.8 g/kg general recommendation, which is a common distractor. Note the tension: the ADA 2026 older-adults standards say only “at least 0.8 g/kg/day, potentially higher and individualised”, and state there is no current evidence that going beyond 0.8–1.5 g/kg improves glycaemic or cardiovascular outcomes. The geriatric nutrition societies are more assertive than the diabetes one; answer to whichever the stem names
  • Deprescribing, correction of vitamin D deficiency, treating depression, and addressing vision, hearing and dentition
  • Comprehensive geriatric assessment is the intervention with the best evidence at the system level — it increases the chance of being alive and in your own home
  • Testosterone, growth hormone and appetite stimulants: not recommended. Megestrol and dronabinol are Beers items

Frailty as a decision tool

It changes what you offer, not merely what you predict: surgical risk, chemotherapy tolerance, dialysis initiation, anticoagulation, intensity of glycaemic and blood-pressure control, and where the time-to-benefit argument bites. STOPP B16 encodes one version of it, and all three clauses are in the criterion: “Statins for primary cardiovascular prevention in persons aged ≥ 85 and established frailty with expected life expectancy likely less than 3 years”. Age alone is not the rule — a fit 88-year-old on a primary-prevention statin does not trip B16.

The comprehensive geriatric assessment

Frailty is the problem; CGA is the instrument with the best evidence against it. It is a multidimensional, multidisciplinary process producing a coordinated plan, and in hospitalised older people it increases the chance of being alive and in your own home at follow-up. Know the domains, because a stem describing a “thorough history” that omits three of them is testing exactly this.

DomainWhat is actually assessed
MedicalProblem list, comorbidity, nutrition, continence, pain, sensory impairment, medication review
FunctionalBADL and IADL, gait and balance, falls history, driving
Cognitive and psychologicalCognition, delirium, mood, alcohol, capacity where relevant
Social and environmentalCarer, housing, finances, safeguarding, goals of care and advance planning

Weight loss and the anorexia of ageing

Unintentional loss of 5% in a month or 10% in six is significant and is the entry point of the Fried phenotype. Screen with MNA-SF. Before investigating a cancer, work through the mechanisms that are commoner and fixable: drugs (digoxin, metformin, SSRIs, opioids, anticholinergic dry mouth), dentition and swallowing, depression, dementia at the stage where eating is forgotten, constipation, pain, thyroid disease, and the practical questions — who buys the food, who cooks it, can the patient reach the kitchen and afford the shopping.

Oral nutritional supplements increase intake and weight; they do not reliably change function or mortality, and they work best given between meals, not with them. Appetite stimulants are not recommended — megestrol and dronabinol are Beers items. Protein and resistance exercise together beat either alone.

The deficit index, and its ceiling

The deficit index is a proportion — deficits present divided by deficits counted — so it is the fraction that matters, not which particular deficits a person has. Three properties worth knowing: it rises non-linearly with age in a Gompertz-like curve, it runs higher in women, and it has a universal ceiling at about 0.7. Nobody is observed above it, which is read as the limit of deficits a human can accumulate and remain alive. It correlates strongly with mortality and is unwieldy at the bedside, which is why the Clinical Frailty Scale is what actually gets recorded.

The Fried criteria, operationalised

Table 42-2 is the single most-cited table in the recent papers — four times across four sittings — which means the committee treats it as the definition. It is worth knowing not just as five words but as the five measurements the Cardiovascular Health Study actually used.

CharacteristicHow CHS measured it
Unintentional weight loss / sarcopeniaMore than 10 lb (about 4.5 kg) lost unintentionally in the previous year
WeaknessGrip strength in the lowest 20%, adjusted for sex and body mass index
Exhaustion / poor enduranceSelf-reported, from two questions on a depression scale
SlownessTime to walk 15 feet, slowest 20%, adjusted for sex and height
Low activityWeekly energy expenditure in the lowest 20% — under about 383 kcal/week in men, 270 in women

Three or more is frail; one or two is pre-frail; none is robust. Notice what the cut-points are: population quintiles adjusted for sex, and for BMI or height — not absolute numbers. That is why a grip strength in kilograms is not by itself a Fried criterion, and it is the sort of detail a table-cited question is built on.

What the chapter says is wrong with it

  • Cognition is excluded, which sits badly against the clinical experience that cognitive impairment usually travels with frailty. The subgroup with dual decline — mobility and cognition together — is at very high risk of disability, and the phenotype does not capture them
  • Weight loss is a problem as a criterion as obesity becomes commoner: sarcopenic obesity is frailty with a rising weight, and the phenotype misses it
  • The phenotype is deliberately physical, so it excludes disability and comorbidity in order to predict them — a strength for research and a limitation at the bedside, which is why the Clinical Frailty Scale is what actually gets recorded

What the chapter will not claim

Ch 42 is more cautious than most revision material, and the caution is quotable: there is no strong evidence that frailty can be prevented — observational data associate a Mediterranean-style diet and physical activity with lower risk — and no randomised trial has yet shown that frailty and its consequences can be reversed. The chapter calls that gap the most important obstacle to putting frailty into routine practice.

That sits alongside, not against, the exercise evidence below: progressive resistance training reliably improves strength, gait speed and function, including in the very old. What has not been shown is that it moves a person out of the frailty state. If a stem asks what reverses frailty, the honest answer from this chapter is that nothing has been shown to.

Three layers, not one thing

The chapter frames frailty as a construct with three overlaying dimensions, like the layers of an onion. It is worth holding because it explains why the definitions disagree: each of them is measuring a different layer.

So the Fried phenotype samples the outer layer and nothing else; the deficit index samples the outer layer more broadly; and everything being researched — inflammatory markers, anabolic hormones, mitochondrial function, senescence — belongs to the layers underneath, which is why no blood test diagnoses frailty and why none is likely to soon.

Hazzard ch 57, p853 — 8 questions across four sittings. The chapter before dementia, and the one that decides whether the patient in the stem has a disease at all.

Normal ageing

DeclinesPreserved
Processing speed — the dominant change, and it contaminates every timed testCrystallised intelligence: vocabulary, general knowledge, expertise
Working memory and divided attentionRecognition memory — cueing helps, which is the discriminator
Free recall and name retrievalProcedural memory, semantic memory
Executive flexibility, set-shiftingSimple attention, language comprehension

The cueing rule. In normal ageing and in depression, a cue helps retrieval. In amnestic MCI and Alzheimer disease, storage has failed and a cue does not help. That single distinction answers more stems than any test score.

Subjective decline, MCI, dementia

  • Subjective cognitive decline — the complaint without objective impairment. It carries some risk, and the patients who complain and test normally worry more than those brought in by a worried family, who test worse
  • Mild cognitive impairment — objective decline in one or more domains, independence preserved. Amnestic subtypes more often progress to Alzheimer disease, non-amnestic to the other pathologies. Progression runs at roughly 10–15% a year in clinic populations, and a meaningful minority revert to normal — usually those whose deficit was drugs, depression, sleep or thyroid all along
  • Major neurocognitive disorder — the decline interferes with independence in everyday activities. Not the score; the interference. Neither is diagnosed during delirium

The instruments, and what they are for

TestCommonly used cut-offNote
MMSE24/30Insensitive to executive and visuospatial deficit; ceiling effect in the educated
MoCA26/30, add 1 point for ≤12 years of educationBetter for MCI and for executive/vascular patterns
Mini-Cog3-word recall + clockTwo minutes, no licence, good screening performance
Clock drawing—Executive and visuospatial in one item; normal in early amnestic disease
IQCODE, AD8informantAsk the informant about change; independent of education and language

These thresholds are the ones in common use rather than diagnostic criteria. Education, language and sensory impairment shift all of them, and testing a patient without their hearing aids produces a number about the hearing aids.

Normal ageing, split more finely than most notes split it

Ch 57 Table 57-1 makes two distinctions worth having, because both are the difference between a worried patient and a patient with disease:

  • Executive function: real-world executive function is preserved; it is novel executive tasks that decline. The patient who still runs the household but fails a lab task they have never seen is showing normal ageing
  • Visuospatial: simple construction and simple copying are preserved; mental rotation, complex copy and mental assembly decline

The chapter's framing of the whole table: normal ageing produces mild changes in circumscribed aspects of cognition, and those changes are much smaller than the effects of age-related medical conditions or neurodegenerative disease. If the change is not mild and not circumscribed, stop calling it ageing.

Before you label anything

Exam pearl

When the stem hands you a drug list and a memory complaint in the same paragraph, the drug list is the answer.

B12, thyroid, sodium, calcium, depression, obstructive sleep apnoea, alcohol, subdural haematoma, normal-pressure hydrocephalus — and drugs, which is the one you can fix that day: anticholinergics, benzodiazepines, Z-drugs, opioids, antiepileptics. Check Beers Table 7 and STOPP Section M before ordering the MRI.

What to offer in MCI

No drug is approved or recommended for MCI — cholinesterase inhibitors do not prevent progression and carry their own harms, and that is a recurring stem. What is defensible: treat the reversible contributors, deprescribe, aerobic and resistance exercise, hearing and vision correction, vascular risk-factor control, alcohol reduction, social and cognitive engagement, and planned review. The Lancet Commission's modifiable risk factors — hearing loss, education, hypertension, smoking, obesity, depression, physical inactivity, diabetes, alcohol, head injury, air pollution, social isolation, and the 2024 additions of untreated vision loss and high LDL cholesterol — are cited by name in this exam and are worth holding as a list.

Numbers from ch 57 worth carrying

  • Visual hallucinations with an MMSE above 20 are highly suggestive of dementia with Lewy bodies. Hallucinations that early, with cognition that intact, do not fit Alzheimer disease
  • Post-operative cognitive dysfunction after cardiac surgery is reported in 30–70% at discharge and remains at 15–25% at twelve months
  • Normal-pressure hydrocephalus is about 6% of dementia cases. After shunting, at six months 83% improved in gait and 46% in memory; among survivors at five years, 39% still had better gait and fewer than 10% still showed cognitive improvement. Gait is what shunting buys, and it buys it far more reliably than cognition
  • Behavioural-variant FTD is 50–60% of all FTLD diagnoses
  • Late-onset depression may itself be a prodromal symptom of neurodegenerative disease, not merely a mimic of it or a reaction to it

The rarer dementias the exam has drawn from ch 57

  • Prion disease (Creutzfeldt–Jakob the best known): profound, rapidly progressive dementia, sporadic cases in the 60s, early symptoms vague — poor memory and concentration, apathy, lability, sleep and appetite loss — with hyperreflexia, incoordination, saccadic abnormalities and incontinence as it advances over months; EEG changes, MRI hyperintensities and CSF 14-3-3 protein. The 2023 examination finding was the hyperreflexia; the 2024 stem (a retired engineer, months, hyperreflexia, MRI hyperintensity) wanted palliative referral, because diagnosis comes late and the course is fast
  • Corticobasal syndrome: tau pathology, asymmetric frontoparietal atrophy, onset in the early 60s; progressive asymmetric tremor, incoordination, rigidity, myoclonus, alien limb and unilateral ideomotor apraxia, with memory relatively preserved early — the 2025 answer for asymmetric tremor plus apraxia
  • Neurosyphilis: dementia 5–25 years after infection with hallucinations, delusions, mood change, personality change, strokes, ataxia and global decline; classed as reversible but with only limited cognitive benefit from penicillin; think of it with HIV and in any dementia of unclear cause (2025)
  • Normal ageing (Table 57-1): processing speed, new learning and retrieval, word-finding and fluency all decline; syntax, vocabulary and semantic knowledge are preserved — the 2024 “which is not a normal change” answer was the grammatical ability

Driving

A dementia diagnosis is not by itself a bar to driving, and early Alzheimer disease with mild impairment may be compatible with it; moderate or severe impairment is not. What predicts risk better than any score is the informant's account, a history of near-misses, getting lost on familiar routes, and executive and visuospatial deficit rather than memory. Practical tools: clock drawing and Trail Making B as flags, then an on-road assessment, which is the only real test.

In Israel this is a statutory matter and is examined as one. Medical fitness to drive is governed by the Ministry of Health circular (כשירות רפואית לנהיגה), with a duty to report to the medical institute for road safety (המכון הרפואי לבטיחות בדרכים, מרב"ד). Reporting is a defined duty, not a breach of confidence, and it is the physician's, not the family's. See Ethics & EOL law.

Telling the patient

Disclosure is the default: a person with capacity has a right to their diagnosis, and hiding it removes their chance to plan while they still can — an enduring power of attorney (ייפוי כוח מתמשך), advance directives, finances, driving, and the conversation about where they want to live. When family ask you not to tell, the correct move is to ask the patient how much they want to know and whom they want told, which respects autonomy without imposing disclosure. Pair the diagnosis with what happens next — follow-up, support services, and the reversible contributors you are still treating.

What counts as abnormal, and what MCI actually does next

  • On formal neuropsychological testing, scores 1 to 1.5 standard deviations below the mean for age- and education-matched peers are treated as abnormal — though the chapter notes there is no universally agreed cut-off. Age and education matching is the part that matters: a raw score means nothing without them
  • 80% of people diagnosed with MCI go on to develop Alzheimer disease within 5 to 8 years
  • They convert at roughly 10–15% a year, against a general-population conversion rate of 1–2%. That contrast is the reason the diagnosis is worth making
  • But 15–40% of those diagnosed with MCI later test in the normal range — reversion is inherent to the construct, not a sign someone got it wrong
  • Alzheimer pathology is present years to decades before symptoms are noticed, which is what makes the prodromal categories meaningful at all

The fourteen risk factors, with the numbers

The Lancet standing Commission's 2024 report adds untreated vision loss and high LDL cholesterol to the twelve named in 2020. Together the fourteen carry a weighted population attributable fraction of 45% — nearly half of dementia worldwide could in theory be prevented or delayed. These are the Commission's own weighted figures, which is what a question citing this paper is likely to be built on.

Risk factorLife stagePrevalenceRelative riskWeighted PAF
Hearing lossmidlife59.0%1.47%
High LDL cholesterol — new in 2024midlife76.5%1.37%
Less educationearly life23.2%1.65%
Social isolationlate life24.0%1.65%
Depressionmidlife7.2%2.23%
Traumatic brain injurymidlife12.1%1.73%
Air pollutionlate life75.0%1.13%
Physical inactivitymidlife27.5%1.22%
Smokingmidlife22.3%1.32%
Diabetesmidlife9.3%1.72%
Hypertensionmidlife31.1%1.22%
Untreated vision loss — new in 2024late life12.7%1.52%
Obesitymidlife13.0%1.31%
Excessive alcohol — over 21 UK units a weekmidlife13.3%1.21%
All fourteen———45%

The Commission groups the fourteen by life stage, and a stem can ask which stage a factor belongs to: one early-life factor (education), ten midlife, and three late-life (social isolation, air pollution, untreated vision loss). The prevalence column is the other half of the arithmetic — PAF is driven by it, not by the relative risk.

Two things that are easy to get backwards. Depression has the highest relative risk of the fourteen (2.2) but a small attributable fraction, because it is uncommon; hearing loss has a modest relative risk (1.4) and the largest fraction, because 59% of the population has it. Prevalence, not strength of association, drives the ranking. And the risk is modifiable irrespective of APOE status — genotype does not exempt anyone from the advice or waste it on them.

What the Commission actually tells you to do

  • Make hearing aids accessible; reduce harmful noise exposure
  • Keep systolic blood pressure at or below 130 mmHg from the age of 40
  • Detect and treat high LDL cholesterol from midlife
  • Treat depression effectively; screen and treat vision loss
  • Helmets in contact sports and on bicycles; exercise; smoking cessation; weight and diabetes control; reduce heavy drinking; reduce air pollution
  • Age-friendly housing and communities, and reduce social isolation by facilitating living with others and joining in

Because risk clusters in the same individuals, the Commission argues that interventions should usually be multicomponent rather than single-factor, and should start early and continue across life. After diagnosis it is equally explicit: cholinesterase inhibitors and memantine for Alzheimer disease and Lewy body dementia; multicomponent coping interventions for family carers; activity interventions for neuropsychiatric symptoms — and no evidence for exercise as a treatment for neuropsychiatric symptoms, which is the trap in that sentence.

Hazzard ch 45, p665 — 5 questions across three of four sittings. In an older patient the presentation is usually a fall, and the amnesia for the event is why the distinction matters.

An unwitnessed fall with no memory of hitting the floor is syncope until proven otherwise. Retrograde amnesia for the loss of consciousness is common with age, so “I just tripped” is not evidence.

The three that matter

CauseClueFirst move
Orthostatic hypotensionOn standing, after meals, after a dose change, in the morningLying and standing pressures at 1 and 3 minutes; then the drug list
Reflex / neurally mediatedSituational — micturition, cough, defecation, pain, prolonged standing · prodrome of warmth, nausea, greying visionReassure, hydrate, counterpressure manoeuvres, withdraw vasoactive drugs
CardiacOn exertion or supine · no prodrome, so injury · palpitations · structural disease · abnormal ECG · family history of sudden deathECG, monitoring, echocardiography — admit

The physiology behind the stems: standing pools 500–1000 mL in the legs and splanchnic bed; the fall in pressure unloads the carotid and aortic baroreceptors, whose reflex raises sympathetic outflow, cuts vagal tone, and lifts heart rate, resistance and venous return. Ageing blunts baroreflex sensitivity — the 2026 “normal autonomic ageing” answer — and a disrupted baroreflex causes OH. Postprandial hypotension is splanchnic pooling with a failure to raise sympathetic activity, heart rate and resistance, plus vasodilatory gut peptides — asked in 2024 and 2026.

Definitions worth being exact about

  • Orthostatic hypotension: a fall of 20 mmHg systolic or 10 mmHg diastolic within three minutes of standing. Measure supine after five minutes' rest, then at 1 and 3 minutes standing
  • Postprandial hypotension: a 20 mmHg systolic fall within two hours of the start of a meal. Prevalence 24–36% of nursing-home residents, 23% of older adults admitted with syncope or falls, and 50% of those with unexplained syncope — usually missed because nobody measures after lunch. It may or may not coexist with OH
  • Carotid sinus hypersensitivity: on 5–10 seconds of carotid sinus massage, asystole of 3 seconds or more (cardioinhibitory), a systolic fall of more than 50 mmHg (vasodepressor), or both (mixed) — with or without symptoms. When massage reproduces syncope it is carotid sinus syndrome, and that is the distinction the chapter draws. Most susceptible: coronary disease, hypertension, digoxin, beta-blockers, methyldopa; a third also have vasovagal syncope or OH. Do not massage over a bruit or soon after stroke or infarction. Dual-chamber pacing abolishes syncope in 85–90% of cardioinhibitory cases; midodrine helped the vasodepressor form in one small trial

The workup that is actually indicated

History from a witness, examination including lying and standing pressures, and a 12-lead ECG answer most of it. Add echocardiography where structural disease is suspected, prolonged monitoring or an implantable loop recorder where an arrhythmia is suspected but intermittent, and carotid sinus massage in unexplained syncope or falls in the older patient. Tilt testing is for recurrent unexplained episodes, not first-line. Routine head CT, carotid Dopplers, EEG and blood panels have a very low yield in undifferentiated syncope and are a favourite wrong answer.

Treatment of orthostatic hypotension, in order

  1. Withdraw the offending drug — antihypertensives, alpha blockers, nitrates, diuretics, tricyclics, antipsychotics, dopaminergics
  2. Non-pharmacological: squat or cross the legs when symptoms start, hydration and salt, waist-high graded stockings or an abdominal binder, sleep 30–45° head-up, avoid heat, straining and alcohol. For the postprandial form: antihypertensives between meals rather than with them, no diuretics or prolonged sitting before eating, small frequent meals high in protein and fat, cold rather than warm, and a walk afterwards
  3. Then, for severe OH or PPH, the chapter's four: caffeine 250 mg (two brewed cups) in the morning, fludrocortisone 0.1–0.5 mg daily, midodrine 2.5–10 mg three times daily, and octreotide 50 µg subcutaneously 30 minutes before meals — watching supine hypertension, oedema and heart failure. Droxidopa is not in ch 45 — its source is Kaufmann et al., Neurology 2014;83:328 (NOH301, read from the paper; 162 responders randomised for one week): OHQ composite improved 0.90 units over placebo, standing systolic up 11.2 vs 3.9 mmHg, supine systolic over 180 in 4.9% vs 2.5%, headache the commonest adverse effect

Driving: an episode of syncope has licensing consequences under the Ministry of Health circular on fitness to drive (כשירות לנהיגה), which the law block examines. The reporting duty and the thresholds are in Ethics & EOL law.

Dizziness is four complaints, not one

Exam pearl

Ask which of the four they mean before anything else. Half the stems are decided by that question alone, and the fall that nobody witnessed is syncope until proven otherwise.

The word means whatever the patient means by it, and the first job is to find out which. In older patients the causes are frequently multiple, which is itself the answer to some stems.

What they meanPoints to
Vertigo — the room movesVestibular: BPPV, vestibular neuritis, Ménière, or a central cause
Presyncope — about to faintOrthostatic hypotension, arrhythmia, drugs — treat it as syncope
Disequilibrium — unsteady on the feet, not in the headMultisensory: neuropathy, vision, cervical spine, cerebellar, parkinsonism, deconditioning
Light-headed or floatingAnxiety, hyperventilation, drugs — a diagnosis of exclusion in this age group
  • BPPV is the commonest and the most rewarding: seconds of vertigo on turning in bed or looking up. Dix–Hallpike provokes it — upbeating torsional nystagmus with a latency of 1–5 seconds, a burst of 10–20 seconds, and fatigability — and the Epley manoeuvre treats it, repeated until the Dix–Hallpike is negative. Duration sorts the episodic causes: under a minute BPPV; 20–120 minutes TIA or migraine; 2 hours to 2 days Ménière or recurrent vestibulopathy. Vestibular suppressants — meclizine, scopolamine, benzodiazepines — are dangerous in the old, cause falls and confusion, and with prolonged use paradoxically prolong the dizziness by blocking central compensation; low dose, acute episodes only
  • Acute vestibular syndrome — continuous vertigo over days — is where you separate neuritis from stroke. The HINTS examination (not in ch 45; Kattah et al., Stroke 2009;40:3504, read from the paper — 101 high-risk patients, 76 central: a normal head impulse, direction-changing nystagmus or skew was 100% sensitive and 96% specific for stroke, and early DWI-MRI was falsely negative in 12%, all under 48 hours) does it better than early imaging: a normal head-impulse test, direction-changing nystagmus, or skew deviation each point central. Remember that a posterior-circulation stroke can present with dizziness and almost nothing else, and that an early CT will be normal

Hazzard ch 51, p759 — 5 questions across three of four sittings. The examinable content is who to treat, with what, and when to stop — and the one drug you can never simply stop.

Who gets treated

  • A hip or vertebral fragility fracture — treat, whatever the T-score. No DXA required to make the decision
  • T-score −2.5 or below at femoral neck, total hip or lumbar spine
  • Osteopenia with a FRAX 10-year probability above the national intervention threshold

T-score compares with a young adult; Z-score compares with age-matched peers and a Z below −2.0 should send you looking for a secondary cause. Degenerative change, aortic calcification and vertebral fracture all falsely raise the lumbar reading in the old, which is why the hip site is preferred.

Secondary causes to exclude first

Vitamin D deficiency, hyperparathyroidism, coeliac disease, myeloma, hyperthyroidism and over-replacement, hypogonadism, CKD, and drugs — glucocorticoids above all, plus aromatase inhibitors, androgen deprivation, anticonvulsants, long-term heparin, and the proton pump inhibitors and SSRIs whose association is weaker but real.

The drugs

AgentPlaceWatch
Bisphosphonates — alendronate, risedronate, zoledronateFirst-lineOral dosing ritual and upper GI intolerance; the eGFR 30–35 floor is label convention, not stated in ch 51. Zoledronate 5 mg yearly: flu-like reaction after the first infusion that fades with later ones, 35% fewer clinical fractures, and lower all-cause mortality (9.6% vs 13%) in the trial — and the antifracture effect persists after stopping, which is what makes the holiday possible
DenosumabRenal impairment, intolerance, high risk60 µg six-monthly; hip fracture down 40% over 3 years, effective at 75 and over, and the chapter's preferred agent in long-term care for its route and tolerability. Never simply stop: it is not retained in bone, the antifracture effect is back to baseline 12 months after the last dose, and fracture risk rises markedly in those with a prior vertebral fracture. Cover with a bisphosphonate on stopping (START H6). Hypocalcaemia risk, especially in CKD
Anabolics — teriparatide, abaloparatide, romosozumabT-score worse than −3.5; fracture with T worse than −2.5; fracture or bone loss after 2 years of bisphosphonateAnabolic first, then antiresorptive — the gain is lost if it is not consolidated, and a concurrent bisphosphonate blunts teriparatide. Teriparatide 20 µg daily and abaloparatide: 2 years maximum (rodent osteosarcoma); not in Paget disease or unexplained raised alkaline phosphatase. Romosozumab 210 mg monthly: 12 months maximum, cardiovascular signal in one phase 3 trial, vertebral fracture down 75% when followed by denosumab. All need the cognition, motivation and independence to self-inject
RaloxifeneNot discussed in ch 51 — conventionalVTE, hot flushes, no hip-fracture data
Calcium and vitamin DRecommended for everyone in the chapter, and every drug trial ran on top of themElemental calcium 1200–1500 mg/day, vitamin D at least 800 IU/day, up to 2000 IU. Check 25(OH)D first in the frail: at or under 50 nmol/L start 2000 IU; at or under 30 nmol/L a 50,000 IU loading dose then 1000–4000 IU daily. Never the bolus regimens

Duration and the holiday

Exam pearl

Denosumab is the one you can never simply stop. A drug holiday applies to bisphosphonates; stopping denosumab without a bisphosphonate behind it causes vertebral fractures.

The chapter's rule: a holiday may be considered after 3 to 5 years of antiresorptive therapy in moderate or low fracture risk, because a short break costs little. In high-risk patients — prior hip or vertebral fracture, T-score still very low, continuing glucocorticoids — benefit continues beyond 5 years and the timing needs care. The evidence behind it: in pooled extension trials, 6 or more years of bisphosphonate gave fracture rates of 9.3–11% against 8.0–8.8% on placebo. The holiday rests on the skeletal retention of bisphosphonates and it does not apply to denosumab, which is the trap. The oral-five / IV-three split is a common convention, not ch 51.

The rare harms, in proportion

Atypical femoral fracture — risk rises with duration of any bisphosphonate (and of denosumab), and falls rapidly once it is stopped. Radiograph any groin or thigh pain on treatment, then bone scan or MRI if needed; the chapter notes that the fracture precedes the pain in most cases. Osteonecrosis of the jaw — exposed necrotic maxillofacial bone that fails to heal; at osteoporosis doses the incidence is 0.001–0.01%, against the frequent high doses of oncology. Both are rare enough that fear of them causes more fractures than the drugs do, and saying so in proportion is usually the answer being tested.

Do not forget the falls half. A drug reduces fracture risk by about half at best; the fracture still needs a fall. Exercise with balance training, medication review, vision, footwear and home hazards belong in the same plan — see 43 Falls.

Vertebral fracture

Most are silent: the presentation is height loss, progressive kyphosis, and chronic back pain rather than an event, and the diagnosis is often made on a chest film. They matter because they predict the next one — half of patients refracture within 10 years, and half of those within 2 years of the first, a risk equal to that of a woman 10 years older — which is what “imminent risk” means and why the chapter says most older patients with a prior fracture are treatment candidates now, not after the DXA.

  • Management is analgesia, early mobilisation, and starting bone treatment. Bed rest costs more than it relieves
  • Vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty did not beat sham in the better trials and are not recommended routinely — a favourite question, though ch 51 does not discuss them
  • Suspect something other than osteoporosis if there is fever, a known cancer, neurological signs, thoracic pain in a young-old patient, or a fracture above T4

Calcium and vitamin D, in proportion

Ch 51 holds both halves of this at once, and the exam can ask either. On one side: calcium and vitamin D are “an essential component of any treatment”, recommended for all, and every drug trial supplemented both. On the other: calcium from diet or supplements produced only small BMD gains; vitamin D supplements have no clear effect on fracture; and high-dose bolus vitamin D — 500,000 IU yearly or 60,000 IU monthly — consistently increased falls and fractures. Dietary calcium is associated with lower all-cause mortality; very high supplemental calcium carries a possible cardiovascular signal. So: diet first, daily doses in the ranges above, measure the level in the frail, and never the bolus.

Hazzard ch 87, p1353 — 7 questions across three of four sittings. A cheap chapter with two expensive traps: fibre in the wrong patient, and diarrhoea that is actually impaction.

Define it properly

Not frequency alone. Rome-type criteria require two or more of: straining, lumpy or hard stools, sensation of incomplete evacuation, sensation of anorectal blockage, manual manoeuvres, and fewer than three spontaneous bowel movements a week — in at least a quarter of defecations. Colonic transit changes little with age; what changes is mobility, fluid, drugs, and the pelvic floor.

Red flags before treating

New onset in someone previously regular, weight loss, rectal bleeding or iron-deficiency anaemia, a change in stool calibre, a family history of colorectal cancer, or an abdominal or rectal mass. These earn a colonoscopy, weighed against life expectancy. Everyone gets a rectal examination — tone, impaction, mass, and the paradoxical contraction of dyssynergia.

Secondary causes

CategoryExamples
DrugsOpioids, anticholinergics, calcium-channel blockers (verapamil), iron, calcium, aluminium antacids, diuretics, antipsychotics, tricyclics, ondansetron
MetabolicHypothyroidism, hypercalcaemia, hypokalaemia, diabetes, uraemia
NeurologicalParkinson disease — often years before the motor signs — stroke, cord lesion, autonomic neuropathy
Structural / functionalObstruction, stricture, rectocele, dyssynergic defecation, immobility, inaccessible or undignified toilet arrangements

How common, and how slow the gut actually gets

  • Prevalence 12–19% in North America, rising with age. Asked directly about recurrent constipation: 26% of women and 16% of men, and at 84 and over, 34% and 26%
  • Total gut transit is normally under 72 hours. In ambulant older patients it runs to about 3 days; in bedridden patients, 3 weeks; and in institutionalised or bedridden patients with constipation, 6 to more than 14 days. In immobile older people with diabetes it reaches 200 ± 144 hours
  • Just one week of bed rest slows transit in healthy young volunteers — the point being that immobility alone does this, before any drug or disease is involved

The chapter's diagnostic definition is stricter than the symptom list alone: two or more of the symptoms, present on more than 25% of occasions, for at least 12 weeks in the last 12 months. Hard stool means Bristol type 1–2. Normal perineal descent is under 4 cm.

Treatment, in the order it is examined

Exam pearl

Liquid stool in a constipated patient is overflow. Loperamide is the harm the question is testing for.

  1. Non-drug: mobility, fluid, a toilet routine exploiting the gastrocolic reflex after breakfast, footstool for posture, privacy and time. Removing the commode-behind-a-curtain problem is a real intervention
  2. Osmotic: polyethylene glycol carries the chapter's only level 1 evidence and out-performs lactulose on frequency and straining, at the cost of more liquid stools — but ch 87 places it, for older people, at acute disimpaction (1 L or 8 sachets daily for 3 days cleared 89% of impactions) and at regular use only in high-risk patients resistant to milder, cheaper agents. Lactulose and sorbitol are equally effective and sorbitol is much cheaper; that is the exam answer on cost. Docusate has no effect on motility and little or no laxative action even at 300 mg/day
  3. Stimulant: senna or bisacodyl, alone or added. Senna acts in 8–12 hours, so at bedtime; 20 mg daily for six months in the over-80s lost no protein or electrolytes, and in patients with weak sphincters senna alone may treat the constipation without the soiling that softeners cause. Bisacodyl 10 mg daily is the alternative; bisacodyl carries an ischaemic-colitis risk in the old. Long-term senna is not known to damage the bowel — the “lazy colon” is folklore and a common distractor
  4. Secretagogues — lubiprostone, linaclotide, prucalopride — for refractory chronic constipation
  5. Opioid-induced constipation that fails laxatives: a peripherally acting mu-opioid receptor antagonist (naloxegol, naldemedine, methylnaltrexone). This is the specific answer, and every regular opioid needs a laxative from day one — STOPP L2

Two traps. Fibre in an immobile patient with poor fluid intake makes things worse, and it is contraindicated in suspected obstruction and in opioid-induced constipation. Overflow diarrhoea from impaction treated as diarrhoea — with loperamide — is the classic harm; liquid stool around a hard mass needs disimpaction, not an antimotility drug.

Mineral oil by mouth is a Beers item — and the committee's laxative–side-effect pairing answer, twice — in anyone with swallowing or reflux risk: aspiration lipoid pneumonia.

Opioid-induced constipation, by the numbers

The PAMORA numbers from ch 87: naldemedine raised the response rate to 52% against 35% on placebo (RR 1.51, 95% CI 1.32–1.72); naloxegol to 42% against 29% (RR 1.43, 1.19–1.71), response defined as three or more spontaneous bowel movements a week. Methylnaltrexone improved frequency across five trials but the evidence was graded low quality. For refractory constipation the chapter offers transanal irrigation, with a pooled response rate of about 50%.

Three mechanism answers from ch 87. Transit slows because of a loss of colonic enteric neurons producing nitric oxide and acetylcholine (2024). Rectal dysmotility — the loaded rectum that cannot contract, elicitable in only 14% with a history of impaction — is attributed to diminished parasympathetic outflow from sacral cord damage, or to years of suppressing the urge (2026). And acute colonic pseudo-obstruction (Ogilvie), the caecum at 10 cm or more in the frail, acutely ill or postoperative patient: nil by mouth, flatus tube, correct potassium and magnesium, then neostigmine if the heart allows, then endoscopic decompression, with PEG afterwards to prevent recurrence (2025).

Faecal incontinence, briefly

It is on the official exam topic list with no frequency behind it. Commonest mechanism in the old is overflow from impaction; then sphincter and pudendal injury, diarrhoeal states, cognitive and mobility causes. Treat impaction, firm the stool, schedule toileting, and consider biofeedback where there is a functioning sphincter and cognition to use it.

Hazzard's stepwise ladder, which does not start with PEG

A real difference between sources, worth knowing before you answer. This file says polyethylene glycol is the osmotic first-line, which follows the gastroenterology guidelines. Ch 87 Table 87-11 does not. It starts cheaper and milder and reserves PEG for what does not respond.

GroupThe chapter's sequence
Ambulant older people Bulk laxative — psyllium, 1–3 times daily with fluids → if symptoms persist add senna 1–3 tablets at bedtime → if still persisting add sorbitol or lactulose 15 mL daily, titrated to regular (three or more a week) and comfortable evacuation
Questionable fluid intake, or bulk laxatives not tolerated Skip the bulking agent — start with senna 1–2 tablets at bedtime
High risk — bedridden, neurological disease, previous faecal impaction Senna 2–3 tablets at bedtime plus sorbitol or lactulose 30 mL

Note what the ladder does with a bulking agent: it is first in the ambulant patient and skipped entirely where fluid intake is doubtful — which is the same judgement the file makes elsewhere about fibre in the immobile, arrived at from the other side. Targets from the chapter: fibre 20–35 g/day, starting at 3–4 g and building; fluid 1.5–2 L/day.

Dyssynergic defecation

A quarter or more of refractory constipation is not slow transit at all but a failure to coordinate the pelvic floor: the patient strains, the puborectalis and external sphincter contract instead of relaxing, and no laxative will fix it. You detect it with your finger — ask the patient to bear down and feel for paradoxical contraction and inadequate perineal descent — and confirm it with anorectal manometry and a balloon-expulsion test. Biofeedback is first-line and outperforms laxatives in this group, which is a question that rewards knowing the mechanism rather than the drug ladder.

Bowel care in the frail and the dying

  • The regimen follows the opioid, not the complaint: start the laxative with the opioid, and titrate it with the opioid
  • Osmotic plus stimulant is the usual combination; bulk-forming agents are wrong here
  • Rectal measures — suppository or enema — when the rectum is loaded, and manual disimpaction when it is hard and the patient cannot evacuate. Distressing, and more distressing if it is delayed for three days
  • Constipation is a common and reversible cause of delirium, of agitation in advanced dementia, of urinary retention and of overflow incontinence. It belongs on every one of those checklists

Hazzard ch 99, p1559 — 12 questions across three of four sittings, the highest count outside the core nine, and the exam also cites the ADA older-adults standards by name. The whole chapter is one argument: in this population the danger is overtreatment.

Targets by health status

CategoryDescriptionA1c, in common use
HealthyFew chronic illnesses, intact cognition and functionabout 7.0–7.5%
Complex / intermediateMultiple comorbidities, or mild-to-moderate cognitive or functional impairment, or 2 or more IADL dependenciesbelow about 8.0%
Very complex / poor healthEnd-stage chronic illness, moderate-to-severe cognitive impairment, or 2 or more ADL dependenciesstop relying on A1c — manage to avoid hypoglycaemia and symptomatic hyperglycaemia

A1c is also less reliable here: anaemia, transfusion, CKD and altered red-cell survival all distort it. Where it is doubtful, use glucose patterns or continuous monitoring.

Deintensification is an intervention. An A1c of 6.2% on a sulfonylurea or insulin in an 84-year-old is a problem to be fixed, not a target achieved. Look for hypoglycaemia unawareness — autonomic warning symptoms are blunted with age and with duration of disease, so the first sign is confusion, a fall or a seizure.

Drug choice

AgentStanding in older adults
MetforminFirst-line, down to eGFR 30 with dose reduction. Watch weight loss, anorexia and B12 deficiency on long-term use
DPP-4 inhibitorsWell tolerated, weight-neutral, no hypoglycaemia. The safe choice when frailty dominates
SGLT2 inhibitorsCardiorenal benefit that applies at any age — against volume depletion, genital mycotic infection, euglycaemic ketoacidosis and weight loss in an already sarcopenic patient
GLP-1 agonistsEffective with cardiovascular benefit; nausea and weight loss are a cost, not always a benefit, in this group
SulfonylureasBeers avoids the class first- or second-line. STOPP J1 names the long half-life agents — glibenclamide, chlorpropamide, glimepiride. If one must be used, short-acting glipizide
Sliding-scale insulinNot a regimen. If it has produced no insulin for 24–48 hours, stop it; otherwise add basal and discontinue it
ThiazolidinedionesHeart failure, oedema, fractures

Simplify insulin: once-daily basal rather than premixed or multiple daily injections where a carer administers it; match the regimen to who is actually giving it and to whether meals are eaten.

Complications, weighted for age

Albuminuria (over 30 mg/g creatinine) is the first clinical sign of diabetic kidney disease, a marker of cardiovascular risk, and — the 2024 committee answer — a prognostic tool and a measure of response to treatment; a raised creatinine means the damage is already irreversible. Confirm it more than once. Combined albuminuria and reduced GFR is far commoner in the old, and about half of older people with diabetes have kidney disease.

Screen feet and vision, treat blood pressure and lipids with the same time-to-benefit reasoning used everywhere else, and remember the geriatric complications the chapter singles out: falls, cognitive impairment, depression, incontinence, persistent pain, and polypharmacy. Diabetes doubles the risk of cognitive decline, and cognitive impairment is itself a reason to loosen targets and simplify the regimen.

Ageing physiology the exam keeps asking (ch 99): in people without diabetes there is a slight rise in fasting glucose and a much more marked slowing of the return to normal after an oral glucose load (2026); insulin sensitivity falls, and the rise in central adiposity accounts for most of that insulin resistance, with inactivity adding to it (2024). Cardiovascular protection: statins have a prognostic benefit within a few years and are recommended for most (2024); the SGLT2 inhibitor is the change with a prognostic effect in the patient with coronary disease, albuminuria and an eGFR of 40 (2024 stem: start empagliflozin, not stop the statin, not more insulin). Prediabetes: follow-up screening every 2 to 3 years, yearly in the high-risk; lifestyle change beats metformin at delaying progression, including over 60 (DPP). In the nursing-home patient with limited life expectancy, a restrictive low-salt, low-cholesterol diet is a cause of weight loss — liberalise the diet and prioritise appetite and enjoyment (2025).

Why hypoglycaemia recovery fails in this population

Table 99-15 lists the risk factors, and they are worth reading as four groups rather than one list, because the therapeutic group is the only one you prescribe:

  • Therapeutic: insulin, sulphonylurea
  • Physiologic: impaired autonomic function, diminished glucagon secretion, kidney or liver failure
  • Functional and cognitive: cognitive disorder, sensory impairment (vision, hearing), impaired mobility or hand dexterity
  • Behavioural and other: poor or irregular nutrition, alcohol or another sedating agent, polypharmacy

The counter-regulatory failure is the part to understand rather than memorise: the catecholamine response that should raise glucose rapidly is blunted — by autonomic neuropathy from long-standing diabetes, and by the β-blockers so many of these patients take for cardiovascular disease. The drug that masks the warning also impairs the recovery.

The threshold shifts, which is why they feel it early

A patient with diabetes may begin to feel hypoglycaemic at a glucose of 80–100 mg/dL — well above the symptomatic threshold in people without diabetes, which is 50–60 mg/dL. Long-standing hyperglycaemia resets the alarm upward, so a patient reporting symptoms at a normal glucose is not imagining it, and a patient comfortable at 55 has lost the alarm altogether.

Hypoglycaemia is the outcome that matters

Exam pearl

An A1c of 6.2% on insulin or a sulfonylurea is a problem, not an achievement. The correct action is to take treatment away.

  • Under 70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L) is the alert value; under 54 is clinically significant; severe is defined by needing another person's help, whatever the number
  • Autonomic warning symptoms are blunted by age, by duration of disease and by beta-blockers, so the presentation is confusion, a fall, a seizure or a collapse — and it is routinely admitted as delirium or stroke
  • Sulfonylurea and insulin are the only common causes. A long-acting sulfonylurea in renal impairment can produce hypoglycaemia lasting a day or more, so those patients are admitted and observed, not treated and sent home
  • Treat with 15 g of fast carbohydrate, recheck at 15 minutes, then give a longer-acting snack. Intramuscular glucagon works poorly in the malnourished, in liver disease and in sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia
  • One episode is a reason to loosen the target and simplify the regimen, not to add a monitoring instruction

Simplify, do not intensify. Premixed insulin and multiple daily injections in a patient who eats erratically or whose carer visits once a day is a hypoglycaemia machine. Move to once-daily basal, dose to the fasting glucose, and accept a higher A1c for it. Continuous glucose monitoring is genuinely useful where hypoglycaemia is suspected and unwitnessed.

How common it is, and what it brings with it

  • Among people 65 and over in the US, total diabetes prevalence is about 27% and prediabetes nearly 50% — both higher than in younger groups
  • About 20% of people who meet the criteria are undiagnosed
  • Cardiovascular burden rises steeply with age: of US adults with diabetes reporting heart disease or stroke, 28% of those aged 35–64, 43% at 65–74 and 55% at 75 or over
  • Diabetic kidney disease is the leading cause of CKD in the United States

Diagnosis, and the drugs that fake it

Ch 99 Table 99-1 gives three routes to the diagnosis, and they apply regardless of age — there is no separate older-adult threshold.

A1cFasting plasma glucoseOGTT, 2-hour
Diabetes≥6.5%≥126 mg/dL (7.0 mmol/L)≥200 mg/dL (11.1 mmol/L)
Prediabetes5.7–6.4%100–125 mg/dL140–199 mg/dL
Normal<5.7%<100 mg/dL<140 mg/dL

Fasting means no caloric intake for at least eight hours, and any criterion should be confirmed on a separate day unless the patient is frankly symptomatic. About 90% of older adults with diabetes have type 2, where asymptomatic hyperglycaemia is the hallmark and ketoacidosis is not part of the syndrome.

Drugs that raise glucose and can manufacture a diagnosis (Table 99-2): diuretics, α-adrenergic agonists, β-blockers, alcohol, calcium-channel blockers, clozapine — alongside the corticosteroids everyone remembers.

Hazzard's own framework, which is not the ADA's

Table 99-6 sorts patients into three health groups and gives glucose ranges for each, with a second, higher set of targets where sulphonylureas or insulin are in use — a distinction the ADA table does not make, and the sort of thing a chapter-referenced stem is built on.

GroupWithout SU or insulinOn SU or insulin
1 — good health
no or 1–2 non-diabetes illnesses, no ADL impairment, ≤1 IADL		 fasting 90–130, bedtime 90–150, A1c <7.5% fasting 90–150, bedtime 100–180, A1c ≥7.0 and <7.5%
2 — intermediate
3+ non-diabetes illnesses, or MCI/early dementia, or ≥2 IADL impairments		 fasting 90–150, bedtime 100–180, A1c <8% fasting 100–150, bedtime 150–180, A1c ≥7.5 and <8.0%
3 — poor health
end-stage illness, moderate-severe dementia, ≥2 ADL impairments, or long-term care		 fasting 100–180, bedtime 110–200, A1c <8.5% fasting 100–180, bedtime 150–250, A1c ≥8.0 and <8.5%

Note the lower bounds in the right-hand column. On a sulphonylurea or insulin the chapter sets a floor as well as a ceiling — an A1c of 6.8% in group 2 is a target breached downward, which is the point the ADA makes in prose and Hazzard makes in a number.

The ADA targets, exactly as written

The exam cites this section by name. The 2026 edition numbers the recommendations, and the table below is its Table 13.2 reduced to what gets examined.

Health statusA1cCGMFastingBedtimeBlood pressure
Healthy — few chronic illnesses, intact cognition and function <7.0–7.5%TIR ≥70%, TBR ≤4% 80–13080–180<130/80
Complex / intermediate — multiple illnesses, or 2+ ADL impairments, or mild-to-moderate cognitive impairment <8.0%TIR ≥50%, TBR <1% 90–150100–180<130/80
Very complex / poor health — long-term care, end-stage illness, moderate-to-severe cognitive impairment, or 2+ ADL impairments Avoid reliance on A1c— 100–180110–200<140/90

Glucose in mg/dL. “Multiple” chronic illnesses means at least three. Statin unless contraindicated in the first two rows; in the third, consider the likelihood of benefit — the time to benefit for a statin is 2.5 years, which is the number that decides it. A1c is unreliable after transfusion and in conditions altering red-cell turnover, which in this population means kidney failure, recent blood loss and erythropoietin.

Prevention, and the exercise prescription

  • In the Diabetes Prevention Program, caloric restriction plus exercise cut progression from prediabetes to type 2 diabetes despite only 5–7% weight reduction being achieved — the modest number is the point, because it is attainable
  • The activity prescription, stated exactly: at least 150 minutes a week of moderate-intensity aerobic activity, spread over at least 3 days, with no more than 2 consecutive days without exercise, plus resistance training at least twice a week

Screening: the tools and their cut-points

Recommendation 13.2 is to screen at least annually for geriatric syndromes. Table 13.1 names the instrument and the number for each, and it doubles as a revision list for the whole syllabus.

DomainInstrumentCut-point
CognitionMini-Cog<3 of 5
Delirium4AT≥4 of 12
DepressionGDS-5≥2 of 5
FallsSTEADIany single “yes” of 3
FrailtyClinical Frailty Scale≥5 of 9
MalnutritionMNA-SF12–14 normal · 8–11 at risk · 0–7 malnourished
SarcopeniaSARC-F≥4 of 10
InsomniaISI-7≥8 of 28
