Screening for mild cognitive impairment or dementia is recommended from age 65, at the first visit and annually — and again whenever self-care slips: insulin dose errors, skipped meals, failure to recognise a hypo.

Simplifying insulin, by the algorithm

  • Move the basal dose from bedtime to morning, and titrate on fasting glucose over a week to a target of 90–150 mg/dL: up by 2 or more units if half the fasting values are above goal, down by 2 or more if more than two a week fall below 80
  • Premixed insulin: take 70% of the total premixed dose and give it as basal only, in the morning
  • Prandial above 10 units a dose: halve it and add a non-insulin agent, then titrate the prandial down as the other agent goes up. Prandial at 10 units or less: stop it and add a non-insulin agent
  • Add metformin 500 mg daily if eGFR is 45 or above; otherwise go to a second-line agent chosen on comorbidity
  • No rapid- or short-acting insulin at bedtime, and stop the correction scale once it is not needed daily

The 4S pathway, which is the framework the 2026 edition builds on. Step one, investigate red flags — a medical or life event, a change in physical, cognitive or mental status, medication adverse effects, changed medication-taking behaviour, signs of unrecognised hypoglycaemia, symptoms of hyperglycaemia. Step two, re-evaluate the glycaemic goal with the patient and the care partner. Step three, deintensify, simplify or modify. Step four, reassess — two weeks of continuous glucose monitoring to see the actual pattern.

Where Hazzard and the ADA differ — answer to the stem's source

Hazzard ch 99ADA 2026 §13
Blood pressureTarget <140/90; consider 130/80 in high-risk patients<130/80 for most; relaxed to <140/90 in poor health
Statin time to benefitCVD prevention benefit apparent within 1–2 years2.5 years (Yourman)

Neither is wrong; they are different documents written at different times. If the מראה מקום points at ch 99, answer 140/90. If it points at the ADA standards, answer 130/80. Knowing that the two disagree is worth more than knowing either number.

Doses the chapter states outright: metformin 500–1000 mg twice daily, maximum 2500 mg/day (ER 500–2000 mg once daily); low-dose aspirin 75–162 mg/day for secondary prevention after assessing bleeding risk; SGLT2 inhibitors need renal dose adjustment and are avoided below eGFR 25–30.

Drugs, with the 2026 caveats

  • Metformin down to eGFR 30, reduced dose at 30–45, eGFR every 3–6 months if kidney function is falling. Check B12 periodically, particularly where there is anaemia or peripheral neuropathy — that is the ADA's wording; the four-year mark often quoted alongside it comes from observational data (DPPOS) rather than from the Standards. Watch the appetite suppression in someone already losing weight
  • Sulfonylureas: glyburide avoided outright; glipizide preferred for its shorter action, though a recent analysis found the highest rate of major adverse cardiovascular events with glipizide. Antimicrobials — fluoroquinolones and co-trimoxazole above all — raise the effective dose and precipitate hypoglycaemia, so reduce or hold the sulfonylurea
  • DPP-4 inhibitors: weak but safe; linagliptin needs no renal adjustment
  • GLP-1 receptor agonists: not preferred where there is unexplained weight loss, undernutrition, problematic constipation, gastroparesis or prior bowel obstruction; monitor for dehydration and loss of muscle mass
  • SGLT2 inhibitors: volume depletion in the frail or orthostatic, genital mycotic infection, more urinary frequency — ask about incontinence before and after starting — and euglycaemic ketoacidosis, most often triggered by infection in long-term care
  • Pioglitazone: heart failure, fluid retention, weight gain, osteoporosis, macular oedema

In long-term care, and at the end of life

Ch 99's end-of-life goals (Table 99-16) add a target the ADA section leaves in prose: be respectful and supportive, match the level of intervention to the stage of illness, support self-management as long as possible, and aim for a painless and symptom-free death — while avoiding metabolic decompensation, that is hypoglycaemia, ketoacidosis, hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state and persistent symptomatic hyperglycaemia. The chapter names a working glucose range rather than an A1c: 6–15 mmol/L, that is 108–270 mg/dL. It also names two goals that are easy to forget at this stage — avoiding foot complications in the frail, bed-bound patient, and avoiding symptomatic volume depletion.

The long-term-care alert thresholds above come from ADA 2026 §13, not from ch 99. Both documents cover this ground and a stem may cite either.

The alert thresholds are specified, and the reason they exist is that a resident may be reviewed only every 30 to 60 days. Call immediately for a glucose below 70 — but treat first. Call as soon as possible for values of 70–100, for two readings above 250 within 24 hours alongside a change in clinical status, for values consistently above 250 over 24 hours or above 300 over two days, for an unreadably high result, or for illness with vomiting, fever, lethargy or poor intake.

At the end of life the 2026 text sets out three states. The stable patient continues their plan with hypoglycaemia prevention as the priority and no role for A1c. The patient in organ failure has hypoglycaemia-causing agents reduced and dehydration prevented — in type 1 diabetes insulin is reduced as intake falls but never stopped. The dying patient with type 2 diabetes can reasonably have all agents discontinued; in type 1 there is no consensus, and a small amount of basal insulin may still be given to prevent ketoacidosis and symptoms. Withdrawal of statins in advanced life-limiting illness improved quality of life in a randomised trial.

Hazzard ch 98, p1545 — 5 questions across three of four sittings. Two examinable ideas: the reference range moves with age, and the subclinical states are decided by the number and the age together.

The reference range moves

TSH rises with normal ageing, so a TSH of 5–6 in an 85-year-old may be age-appropriate rather than disease. Treating it to a young adult's range is a recognised harm, and higher TSH in the very old has been associated with better, not worse, survival.

Subclinical hypothyroidism — raised TSH, normal free T4

Exam pearl

A TSH of 6 in an 85-year-old is usually age, not disease. Repeat it in three months and resist the levothyroxine.

  • Prevalence about 10% at 65 and over, more in women. Repeat first: in 1 to 3 months if the TSH is 4.5–14.9, in 1 to 2 weeks if 15 or higher — recovery from silent thyroiditis or non-thyroidal illness explains many of them
  • Figure 98-4, the chapter's rule at 65 and over: treat at a persistent TSH of 10 or higher, consider treating at 7.0–9.9, observe below 7. TSH of 10 or more predicts cardiovascular mortality, coronary disease and heart failure independent of age; 7 or more predicts cardiovascular mortality. It is not associated with fractures, dementia or depression, and one study found lower mortality in older people with it. The randomised trial in the over-60s showed no benefit in fatigue or symptoms, and no trial has clinical endpoints
  • Start at 25 or 50 µg — the smallest tablets, and the chapter's stated starting dose; “start low, go slow” in cardiac disease is convention never tested in a trial. Recheck TSH at 7 to 8 weeks in the old (6 elsewhere), increments of 25 µg early and 12 µg above 75–100 µg. Target TSH toward the upper limit of normal, as high as 4–6 mU/L over 80 — the 2025 committee answer. Subclinical replacement averages 1 µg/kg/day; full replacement in the old is below the young adult's 1.6. No T3, no desiccated thyroid

Absorption: take it fasting, separated from calcium, iron, proton pump inhibitors and soya. A rising dose requirement usually means an interaction or adherence, not progression — Table 98-7 groups the culprits as drugs that reduce absorption (calcium carbonate, iron, PPIs), drugs that increase metabolism (carbamazepine, phenytoin, rifampicin), and conditions that raise TBG; the 2024 answer was “all of the above”.

Subclinical hyperthyroidism — suppressed TSH, normal free hormones

Prevalence 1–6% on a single test and it persists in more than half on repeat at 3 to 6 months. Ch 98's position is unqualified: treat older people with subclinical hyperthyroidism to laboratory euthyroidism, because it raises atrial fibrillation, heart failure, overall cardiovascular mortality, fracture and dementia. The 0.1 versus 0.1–0.4 split is guideline convention, not the chapter. The causes are those of overt disease: autonomous nodules in a nodular gland (commoner with age, and the one an iodine load unmasks), Graves, over-replacement, amiodarone. Methimazole is preferred over PTU for half-life and safety; agranulocytosis in 0.1–0.5% with either; radioiodine is definitive for an autonomous nodule and often leaves the rest of the gland euthyroid.

Presentation is atypical, and that is the question

What you expectWhat you get in the old
Hyperthyroidism: tremor, heat intolerance, hyperkinesisApathetic thyrotoxicosis — weight loss, depression, apathy, atrial fibrillation, heart failure. Fewer symptoms, and often only one
Hypothyroidism: cold, weight gain, coarse skinFatigue, cognitive slowing, constipation, falls, depression — read as ageing or as dementia

New atrial fibrillation, unexplained weight loss or a change in cognition all justify a TSH. Myxoedema coma — hypothermia, hyponatraemia, hypoventilation, bradycardia, depressed consciousness, usually precipitated by infection, cold, alcohol, or narcotics, sedatives and antipsychotics — is treated by drawing a cortisol, giving intravenous hydrocortisone first (thyroid hormone without it can precipitate adrenal crisis; stop it once cortisol is adequate), then levothyroxine 200–400 µg followed by 75–100 µg daily. T3 is discouraged in the old for cardiac risk, and sedatives are avoided because every drug is cleared slowly. The committee's 2020 answer was the hydrocortisone. Hypoglycaemia and a raised CK are part of the picture.

Do not screen thyroid function during acute illness if it can wait: non-thyroidal illness syndrome produces low T3, sometimes low T4 and a variably low TSH, and it recovers with the illness. Thyroid nodules are common with age and most are benign; ultrasound and selective fine-needle aspiration, with less aggression as life expectancy shortens.

Amiodarone, which is a separate disease

Type 1Type 2
MechanismIodine-induced excess synthesis in an abnormal gland — nodular goitre, latent GravesDestructive thyroiditis in a normal gland, releasing stored hormone
Doppler flowNormal or increased vascularityAbsent vascularity
TreatmentThionamideGlucocorticoid

Ch 98 says the two cannot be told apart at presentation — radioiodine scanning is blocked by the drug's own iodide (37% by weight) — so patients are often started on both corticosteroid and methimazole. The Doppler-flow distinction is guideline teaching, not the chapter — the 2018 European Thyroid Association guideline (Bartalena et al., Eur Thyroid J 2018;7:55, read from the paper), which also says glucocorticoids can be added from the start when the type is uncertain and that stopping amiodarone is a joint cardiology–endocrine decision. Expect a benign transient TSH rise and a chronically higher free T4 with lower T3 that need no treatment — the committee's 2021 answer was “common side effect, observe”. In most cases amiodarone is not stopped: the effects take months to wear off and thyroid dysfunction is managed alongside it. Hypothyroidism arises in those with Hashimoto disease and is often reversible on cessation.

Nodules, and how hard to look

Ultrasound documents size in three dimensions and the high-risk features: hypoechogenicity, irregular margins, taller-than-wide shape, intranodular vascularity and microcalcifications (the 2025 answer); spongiform or mixed cystic–solid appearance is low risk. Lymph nodes are assessed and a TSH drawn.

Thyroid nodules become the rule rather than the exception with age and the great majority are benign. Check TSH first: a suppressed TSH points to an autonomously functioning nodule, which is scanned rather than biopsied. Otherwise ultrasound decides who needs fine-needle aspiration, by size and by sonographic pattern. Anaplastic carcinoma is a disease of the old — a rapidly enlarging, hard, fixed neck mass with hoarseness or stridor is an emergency, not a routine referral. Against that, a small papillary carcinoma in an 88-year-old may reasonably be watched: the same life-expectancy reasoning that governs screening governs this too.

Hazzard ch 81, p1235 — 5 questions across three of four sittings. In this population the examinable content is less about the drugs than about diagnosis at the margins and about whether the patient can physically use the device.

Diagnosis, with the age caveat

Post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC below 0.70 confirms persistent airflow limitation. But that fixed ratio overdiagnoses in the old, because the ratio falls with normal ageing and a ratio under 0.70 is frequent in healthy never-smokers over 65; ch 81 calls this GOLD's first flaw, and expressing FEV1 as percent-predicted its second. The lower limit of normal — the fifth percentile, or a Z-score — halves the prevalence: 37.7% by GOLD against 15.4% by Z-score in older persons, and the excess is not associated with worse outcomes. A breathless older patient without a smoking history is more often in heart failure, deconditioned, anaemic or obese — and the two commonly coexist, which is why an unexplained response to diuresis does not exclude COPD and vice versa.

Assessment and grouping

Grade symptoms with mMRC or CAT, then group by exacerbation history. Ch 81 was written to the older A–D scheme (it puts the eosinophil rule in “Group D”); the current GOLD scheme is A, B and E, with E for two or more moderate exacerbations or one hospitalisation in a year, whatever the symptom burden. Spirometric grade and symptom group are separate axes and questions exploit the confusion. The chapter adds its own screen: blood eosinophils and an α1-antitrypsin level at diagnosis.

Treatment

  • Long-acting bronchodilators are the backbone — LAMA, LABA, or the combination. Inhaled anticholinergics are not a Beers problem; systemic ones are. Theophylline is third or fourth line at best — narrow window, arrhythmia and seizures, and ciprofloxacin raises the level (asked in 2024)
  • Inhaled corticosteroids where exacerbations persist, especially with blood eosinophils above about 300, or with asthma overlap. Against that: pneumonia risk, oral candidiasis, bruising and bone loss, all of which matter more here
  • Pulmonary rehabilitation is the intervention with the largest effect on dyspnoea, exercise capacity and quality of life, and it is under-referred at this age. After an exacerbation it also reduces readmission
  • Long-term oxygen (Table 81-11, asked twice) for resting hypoxaemia — PaO2 at or below 55 mmHg, or at or below 59 with cor pulmonale, right heart failure or a haematocrit above 55%. Worn more than 16 hours a day it improves survival in severe resting hypoxaemia. For isolated moderate resting or exertional desaturation an RCT found no benefit in lung function, exercise, quality of life, admissions or mortality — the chapter permits it only for exertional desaturation under 88% or PaO2 under 55 and a demonstrated gain in dyspnoea or exercise capacity. Nocturnal-only oxygen without daytime hypoxaemia: unclear. Home NIV added to oxygen for persistent hypercapnia (PaCO2 over 53) within four weeks of a hypercapnic exacerbation lengthens time to readmission and cuts death over the next year
  • Vaccinate. START v3 names four and only four: seasonal influenza annually, pneumococcal, varicella-zoster, and SARS-CoV-2. RSV and a pertussis-containing booster are recommended for older adults by public-health bodies but are not START criteria — on a criteria-specific stem, picking them loses the mark
  • Smoking cessation is the only thing that changes the slope of decline, at any age

The device is the intervention

Exam pearl

Before escalating any inhaler, watch the patient use the one they have. A trial of a new drug in a patient with poor technique tests the technique.

Arthritic hands cannot fire a pressurised inhaler; low inspiratory flow defeats a dry-powder device — a DPI needs a peak inspiratory flow above 45 L/min to disaggregate the powder, deposits 10–40% in the lung against 10–20% for a pressurised inhaler, but up to 80% in the oropharynx; a pressurised inhaler needs a slow deep breath, preferably through a spacer; a soft-mist inhaler needs only a gentle breath and suits low flow or poor coordination; and a nebuliser is the easiest of all (Figure 81-2, the committee's 2023 algorithm question). Cognitive impairment defeats anything needing coordination. Check the technique in front of you at every visit, and choose a spacer or a nebuliser rather than escalating a drug the patient is not receiving. A trial of a new inhaler in a patient with poor technique tests the technique, not the drug.

Exacerbations and what follows

Intensified bronchodilator first, withholding the long-acting agents temporarily if the patient is on frequent nebulised doses. Systemic corticosteroid for severe exacerbations — the five-day oral course is GOLD, not the chapter; what ch 81 says is that delirium is more common above 60 mg daily. Antibiotics where sputum purulence or volume increases, especially in moderate or severe exacerbations, for 3 to 7 days in the absence of pneumonia or bronchiectasis. Sputum culture is not needed in a routine exacerbation — it cannot separate colonisers from pathogens — but it earns its place after failed outpatient treatment or with Pseudomonas risk: admission in the past 3 months, four or more antibiotic courses in a year, or severe obstruction (the 2025 answer for the winter admission). Expect resistant organisms (MRSA, Pseudomonas) in nursing-home residents, anyone in acute or subacute care within 90 days, and FEV1 under 30%. Non-invasive ventilation for acute hypercapnia reduces intubation, length of stay, ventilator pneumonia and death, and is not withheld on age alone. Discharge means pulmonary rehabilitation referral, an oxygen and NIV decision, and a step-up in maintenance therapy. In advanced disease, low-dose opioids relieve refractory breathlessness, oxygen helps only the hypoxaemic, and a handheld fan genuinely works. Advance care planning belongs at the second admission, not the last one.

Breathlessness in an older patient is rarely one disease

COPD, heart failure, deconditioning, anaemia, obesity, pulmonary hypertension, thromboembolism and anxiety coexist, and treating one to the exclusion of the others is why patients stop improving. Two practical consequences: natriuretic peptides and echocardiography earn their place when the response to bronchodilators is poor, and a six-minute walk or a sit-to-stand test tells you more about function than any spirometric number.

The company COPD keeps

  • Cardiovascular disease — the commonest cause of death in mild-to-moderate COPD. Cardioselective beta-blockers are not contraindicated and are systematically withheld
  • Muscle wasting and weight loss — independent predictors of mortality; resistance training and nutrition, not just inhalers
  • Osteoporosis — from steroids, smoking, inactivity and low body weight
  • Anxiety and depression — present in a large minority, under-treated, and a major driver of readmission
  • Lung cancer — the risk is concentrated in exactly this group, and screening decisions turn on life expectancy and fitness for treatment rather than age

Advance care planning belongs in the clinic during a good spell: what the patient wants if ventilation is needed, whether non-invasive ventilation is a ceiling or a bridge, and who decides if they cannot. Deciding it at three in the morning during a hypercapnic exacerbation is how it usually happens, and it is the wrong time.

Hazzard ch 101 p1607 and ch 100 p1589 — 6 q across three of four sittings

Three entities that overlap in the same patient and are separated by where the pain is, how fast it came, and what the serology does. RA, lupus and the drug-induced syndromes are ch 101; polymyalgia and giant cell arteritis are ch 100. Gout has no Hazzard chapter of its own — the committee's gout questions cite the AGS Geriatrics Review Syllabus.

Late-onset rheumatoid arthritis, and what the chapter says is different

Late-onset RA (ch 101, Table 101-2)Polymyalgia rheumatica (ch 100)
WhoPrevalence highest in the oldest groups; about 5% of women over 55 have RA; incidence peaks in the sixth to eighth decades. Equal sex distribution, unlike the 2–3:1 female excess of younger onsetOver 50, 90% over 60, women 2:1, northern European ancestry; two to three times commoner than GCA
DistributionLarge joints and the shoulder more often involved at presentation; small-foot-joint synovitis commoner than in PMR. A PMR-like girdle onset is recognisedNeck and limb-girdle aching and stiffness for at least a month; shoulder (75–90%) more than hip (50–70%). A mild non-erosive polyarthritis of hands, wrists and knees in a third; dorsal hand pitting oedema in up to 8%
Onset“Benign polyarthritis of older adults” in up to a third: explosive, infection-like, with fever and night sweats, remitting within a year with or without treatment. RS3PE — remitting seronegative symmetric synovitis with pitting oedema — is the male-predominant (2–3:1) extreme of it, ESR high, prednisone-responsiveAbrupt or slowly progressive; constitutional symptoms in a third but high fever uncommon; no true weakness on examination
SerologyESR rises with age anyway, and RF positivity reaches 30% of healthy 90-year-olds. Earlier reports of more seronegative disease in late onset were not confirmed. Anti-CCP is as sensitive as RF (70–78%) and more specific (88–96%), does not rise with normal ageing, marks erosive disease — and separates late-onset RA from PMR: 65% of LORA positive, no PMR patient positiveRF and ANA negative. ESR over 40, often 100; normocytic anaemia in two-thirds; CK normal. Acute-phase reactant raised in 80–90% at presentation — a normal one does not exclude it
PrognosisSeropositive disease is more severe, more erosive, worse function, higher mortality — in the old as in the young. Very high RF: think cryoglobulinaemia. Sicca symptoms: work up secondary SjögrenImprovement within 2 weeks, near-complete by 4. No response should prompt a search for another diagnosis — including GCA, which is present in 15–20%

The mimics ch 101 lists for a new polyarthritis in an old patient: PMR, osteoarthritis (including the erosive inflammatory form), crystal arthritis, malignancy-associated arthritis, late-onset spondyloarthropathy, hypothyroidism, hyperparathyroidism, diabetic cheiroarthropathy, amyloid, oedematous scleroderma. ESR, not RF titre, tracks disease activity; anti-CCP titre is not used for follow-up.

Polymyalgia: the steroid course, by the numbers

  • Start at the lowest effective dose in the range 12.5–25 mg prednisone daily — the higher end for those at high relapse risk. Reduce to 10 mg within 4 to 8 weeks, then 1 mg every 4 weeks once in remission. Symptoms, not the ESR, guide the taper; alternate-day dosing is inferior
  • A course takes at least 12 to 18 months; three-quarters are off steroids by two years; 10–30% need a low chronic dose; relapse during taper in about a quarter
  • Methotrexate is the only steroid-sparing agent with randomised evidence, considered early where relapse or steroid toxicity is likely; tocilizumab is second line for individual cases. NSAIDs do not lower the ESR and do not suppress a subclinical GCA
  • Screen for GCA at every visit; a rising ESR after initial fall, or failure of low-dose steroid, points to it or to another diagnosis — and biopsy is still worth doing on steroids

Giant cell arteritis — the emergency

Headache in a temporal or occipital distribution (65%), visual disturbance (30%), permanent visual loss 10–15%, jaw claudication 45%, swallowing or tongue claudication, arm claudication, cough. A decreased temporal pulse (46%) is a commoner sign than scalp tenderness (27%). Constitutional symptoms can be the only manifestation, and the fever can meet FUO criteria. PMR in 40–60% and the presenting feature in 25%. Large-vessel disease in a quarter; aortic aneurysm years later, so a yearly chest radiograph.

Treat first, biopsy second — but biopsy within the week. The risk of visual loss mandates steroids on suspicion: prednisone 1 mg/kg (40–60 mg) daily, or 1000 mg IV methylprednisolone daily with active visual symptoms, held for 4 to 8 weeks then tapered over months; most patients need about two years and relapse in up to two-thirds, usually as PMR. Temporal artery biopsy remains the gold standard — at least 1 cm, preferably over 2, sectioned every 3–5 mm because of skip lesions — and its sensitivity holds on steroids but it is ideally not delayed beyond one week. An initial negative biopsy occurs in up to a third; giant cells are found in only half of positives. Doppler halo sign is neither sensitive nor specific enough to replace it. The 1990 ACR criteria (Table 100-5) act as diagnostic criteria when biopsy is unavailable: sensitivity 94%, specificity 91%. Vision lost for more than a few hours very rarely returns.

  • Tocilizumab (GiACTA, FDA-approved) early for new-onset disease at high risk of steroid harm, relapse or prolonged treatment, and at relapse. Methotrexate: modest steroid-sparing effect; infliximab ineffective
  • Low-dose aspirin reduces cranial ischaemic events, particularly anterior ischaemic optic neuropathy
  • Bone protection from day one; Pneumocystis prophylaxis at prednisone 20 mg or more. Twenty to fifty percent develop steroid toxicity; life expectancy is otherwise normal unless there is severe aortitis

Late-onset lupus, and the drugs that imitate it

  • About 10% of lupus begins after 55, and the delay to diagnosis averages 2 to 3 years. Female-to-male 4:1 against 9:1 in the young. Milder: less rash, photosensitivity, alopecia, ulcers, nephritis and lymphadenopathy; more cytopenias, serositis and interstitial pneumonitis. Death is from treatment — infection, cardiovascular disease, stroke
  • Low-titre ANA is present in up to a third of healthy older adults; anti-dsDNA and anti-Sm are specific. The 2019 EULAR/ACR criteria are unvalidated in the old
  • Drug-induced lupus: over 100 drugs, onset 50–70, more often men; antihistone antibodies typical of procainamide and hydralazine, less so of minocycline and anti-TNF. A third on procainamide over a year become symptomatic and nearly all ANA-positive by two; under 20% on hydralazine, dose-dependent above 200 mg/day. Fewer renal, neuropsychiatric and skin features; pleuropulmonary symptoms common with procainamide. It resolves on withdrawal, by definition
  • Antimalarials for arthritis, serositis, mucositis and skin, long term; avoid NSAIDs with renal involvement

Before you start an immunosuppressant

  • Fungal, tuberculous and atypical mycobacterial infection is the chief risk of anticytokine therapy in the old, and infection rates were higher in older RA patients in the CORRONA registry. TB skin test or interferon-gamma release assay plus a chest radiograph before starting; yearly rescreening for those at risk, including nursing-home residents. Hepatitis B reactivation with rituximab
  • Immunise before the DMARD or biologic, especially before rituximab. Influenza and pneumococcal as for the general population; holding methotrexate for 2 weeks after influenza vaccination improves the response without a meaningful flare. Tetanus immunoglobulin rather than toxoid within 24 weeks of rituximab. No live vaccines on biologics; the recombinant zoster vaccine is the safe option, and RA activity, biologics, prednisone and hydroxychloroquine all raise zoster risk
  • Methotrexate is weekly, with folate; parenteral if dyspepsia or dysphagia; extreme caution with any chronic or active infection

Crystal and septic arthritis — not in Hazzard

Exam pearl

Aspirate first. Crystals in the fluid do not exclude infection, and the two coexist often enough to kill someone.

Neither ch 100 nor ch 101 covers gout, pseudogout or septic arthritis beyond listing them as mimics; the committee's gout questions cite the GRS. What follows is conventional teaching, not textbook-cited, and the one sitting that asked it wanted: steroids for polyarticular gout given for 5 to 10 days with a taper.

  • Gout in the old is more often polyarticular, tophaceous, upper-limb and diuretic-related, and mistaken for infection or RA. NSAIDs are usually the wrong answer — renal impairment, heart failure, anticoagulation, GI bleeding; low-dose colchicine, a short steroid course or an intra-articular steroid instead
  • Allopurinol started low and titrated, with colchicine cover for the first months, not stopped during an attack and not started without cover. Calcium pyrophosphate: chondrocalcinosis, wrists and knees, positively birefringent rhomboids, symptomatic treatment only
  • Septic arthritis: often afebrile, often on a damaged or prosthetic joint. Aspirate before treating; Gram stain, culture, cell count; empirical antibiotics after the sample; drainage

Hazzard ch 27, p371 — this is the chapter the analysis could not name. It appeared in every one of the 2024–2026 sittings and had no section here because the number had never been resolved to a title. It is Perioperative Care, and it sits alongside ch 28 Anesthesia (p383) and ch 29 Surgical Quality and Outcomes (p399).

What the preoperative assessment is actually for

Not to clear the patient. To estimate risk, modify what can be modified, and set expectations — and in a geriatric patient the outcome that matters is often function and independence rather than 30-day mortality. Ask what the operation is meant to achieve and whether the patient's goals survive the likely recovery.

InstrumentWhat it adds
Revised Cardiac Risk IndexSix predictors: high-risk surgery, ischaemic heart disease, heart failure, cerebrovascular disease, insulin-treated diabetes, creatinine above 2 mg/dL
Functional capacityUnder 4 METs — cannot climb a flight of stairs or walk up a hill — marks poor capacity. It is the cheapest and most informative question in the assessment
ASA classCrude but universal; see the anaesthetic note below
Frailty — CFS, Fried, EdmontonPredicts complications, institutional discharge and mortality independently of RCRI and ASA, and is the geriatric addition the chapter exists to make
Cognition — Mini-CogPre-existing impairment is the strongest predictor of postoperative delirium. Document a baseline or you cannot diagnose delirium afterwards

Also assess: nutrition (albumin and unintentional weight loss), the medication list, alcohol and tobacco, falls history, sensory impairment, social support and the discharge destination. Routine preoperative testing — ECG, chest radiograph, full panels — in an asymptomatic patient having low-risk surgery does not improve outcomes and generates false trails.

Drugs, held and continued

ContinueHold
Beta-blockers — never stop abruptly; withdrawal causes rebound ischaemia. Do not start one on the day of surgeryACE inhibitors and ARBs on the morning of surgery, to reduce induction hypotension
StatinsSGLT2 inhibitors, 3–4 days before — euglycaemic ketoacidosis
Levodopa, on the patient's own scheduleDiuretics on the morning; most oral hypoglycaemics
Inhalers, thyroid replacement, antiepilepticsConsider holding a GLP-1 agonist — delayed gastric emptying and aspiration at induction

Anticoagulation: most minor procedures do not need interruption; where a DOAC is stopped, timing follows renal function and bleeding risk, and bridging with heparin is usually unnecessary and harmful outside a mechanical valve or very high thrombotic risk. Antiplatelets after a coronary stent: elective surgery is deferred until the mandatory dual-antiplatelet period is complete; aspirin is usually continued through.

The numbers ch 27 gives, and the exam has used

  • 25–30% of all perioperative deaths are cardiac — the 2020 committee answer. LVEF under 40% is an independent MACE risk; heart failure with preserved EF still raises it, and two-thirds of older adults with heart failure have normal systolic function. A prior stroke is a MACE risk factor (2023)
  • In the over-80s after major non-cardiac surgery, any complication multiplies 30-day mortality from 4% to 26%. Postoperative atrial fibrillation in about 25%; a beta-blocker or amiodarone reduces it but is not routinely recommended
  • Delirium in 10–15% after general surgery, 30% after cardiac surgery, up to 50% after hip fracture repair; it predicts worse recovery and long-term decline. Postoperative cognitive dysfunction in 26% at one week in the over-60s after abdominal or orthopaedic surgery (ISPOCD), with older age, lower education and prior cognitive impairment as risks
  • Anticoagulants: warfarin — hold four doses to an INR under 1.5, check on the day, vitamin K 1 mg IV or 2.5 mg oral if needed; LMWH bridging only for the high-thrombotic patient, stopped 24 h before and restarted 24–48 h after; DOACs need no bridging, stopped 1 to 4 days before by renal function and bleeding risk. Elective surgery waits 3 months after a DVT or PE (asked 2024)
  • Transfuse for symptoms, and possibly below 7 g/dL; preoperative IV iron in the anaemic reduces transfusion

Postoperative delirium is the complication of this chapter

Exam pearl

Undertreated pain causes more postoperative delirium than opioids do. The answer is the right analgesia, not less of it.

The commonest surgical complication in older patients, and largely preventable by the same multicomponent programme used on the ward. Prevention beats treatment here more decisively than anywhere else: orientation, glasses and hearing aids back on immediately, early mobilisation, sleep protection, hydration, bowel and bladder care, adequate analgesia — undertreated pain is a delirium precipitant, not a protection against one.

  • Avoid meperidine, benzodiazepines, anticholinergics including scopolamine and promethazine, and high-dose antihistamines
  • Regional versus general anaesthesia has not been shown to change the rate of delirium or of functional recovery after hip fracture in the large trials — a favourite question with a counterintuitive answer
  • Depth-of-anaesthesia monitoring and avoiding excessively deep planes is reasonable, and the evidence for it is softer than it is often presented
  • Remove catheters and lines as early as possible; every one of them is a tether and a source of sepsis

The DNR order does not evaporate in the operating theatre. A blanket suspension is not acceptable practice: the correct approach is a required reconsideration before surgery, documenting which interventions the patient does and does not want and for how long afterwards. This is examinable both as ethics and as procedure.

Hazzard ch 31, p437 — and הפרעות בליעה is on the official exam topic list in its own right. The chapter that connects stroke, Parkinson disease, dementia, pneumonia and the feeding-tube question.

Presbyphagia is not dysphagia

Ageing slows the swallow, reduces tongue pressure and lengthens the pharyngeal phase — presbyphagia, a reduced reserve that is compensated in health and decompensates under any insult. Dysphagia is the symptomatic disorder. The distinction matters because a stroke or a pneumonia unmasks presbyphagia rather than creating a new disease.

OropharyngealOesophageal
ComplaintDifficulty starting the swallow, coughing or choking on swallowing, nasal regurgitation, wet voice, droolingFood sticking after the swallow, seconds later, retrosternal
Causes in the oldStroke, Parkinson disease, dementia, motor neurone disease, myasthenia, cervical osteophytes, Zenker diverticulum, head and neck cancer or its radiotherapy, xerostomia, drugsMotility disorders, stricture including peptic, eosinophilic oesophagitis, malignancy, pill oesophagitis
First testBedside screen, then videofluoroscopy or FEESEndoscopy; barium swallow; manometry

Drug causes are worth a separate sweep: anticholinergics and diuretics through dry mouth, antipsychotics and metoclopramide through drug-induced parkinsonism, benzodiazepines and opioids through sedation, and bisphosphonates, doxycycline, potassium chloride and NSAIDs through direct pill oesophagitis — which is why those are taken upright with a full glass of water.

Assessment

  • Screen before the first oral intake after a stroke. A simple water-swallow screen with a trained observer reduces pneumonia
  • Videofluoroscopy is the gold standard, and is the only way to see silent aspiration — passage below the cords with no cough. FEES is the bedside alternative and needs no radiation, useful in a patient who cannot be transported
  • Look for the consequences as well as the cause: weight loss, dehydration, recurrent chest infection, food avoidance, and the social loss of eating with other people

Management, and what the evidence does not support

Exam pearl

Oral hygiene beats thickened fluids for preventing aspiration pneumonia. The intuitive answer and the evidenced one point in different directions.

  • Postural and manoeuvre strategies — chin tuck, head turn to the weak side, supraglottic swallow — taught by a speech and language therapist, and effective in the patients who can follow them
  • Texture modification and thickened fluids reduce visible aspiration but the evidence that they reduce pneumonia is weak, and they reduce palatability, intake and hydration. They are not a free intervention
  • Oral hygiene is one of the few measures with real evidence against aspiration pneumonia — it is the oral flora that is aspirated, and this is the cheapest thing on the list
  • Upright positioning for the meal and for 30 minutes after; unhurried, small mouthfuls; self-feeding where safe; minimise sedating drugs at mealtimes
  • In advanced dementia, tube feeding does none of what it is used for — no better survival, no fewer aspiration pneumonias, no pressure-ulcer benefit, no comfort. Careful hand feeding, offered as an active choice, is the alternative. See 67–70 Palliative. Do not generalise that to all dysphagia: the evidence is specific to advanced dementia, where the swallow fails as part of a terminal illness. In acute stroke with a swallow expected to recover, and in motor neurone disease, enteral feeding is standard and gastrostomy is offered deliberately — the question is whether the underlying course is recoverable

Hazzard ch 48 p719 — and the MoH procedure the exam names

In Israel this is not only a clinical topic but a statutory reporting duty, and the MoH procedure on abuse of the helpless (נוהל התעמרות בחסרי ישע) is named directly in the exam's source tables. The clinical half below is ch 48; the legal half is the procedure.

The categories, and how often each is reported

TypeAnnual prevalence (ch 48)What it looks like
Psychological / emotional4.6–13% — the most reportedThreats, humiliation, isolation from family and services, infantilisation. The patient defers to the carer and will not speak alone
Financial exploitation3.5–6.6%Unexplained withdrawals, a new controlling relationship, a changed will or power of attorney, unpaid bills despite means
Neglect5.1–5.4%Dehydration, malnutrition, pressure injuries, poor hygiene, untreated conditions, missing glasses, hearing aids or dentures, medication not given. Chronic disease that keeps decompensating despite a plan and resources
Physical0.2–2.1%Injuries to head, face, neck and upper limbs; bruises over 5 cm, on the face, lateral right arm or posterior torso. Against a fall: left cheek or zygoma, neck and ear injuries, and facial or dental injury without limb injury
Sexual0.3–0.6%Genital or anal injury, unexplained infection, inner-thigh bruising

Laboratory markers proposed but not validated: malnutrition, dehydration, hypo- or hyperthermia, rhabdomyolysis, toxicology. The chapter's point is that fracture, depression and malnutrition all have a chronic disease explanation and an abuse explanation, and mistreatment sits in the differential of almost every geriatric presentation.

Risk, recognition and outcome

  • Up to 10% of community-dwelling older adults a year; nearly half of people with dementia are mistreated by carers in smaller studies. As few as 1 in 24 cases reaches the authorities — victims are isolated, ill, demented, afraid of reprisal or of the institution, or protecting the abuser
  • The most consistent risk finding is the relationship: spouses and adult children are the usual perpetrators, sons and daughters equally. Two dependencies run in opposite directions — the victim's on the carer, and the perpetrator's financial and housing dependence on the victim. The “stressed caregiver” is one pattern among several; the schizophrenic adult child and the spouse with progressive dementia are different problems needing different plans
  • Physicians are among the least helpful of 17 occupational groups in reporting to protective services, and only a small fraction of reports come from them
  • Outcomes: more ED visits, admissions, dementia, depression and nursing-home placement, and a threefold mortality against non-abused controls. There are no randomised trials of intervention

Interview the patient and the alleged perpetrator separately and alone. A carer who will not leave the room is itself a finding. The EASI (Elder Abuse Suspicion Index) — five questions to the patient and one to the physician, one “yes” triggering assessment — is validated only in cognitively intact primary-care patients, with sensitivity 0.47 and specificity 0.75. It supports the conversation rather than replaces it. A written safety plan (Table 48-4) is part of managing every case of family violence.

The Israeli duty, which is what gets examined

Exam pearl

The duty to report a helpless person at risk does not bend to the patient's wishes. That is what makes it different from everything else in the ethics syllabus.

  • There is a duty to report a reasonable suspicion of harm to a helpless person (חסר ישע) — someone who cannot care for themselves through age, illness or disability. It falls on the professional, and it is not discharged by telling a relative or a colleague
  • The report goes to the police or to the social worker appointed under the law (עובד סוציאלי לפי חוק); the MoH procedure נוהל התעמרות בחסרי ישע sets out the institutional pathway
  • The duty exists irrespective of the patient's wishes, which is what distinguishes it from most of the consent-based material elsewhere in the syllabus, and it is where a vignette will try to catch you with a competent patient who asks you not to report — and with the patient whose designated חוק סיעוד carer is the one neglecting them
  • Document what was observed rather than what was concluded: injuries described and measured, the account given, who gave it, and who was present

Hazzard ch 53 p793 — and the NEJM review the exam cites by name

שברים is an official exam heading, and this is the fracture that carries the syllabus. Written from ch 53, with the perioperative numbers ch 53 defers to ch 27 and the rehabilitation numbers it defers to ch 55.

The numbers that frame it

  • Average age at fracture is 82. Of those who reach 85, about 19% of women and 12% of men will fracture a hip; by 90, 30% and 20%. A quarter to 30% of hip fractures are in men
  • One-year mortality: about 18% of women and 36% of men, concentrated in the first few months and in those in the poorest health. The fracture itself accounts for nine extra deaths per 100 patients over four years, and the excess persists well beyond the first year even in the fittest
  • Delirium occurs in up to 60% after repair; dementia is the major risk factor, and admission from an institution and heart failure are the hip-specific ones. Proactive geriatric consultation cuts the incidence by a third and severe delirium by half in one study
  • The body pays for the fracture: 3–6% of muscle mass lost within two months, fat mass up 3–4% over the year, nearly 3% of total-hip and more than 4.5% of contralateral femoral-neck bone density lost in the first year — 12.5 times the expected loss. Vitamin D deficiency is very common at presentation
  • More than 75% have at least four comorbid conditions before the fracture

The operation follows the blood supply

About half of hip fractures are femoral-neck (intracapsular) and half intertrochanteric (extracapsular); subtrochanteric fractures, within 5 cm below the lesser trochanter, are less common. Intertrochanteric patients tend to be older with more comorbidity. The femoral neck and head are fed by fine retinacular branches of the medial circumflex femoral artery that lie against the neck, so a neck fracture threatens non-union and osteonecrosis; the intertrochanteric region has a plentiful, redundant supply and heals after fixation.

PatternWhat ch 53 says is done
Femoral neck, non-displacedNon-weight-bearing or in-situ fixation to prevent propagation. A patient who can still walk on it with pain has not excluded a fracture; if plain films are negative, MRI (more sensitive than CT) for marrow oedema
Femoral neck, displacedArthroplasty, partial or total. Total hip replacement gives better long-term results and less pain in the active patient — the HEALTH trial (NEJM 2019) is in the chapter's reading list, and the exam has asked it as function after total versus hemiarthroplasty
IntertrochantericInternal fixation — hip plate and screw, or an intramedullary hip screw. All of these allow weight-bearing as tolerated afterwards
SubtrochantericNot detailed in ch 53. If there was prodromal thigh pain on long-term bisphosphonate, think atypical femoral fracture and image the other side — see 51 Osteoporosis

Non-operative management is a real option for a defined group: those who could not walk before the fracture, advanced dementia with contractures, little pain from the fracture, very high surgical risk, or very short life expectancy. The chapter puts the geriatrician in charge of that “big picture” decision and of the palliative pathway that follows it.

The perioperative decisions that are actually examined

Exam pearl

Ch 53 gives no number for time-to-surgery. The number the exam uses comes from the NEJM review it cites by name: surgery within 24 hours lowers mortality. Quote the source with the number.

  • Timing. Ch 53 says only that the geriatrician's job is to get the patient to theatre rapidly and medically stabilised, and that delay for testing that will not change the operation is the thing to avoid. The Management of Acute Hip Fracture review (Bhandari, NEJM) supplies the figure the committee asks for: operating within 24 hours reduces mortality
  • Anticoagulant clearance is ch 27's material, and it is what stops a same-day operation: warfarin — withhold four scheduled doses to bring the INR under 1.5, measure it on the day, and reverse with a small dose of vitamin K (1 mg IV or 2.5 mg orally, acting within 24 hours) or fresh frozen plasma if it cannot wait. DOACs need no bridging and are stopped 1 to 4 days beforehand according to thrombotic risk, bleeding risk and renal function. LMWH is stopped 24 hours before and restarted 24 to 48 hours after, by bleeding risk
  • General versus spinal anaesthesia: no difference in mortality, and the choice is the surgeon's and anaesthetist's by local practice. That is the whole of what ch 53 says. The trial answer — not in Hazzard, cited from the trial — is REGAIN (Neuman et al., N Engl J Med 2021;385:2025, doi 10.1056/NEJMoa2113514, read from the paper; 1,600 patients aged 50 and over): spinal against general made no difference to the composite of death or inability to walk unassisted at 60 days, and the incidence of delirium was similar
  • A preoperative regional nerve block reduces pain, can be placed by an anaesthetist or a trained emergency physician, often makes intravenous opioids unnecessary after surgery — and may make the urinary catheter unnecessary. Catheters are for patients who cannot roll or use a bedpan for pain, and if placed they come out the morning after surgery
  • Transfusion threshold is ch 27's again: reserve transfusion for symptoms, and possibly a haemoglobin below 7 g/dL; preoperative intravenous iron in anaemic patients reduced postoperative transfusion in small trials. The hip-fracture trial — not in Hazzard, cited from the trial — is FOCUS (Carson et al., N Engl J Med 2011;365:2453, doi 10.1056/NEJMoa1012452, read from the paper; 2,016 patients over 50 with cardiovascular disease or risk factors and a haemoglobin under 10 after hip-fracture surgery): a restrictive trigger of symptoms or 8 g/dL was no worse than a liberal 10 g/dL for death or inability to walk across a room at 60 days — 34.7% vs 35.2%, odds ratio 1.01; a median of two units given in the liberal arm and none in the restrictive. So the textbook says 7, the hip-fracture trial used 8, and both say symptoms first; the exam has not yet asked which
  • Mobilise on the day of surgery, and certainly by day one. Deep-breathing exercises with or without an incentive spirometer — postoperative pulmonary complications are among the most lethal. DVT prophylaxis for 21 to 31 days after surgery, continued into the rehabilitation setting. Pressure-injury vigilance: stage 2 or worse in about 5% within 21 days of the fracture. A bowel regimen from the start, because opioids plus immobility make constipation routine
  • Orthogeriatric co-management. A meta-analysis of 18 studies: reduced in-hospital mortality, reduced long-term mortality, shorter stay. A randomised trial of care on a geriatric ward did not reduce delirium but improved mobility at four months. Watch for the postoperative pair the chapter names, atrial fibrillation and heart failure — and expect the heart failure to worsen after discharge

What to tell the family, in the order recovery happens

Recovery follows a sequence. Depression, upper-limb ADL and cognition peak by about 4 months; balance and gait plateau at about 9 months; lower-limb activities and instrumental tasks recover by about a year (Figure 53-5, the Magaziner eight-domain study). Most patients plateau by six months. Depressive symptoms and cognitive limitation are common and often resolve with little intervention within two months, but anyone who reports depressive symptoms even transiently recovers less well, and mild depression is worth treating.

  • At one year, of those who managed alone before the fracture, 20% need help putting on trousers, 40% to cross a room, 66% to use the toilet, 90% to climb five stairs. Housework, getting out of walking distance and shopping: 62%, 53% and 42% newly dependent
  • Up to half of previously independent patients need a cane or walker at one year; fear of falling then limits activity further. A fall injury makes admission to a nursing facility ten times more likely, and the over-85s have longer rehabilitation, worse lower-limb recovery, more long-term care and more persistent pain
  • Slower-than-expected recovery has a checklist: persistent delirium, depression, polypharmacy, vitamin D and other nutritional deficits, social isolation

Rehabilitation eligibility, and after

Services are offered when two conditions hold: a functional loss, and the ability to participate. Severe cognitive impairment, unresolved delirium, severe pre-fracture disability such as being bed-bound, and terminal illness may exclude standard rehabilitation. Acute inpatient rehabilitation demands 3 hours a day and at least two disciplines; subacute care is for those who cannot manage that. Continued exercise after discharge improves function through the first year, progressive-resistance training most of all. Reassess at discharge from rehabilitation and again at the end of home physiotherapy. Hip protectors offer little or no benefit in randomised studies and are not a substitute for falls and bone work. The Israeli framework for who is admitted where is in 55 Rehabilitation.

Do not leave without the bone plan. The chapter is explicit that both women and men need pharmacological prevention of the second fracture, and that vitamin D deficiency is the rule. A hip fracture is the indication to treat, whatever the DXA shows, and the multidisciplinary falls assessment — home, medications, vision, postural blood pressure, gait and balance — goes with it. See 51 Osteoporosis and 43 Falls.

Hazzard ch 62 p953 — with the post-stroke numbers from ch 55 p817

The acute chapter behind 55 Rehabilitation, and the one that decides how much there is to rehabilitate. Fifth leading cause of death, first cause of disability; incidence rises with age and a growing share of strokes occur at 85 and over. Prognosis is worse in the old, yet the mortality decline of the last decades reaches every age group including the over-85s — because the treatments below are given to them.

TIA and minor stroke: the definitions and the score

  • A TIA is focal symptoms resolving within 24 hours with no lesion on diffusion MRI. If DWI is positive it is a stroke, however brief the symptoms — a minor stroke. The distinction does not change the workup; both demand urgent, complete investigation
  • Recurrence after TIA or minor stroke is about 10% in 90 days, highest in the first 48 hours, and as high as 10% in the first week depending on mechanism
  • ABCD2: Age over 60 (1) · Blood pressure over 140/90 (1) · Clinical — speech alone (1), unilateral weakness (2) · Duration — under 10 min (0), 10–59 min (1), 60 min or more (2) · Diabetes (1). A score of 4 or more is elevated risk, and is the entry criterion the DAPT trials used

Acute treatment: the windows and the thresholds ch 62 actually gives

Exam pearl

Age is not a contraindication to thrombolysis or thrombectomy. Pre-stroke function is the ground you stand on when you decline, and the chapter backs you: benefit outweighs risk in older adults, thrombectomy works in octogenarians.

DecisionThreshold or windowWhere it comes from
IV thrombolysis, alteplase 0.9 mg/kg, 10% bolusWithin 4.5 h of onset. NINDS (3 h): 12% absolute gain in good outcome against 6% symptomatic haemorrhage. ECASS III (3–4.5 h): 7.2% absolute gain, sICH 2.4% vs 0.3%, no mortality difference — but it excluded the over-80s and severe strokesNINDS data show the older adult's higher haemorrhage risk does not outweigh benefit. Tenecteplase is arriving as a single-bolus alternative
Thrombolysis when symptoms are nondisablingNot given. PRISMS found no benefit of alteplase over aspirin; guidelines recommend against IVT for deficits that would not interfere with daily lifeThe chapter's operative test is “disabling”, judged clinically — not a number
Unknown onset or wake-up strokeDWI–FLAIR mismatch on MRI (WAKE-UP: 53.3% vs 41.8% excellent outcome, median NIHSS 6), or CT/MR perfusion core–penumbra mismatch out to 9 h (EXTEND)Tissue-based selection replacing clock-based
Mechanical thrombectomyLarge-vessel occlusion — intracranial ICA or M1 — to 6 h routinely; 6–24 h (DAWN: 49% vs 13% independent) and 6–16 h (DEFUSE 3: 41% vs 15%) with a salvageable penumbra on perfusion imagingLevel Ia evidence; effective at all adult ages including octogenarians; the largest effect size in the chapter
ASPECTS on the first CTTen MCA regions, one point lost per region affected. Below 6 predicts a worse outcome and is the usual cut-off for intervention — explicitly not a strict rulePlus CTA of head and neck in every acute stroke, for the LVO and the collaterals

There is no NIHSS threshold in ch 62 — the scale appears once, as the median of a trial. Cut-offs such as “5 or under is minor” are conventions from the trials themselves, not from the textbook; the chapter's thresholds are ASPECTS under 6, ABCD2 of 4 or more, and disabling versus nondisabling. Stroke-unit care improves outcomes over a general ward; avoid hyperthermia; heparin or pneumatic compression until walking.

What causes it here

MechanismGeriatric note
Cardioembolic — atrial fibrillationThree- to fivefold stroke risk; prevalence rises 5% a year after 65, and AF accounts for up to 40% of ischaemic strokes in the oldest old. In an older patient with no lacunar or large-vessel pattern, prolonged rhythm monitoring is mandatory, and reasonable even when another cause is apparent
Small-vessel / lacunarHypertension and diabetes. Antiplatelet early, let the blood pressure autoregulate acutely. Long-term DAPT and anticoagulation are not recommended — SPS3 found aspirin plus clopidogrel no better and more lethal
Large-artery — carotidEndarterectomy or stenting for symptomatic stenosis over 70%. Within two weeks when the infarct is small; deferred after a large infarct for the reperfusion-injury risk. Asymptomatic stenosis: benefit not established against modern medical therapy; case by case
Intracranial atherosclerosisSAMMPRIS: stenting was worse than intensive medical therapy. What survived is the medical arm — aspirin 325 mg plus clopidogrel 75 mg for 90 days, high-intensity statin to LDL under 70, tight blood pressure
Intracerebral haemorrhageBlood-pressure lowering, anticoagulant reversal, neurosurgical opinion. Cerebral amyloid angiopathy is the cause of recurrent lobar haemorrhage in the old, and a reason to think hard before anticoagulating

Secondary antiplatelet therapy: how long, and the two trials

Exam pearl

Aspirin plus clopidogrel for 21 days, started within 24 hours, after a high-risk TIA or minor stroke that did not get thrombolysis. The number is 21 because CHANCE stopped there and POINT paid in bleeding for going to 90.

  • Aspirin 50–325 mg/day as soon as possible; most of its benefit is in the first days. Clopidogrel is an equal first-line alternative (CAPRIE: no difference in the stroke subgroup); ticagrelor was not superior to aspirin at 90 days (SOCRATES). Antiplatelet monotherapy remains the cornerstone for non-cardioembolic stroke
  • CHANCE (China, 5,170 patients): aspirin plus clopidogrel for 3 weeks then aspirin alone, started within 24 hours of a high-risk TIA or minor stroke. Recurrent stroke 8.2% vs 11.7% — a 32% relative reduction — without a significant rise in bleeding
  • POINT (4,881 patients, North America, Europe, Australasia): the same combination for 90 days. Ischaemic stroke, MI or vascular death 5.0% vs 6.5%, but major haemorrhage 0.9% vs 0.4% — attributed to the higher clopidogrel loading dose and the longer course. The benefit was concentrated in the first 30 days; the bleeding accrued after the first week
  • Hence the American Heart Association / American Stroke Association recommendation: DAPT with aspirin and clopidogrel, started within 24 hours, for 21 days, after high-risk TIA or minor stroke, provided the patient did not receive thrombolysis. THALES reproduced the benefit with ticagrelor for 30 days but at the cost of more major, fatal and intracranial haemorrhage
  • Atrial fibrillation: warfarin (INR 2–3) cuts recurrent embolism by close to 70% against aspirin; DOACs are non-inferior with significantly less intracranial haemorrhage and more gastrointestinal bleeding, net benefit in their favour, no monitoring. Not in infective endocarditis. Heart failure in sinus rhythm gets no anticoagulation beyond the acute phase (WARCEF)
  • Blood pressure remains the most effective single measure, lowered after the acute phase; a statin unless life expectancy makes it pointless

Post-stroke depression and the other late complications

Ch 62 lists the late complications as spasticity, contracture, pressure ulcers, shoulder dislocation and depression, and gives the numbers over to ch 55: depression in 15–70% depending on the study, with a significant negative effect on rehabilitation and a response to several antidepressants; bladder incontinence in 50–70% in the first month, returning to population levels by six months with timed voiding and residual monitoring; hemiplegic shoulder pain in 34–84%, managed by positioning, early range of motion, and electrical stimulation with benefit up to six months. Two prescribing points the exam can build on: fluoxetine does not improve functional recovery — the early signal was not reproduced in three trials, and it increased fractures, so it is for mood only; and for central post-stroke pain nortriptyline is preferred over amitriptyline in older adults. Botulinum toxin helps spasticity. Fatigue, sleep-disordered breathing and anxiety are to be sought, not waited for.

The rehabilitation handoff

Every patient with stroke-related disability is assessed by physiotherapy, occupational therapy and speech therapy as appropriate, and a substantial number benefit from inpatient rehabilitation; patients treated in dedicated stroke units by experienced physician, nursing and rehabilitation staff do better than on a general ward. Recovery takes six months to a year or longer, paced by neuroplasticity. Screen the swallow before anything by mouth (31 Disorders of Swallowing). Almost half of stroke deaths in older adults occur in hospital or rehabilitation facilities, so goals of care — which recovery matters to this patient: walking, communicating — are set early and primary palliative care runs alongside. The Israeli admission criteria, the FIM, the Copenhagen recovery numbers and the EBRSR handbook are in 55 Rehabilitation; vascular cognitive impairment is graded by the VasCog-2-WSO criteria in 59 Dementia.

Hazzard ch 102, p1629 — four pooled questions, present in three of four sittings, and Table 102-3 is cited three times, which puts it level with the frailty and continence tables at the top of the cited list. This was the tier-2 chapter with the thinnest coverage in this file.

The differential, split the way the chapter splits it

Mechanical / non-systemicSystemic
Lumbar strain; spondylosis of discs and facet joints; spinal stenosis; spondylolisthesis and spondylolysis; herniated disc; sciatica and piriformis syndrome; osteoporotic vertebral or sacral compression fracture; DISH; kyphosis and scoliosis; and referred pain from hip osteoarthritis Malignancy — myeloma, metastasis, lymphoma, cord or retroperitoneal tumour; infection — osteomyelitis, septic discitis, paraspinal abscess, septic emboli from endocarditis; inflammatory arthritis; Paget disease; visceral — aortic aneurysm, pyelonephritis or perinephric abscess, nephrolithiasis, pancreatitis, cholecystitis, penetrating ulcer, prostatitis

Referred hip osteoarthritis and a leaking aortic aneurysm are on the same page for a reason: the commonest miss and the one that kills. Non-specific low back pain is a diagnosis made after working through this list, not before.

Red flags, and when to image

Exam pearl

Leg pain relieved by leaning forward on a trolley is spinal stenosis, and the posture is worth more than the MRI report. Degeneration on a film in this age group tells you nothing.

The chapter uses the American College of Radiology criteria to decide who gets imaged. Each of these marks a higher probability of systemic disease:

  • Age over 70 — which is most of your clinic, and is why the threshold to image is genuinely lower here than in a younger patient
  • Recent significant trauma, or milder trauma over the age of 50
  • Unexplained weight loss or fever
  • Immunosuppression, including diabetes
  • History of cancer
  • Osteoporosis, or prolonged glucocorticoid use
  • Focal neurological deficit that is progressive or disabling
  • Symptoms lasting six weeks or more
  • Intravenous drug use

And the counterweight. Degenerative change is close to universal — ch 102 puts back-pain prevalence at 27–86% by population, and in an Israeli study 44% of 70-year-olds and 58% of 77-year-olds reported it; the 89%/57% disc-degeneration figure is classic epidemiology, not in the chapter — and imaging findings correlate poorly with pain. Ch 102 says plainly that anatomic abnormalities are often demonstrated regardless of symptoms and that imaging is for red flags. A radiograph reporting spondylosis has told you almost nothing. What a plain film is genuinely good for in an older patient is the thing a younger patient would not have: a compression fracture, DISH, or spondylolisthesis. Get static and dynamic views if instability is the question.

Cauda equina — saddle anaesthesia, urinary retention with overflow, bilateral sciatica, new incontinence, progressive weakness — is an emergency and does not wait for a clinic MRI.

Vertebral compression fracture

  • Severe mechanical pain when the fracture is lower thoracic or lumbar
  • High and mid-thoracic fractures are often asymptomatic and found incidentally — which is why two-thirds of them are never diagnosed at the time
  • The pain typically resolves over four to six weeks. Pain that does not is a reason to look again, not to escalate the analgesia
  • It sharply raises the risk of the next fracture — the “imminent risk” window. It is the indication to treat osteoporosis. See 51 Osteoporosis
  • Vertebroplasty and kyphoplasty did not beat sham in the better trials and are not routine

Lumbar spinal stenosis — the table that gets cited

The whole clinical picture follows one mechanical fact. Flexion opens the canal: the disc bulges less, the ligamentum flavum stretches thin, the cross-sectional area available to the roots increases. Extension closes it: the disc bulges in, the ligamentum flavum buckles and folds into the canal, the roots thicken. Everything else is a consequence.

Worse with extensionBetter with flexion
Prolonged standing · walking · walking downhill · lying prone · extending the back Sitting · bending forward · leaning on a walker or a shopping trolley · lying curled · walking uphill or on a bicycle
  • The presenting complaint is usually leg pain, not back pain: heaviness, numbness, cramping or burning, usually both legs though often worse on one
  • Neurogenic claudication, also called pseudoclaudication, and often an incomplete sciatica rather than a dermatomal one
  • True weakness is uncommon; examination is frequently normal at rest, which is a trap — examine after walking if you can
Neurogenic claudicationVascular claudication
Relieved bySitting or bending forward — postureStanding still — rest
Uphill / cyclingBetter, because the spine flexesWorse, because demand rises
OnsetVariable distance; worse first thing on standingReproducible claudication distance
Pulses and skinNormalAbsent pulses, hair loss, cool foot

Both coexist often enough that finding one does not excuse you from looking for the other — and a third possibility, hip osteoarthritis, refers into the groin and thigh and is worse on weight-bearing regardless of posture.

Management

  • Conservative first for stenosis without progressive deficit: exercise with a flexion bias, physiotherapy, weight reduction, and activity modification. Many patients are stable or improve over years
  • Analgesia is the geriatric problem. NSAIDs collide with renal function, heart failure, anticoagulation and the GI tract; opioids are not first-line for chronic musculoskeletal pain and STOPP names them; paracetamol is modest; a gabapentinoid for the neuropathic component buys sedation and falls. Say so rather than reaching for the next drug
  • Epidural steroid injection gives short-term relief at best for stenosis and does not change the course
  • Surgery — decompression, with fusion only where there is instability — for disabling symptoms after conservative treatment, and urgently for cauda equina or a progressive deficit. Age alone is not the contraindication; frailty and the ability to rehabilitate afterwards are what decide it
